C++ Interview Handbook

Then a full DSA part, pattern by pattern, each with tested C++ templates and a must-do problem list, followed by output puzzles, must-do programs, practice sets, where to practise and a 21-day plan.

How to use this handbook

  • First pass: read in order. Sections build on each other, from compilation and types up to templates, the STL, modern C++ and threads; then the DSA part (28–40) goes pattern by pattern, and the practice part (41–45) drills everything.
  • Every section has the same shape: notes → code → callouts → interview questions.
  • Revise actively. Turn on Quiz mode in the contents panel: every answer folds, so you answer aloud first and open only to check.
  • Track progress. Tick Mark as revised under a section title when you can answer all of its questions. Progress is remembered in this browser.
  • Search with the box at the top (press /): it finds topics, questions and puzzles.
Label Meaning
C++17 The standard in which a feature appeared
verified run Compiled with g++ 13.3 and executed; the output shown is the real output
compiles Compiled but not run (it only declares things, waits forever, or prints addresses)
compile error Rejected by the compiler on purpose; the real error message is shown
reference C++23/26 code that needs a newer compiler than g++ 13; shown so you know the syntax
Pitfall box A trap that loses marks or causes bugs

NoteHow the code samples run

A snippet without its own main runs inside int main() { … } with #include <bits/stdc++.h> and using namespace std; in front of it. In a snippet that contains the comment // in main:, the classes and functions above that line are declared at file scope and the lines below it run inside main. Everything was built with -std=c++20 on 64-bit Linux, with AddressSanitizer and UBSan switched on, so no example here hides a memory bug. Sizes such as sizeof(long) are the 64-bit Linux values.

Service-based companies (mass hiring) Product-based companies C++-heavy roles (systems, embedded, games, trading)
Online test Aptitude, C/C++ MCQs and output questions, one or two coding problems Two or three DSA problems (LeetCode medium, sometimes hard) DSA plus C++ MCQs on pointers, UB, templates and the object model
Technical interview OOP with real-life examples, pointers vs references, constructors and destructors, virtual functions, string/array programs, your project DSA in C++, STL internals, smart pointers, move semantics, OS basics, low-level design Memory layout, vtables, move semantics, templates, atomics and memory order, cache behaviour, UB

Every interviewer will ask you to explain your own project in depth. Prepare it with the template at the end of section 45.

Ways through this page

  • Three weeks — follow the 21-day plan in section 45: one C++ section and one DSA pattern every day.
  • One week — the 7-day crash plan in section 45, quiz mode only.
  • The night before — the Remember boxes, the cheat sheet in section 45, and the puzzles you got wrong.
  • Coding round tomorrow — the pattern table in section 28, the C++ toolkit in 29, and the must-do lists at the end of sections 30–40. Tick problems as you solve them; the counter at the top of section 28 tracks your progress.
  • You also know Java — the C++ vs Java table in section 01 and the ownership sections (09, 10, 14) are where the two languages differ most.

How to answer a C++ question

  1. Define it in one sentence. "A virtual function is a member function whose call is resolved at run time from the object's dynamic type."
  2. Say why it exists. Which problem does it solve?
  3. Show a tiny example. Write five lines on the whiteboard or say them.
  4. Mention the cost and the trap. One extra pointer per object, an indirect call, the base-class destructor that must be virtual.
  5. Tie it to real code. Where you used it in a project, or where the STL uses it.

Interviewers in C++ listen for three words in particular: ownership (who deletes this?), complexity (what does this cost?) and undefined behaviour (is this even legal?). Use them when they apply.

Compilation, the Toolchain & First Program

What C++ is, how source becomes an executable, the anatomy of a first program, input/output, namespaces, and how C++ differs from C and Java.

What C++ is

  • A compiled, statically typed, multi-paradigm language: procedural, object-oriented, generic (templates) and functional (lambdas) styles all work.
  • Created by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs, starting in 1979 as "C with Classes"; renamed C++ in 1983.
  • Compiles to native machine code — no virtual machine, no garbage collector. You decide where every object lives and when it dies.
  • Design rule: the zero-overhead principle — you don't pay for what you don't use, and what you do use is as fast as hand-written code.
  • Standardized by ISO committee WG21 on a three-year cycle.
Standard Year Headline features
C++98 / C++03 1998 / 2003 Classes, templates, exceptions, the STL; C++03 was a bug-fix release
C++11 2011 auto, range-for, lambdas, move semantics, nullptr, smart pointers, constexpr, std::thread, unordered_map — "modern C++" starts here
C++14 2014 Generic lambdas, make_unique, relaxed constexpr
C++17 2017 Structured bindings, if with initializer, optional/variant/any, string_view, filesystem, fold expressions, CTAD, guaranteed copy elision
C++20 2020 Concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules, <=>, span, format, jthread
C++23 2023 std::print, std::expected, mdspan, deducing this, ranges::to, flat_map
C++26 finished 2026 Static reflection, contracts, std::execution, a hardened standard library, no UB for reading uninitialized locals
RememberWhich standard to say you use

Write interview and DSA code in C++17 or C++20 (-std=c++17 / -std=c++20). Online judges such as LeetCode, Codeforces and CodeChef compile with g++ or clang in C++17/20/23 mode, so everything in this handbook works there.

Your first program

C++verified run
#include <iostream>      // declares std::cout, std::cin

int main() {             // execution starts here; must return int
    std::cout << "Hello, C++!" << '\n';
    int a = 7, b = 5;
    std::cout << a << " + " << b << " = " << a + b << '\n';
    return 0;            // 0 = success; may be omitted in main only
}
Output
Hello, C++!
7 + 5 = 12
  • #include <iostream> is a preprocessor directive: the contents of the header are pasted in before compilation.
  • int main() is the entry point. Valid forms: int main() and int main(int argc, char* argv[]). void main() is not standard C++.
  • std::cout is an object of type std::ostream; << is an overloaded operator that returns the stream, which is why calls chain.
  • std:: is the namespace of the standard library.
  • Reaching the end of main without return behaves like return 0; — this exception exists only for main.

From source to executable

Shell
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 hello.cpp -o hello   # all four stages in one go
./hello

g++ -E hello.cpp -o hello.i    # 1. preprocess only
g++ -S hello.i  -o hello.s     # 2. compile to assembly
g++ -c hello.s  -o hello.o     # 3. assemble to an object file
g++ hello.o     -o hello       # 4. link into an executable
  • A translation unit is one .cpp file after preprocessing. Each is compiled separately into an object file.
  • Compile errors come from one translation unit: syntax, types, overload resolution, templates.
  • Linker errors come from combining them: undefined reference to 'foo()' (declared but never defined, or the file wasn't linked), multiple definition of 'x' (defined in two files).

Declarations vs definitions

C++compiles
extern int counter;          // declaration: "an int called counter exists somewhere"
int square(int x);           // declaration (prototype)
struct Point;                // declaration (incomplete type)

int counter = 0;             // definition: storage is allocated here
int square(int x) {          // definition: the body
    return x * x;
}
struct Point { int x, y; };  // definition
  • A declaration introduces a name and its type; a definition also creates the thing (allocates storage, provides the body).
  • Every definition is also a declaration. You may declare a name many times but define it only once in the program — the One Definition Rule (section 25).
  • Headers (.h/.hpp) normally hold declarations, class definitions, templates and inline functions; .cpp files hold function and variable definitions.

Useful g++ flags

Flag Effect
-std=c++20 Pick the language standard (c++17, c++20, c++23)
-Wall -Wextra Turn on the important warnings — always use them
-O0 / -O2 / -O3 No optimization (debugging) / standard release / aggressive
-g Add debug info for gdb
-fsanitize=address,undefined Catch out-of-bounds, use-after-free and UB at run time
-o name Name the output file (default a.out)
-c Compile to an object file without linking
-I dir / -L dir / -lname Add an include directory / a library directory / link libname
-DDEBUG Define a macro, like #define DEBUG at the top of every file

Input and output

Object Stream Buffered
std::cin Standard input Yes
std::cout Standard output Yes
std::cerr Standard error No — appears immediately
std::clog Standard error Yes
C++verified run
int n;
cin >> n;                       // >> skips leading whitespace
vector<int> v(n);
for (int& x : v) cin >> x;
cin.ignore();                   // drop the '\n' left after the last number
string name;
getline(cin, name);             // reads a whole line, spaces included
cout << "sum = " << accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) << '\n';
cout << "name = " << name << '\n';
Output (input: 3 ⏎ 10 20 30 ⏎ Ada Lovelace)
sum = 60
name = Ada Lovelace
Pitfallgetline after cin >> reads an empty line

cin >> n stops at the newline and leaves it in the buffer, so the next getline returns immediately with an empty string. Call cin.ignore() (or cin >> ws) before switching from >> to getline.

endl vs '\n' — both end the line, but std::endl also flushes the buffer. Flushing after every line is slow when you print a lot, so write '\n' and flush only when you must (before a crash-prone step, or in interactive problems).

Fast I/O for competitive programming and big inputs:

C++compiles
ios::sync_with_stdio(false); // stop syncing C++ streams with C stdio
cin.tie(nullptr);            // don't flush cout before every cin

After sync_with_stdio(false), don't mix printf/scanf with cout/cin in the same program.

Namespaces

A namespace groups names to avoid collisions: std::sort and your own sort can coexist.

C++verified run
namespace geometry {
    const double PI = 3.14159;
    double area(double r) { return PI * r * r; }
    namespace units { const char* name = "cm"; }   // nested
}
namespace geo = geometry;                          // alias
// in main:
cout << geometry::area(2.0) << '\n';
cout << geo::units::name << '\n';
using geometry::PI;                                // brings in one name
cout << PI << '\n';
Output
12.5664
cm
3.14159
PitfallNever write using namespace std; in a header

A using-directive in a header leaks every std name into every file that includes it, causing silent overload changes and clashes (your count, distance or size against std::count, std::distance, std::size). In a .cpp file or a contest solution it's a matter of taste; in a header it's a bug waiting to happen.

C vs C++

C C++
Procedural only Procedural, object-oriented, generic, functional
struct holds data only struct/class hold data and functions, with access control
malloc/free new/delete (call constructors/destructors), smart pointers
No function overloading (one name, one function) Overloading and default arguments
Pointers only Pointers and references
Error codes Exceptions
Macros for generic code Templates
printf/scanf iostream (type-safe), plus the C functions
No namespaces Namespaces
Small standard library The STL: containers, algorithms, strings, threads

C++ vs Java

C++ Java
Runs as Native machine code Bytecode on the JVM (JIT-compiled)
Memory Manual / RAII / smart pointers; no garbage collector Garbage collected
Objects Can live on the stack or the heap Always on the heap (references on the stack)
Pointers Raw pointers, pointer arithmetic, references References only; no arithmetic
Inheritance Multiple inheritance of classes Single class inheritance, multiple interfaces
Polymorphism Opt-in with virtual Every non-static, non-private, non-final method is virtual
Generics Templates: code generated per type, at compile time Type erasure: one class, checks at compile time
Operator overloading Yes No (except + on String)
Destructors Deterministic — run at scope exit No destructors; try-with-resources / cleaners
Default parameters Yes No (use overloads)
Header files Yes (declarations separate from definitions) No
Platform Recompile per platform Write once, run anywhere
Undefined behaviour Exists (out-of-bounds, overflow, dangling) Exceptions instead (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
How to say itIs C++ a pure object-oriented language?

"No. C++ is multi-paradigm. You can write free functions outside any class, main itself is a free function, the built-in types like int aren't objects with methods, and you can use procedural and generic styles without any classes. It supports all the OOP features — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism — but doesn't force them."

Interview questions

QWhat happens when you compile and run a C++ program?

The preprocessor expands #includes and macros into a translation unit; the compiler parses and type-checks it and generates assembly; the assembler turns that into an object file with a symbol table; the linker combines all object files and libraries into an executable, resolving each function and variable reference to one definition. At run time the OS loader maps the executable into memory, static objects are constructed, then main runs; after main returns, static objects are destroyed in reverse order.

QWhat is the difference between a compile error and a linker error?

A compile error is found inside one translation unit — bad syntax, a type mismatch, no matching overload. A linker error is found when combining translation units — a function declared and called but never defined (undefined reference), or the same non-inline function or global defined in two files (multiple definition).

QDeclaration vs definition?

A declaration tells the compiler a name exists and what type it has (int f(int);, extern int x;). A definition also creates it — allocates storage or provides the body (int f(int a) { return a; }, int x = 0;). A name can be declared many times but defined once (the One Definition Rule).

QWhat is the zero-overhead principle?

"What you don't use, you don't pay for; what you do use, you couldn't hand-code any better." For example, a class without virtual functions has no vtable pointer, and std::array is exactly as fast as a C array.

QWhy is using namespace std; considered bad practice?

It pulls hundreds of names into the global namespace, which can clash with your names or silently pick a different overload. In a header it affects every file that includes it. Prefer std:: qualification or targeted using std::cout;.

Qendl vs '\n'?

Both write a newline; std::endl also flushes the stream. Flushing is a system call's worth of work, so printing many lines with endl can be several times slower. Use '\n' by default.

QWhat do ios::sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) do?

The first stops C++ streams from synchronizing with C's stdio buffers, so cin/cout get their own fast buffering. The second unties cin from cout, so cout isn't flushed before every input operation. Together they make stream I/O about as fast as scanf/printf. Don't mix the two styles afterwards.

QWhat is the difference between #include <file> and #include "file"?

Angle brackets search only the system/compiler include paths (and -I directories); quotes search the current file's directory first, then the same paths as angle brackets. Use <> for the standard library and third-party headers, "" for your own project headers.

QWhat are the valid signatures of main?

int main() and int main(int argc, char* argv[]) (or char** argv). argc is the argument count including the program name; argv[0] is the program name and argv[argc] is a null pointer. It must return int; falling off the end returns 0.

QGive the main differences between C and C++.

C++ adds classes with access control, constructors and destructors, inheritance and virtual functions, function and operator overloading, references, templates, exceptions, namespaces, new/delete, and the STL. C is procedural only. Most C code compiles as C++, but not all (e.g. implicit void* conversion from malloc is an error in C++).

QGive the main differences between C++ and Java.

C++ compiles to native code and has no garbage collector — objects can be on the stack, destructors run deterministically, and memory is managed with RAII and smart pointers. It has pointers with arithmetic, multiple inheritance, operator overloading, templates (code generated per type) and opt-in virtual. Java runs on the JVM, garbage-collects, has only references, single class inheritance and generics by type erasure, and every instance method is virtual by default.

QWhat is undefined behaviour?

Code the standard puts no requirements on: out-of-bounds access, using a dangling pointer, signed integer overflow, reading an uninitialized variable, data races. The program may crash, print garbage or seem to work — and the optimizer may assume UB never happens, so it can delete whole checks. Section 13 lists the common cases.

QWhat is a translation unit?

One source file after preprocessing: the .cpp with all its #included headers pasted in and macros expanded. The compiler compiles each translation unit independently into an object file.

Qcerr vs clog vs cout?

cout writes to standard output and is buffered. cerr writes to standard error, is unbuffered, and is tied to cout (pending cout output is flushed first), so error messages appear immediately even if the program crashes next. clog also writes to standard error but is buffered, for logging.

Data Types, Variables & Operators

Sizes and ranges, literals, the many ways to initialize, auto, enums, integer promotion and the signed/unsigned traps, overflow, floating point, and the operators you'll be quizzed on.

Fundamental types

Type Size on 64-bit Linux Range / notes
bool 1 true / false
char 1 Always 1 byte by definition; signed on x86, unsigned on ARM
short 2 −32,768 … 32,767
int 4 −2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,647 (about ±2.1 × 10⁹)
long 8 8 on Linux/macOS, but 4 on Windows
long long 8 About ±9.2 × 10¹⁸
unsigned int 4 0 … 4,294,967,295
float 4 About 7 significant digits
double 8 About 15–16 significant digits
long double 16 80-bit extended precision on x86
wchar_t / char16_t / char32_t 4 / 2 / 4 Wide and Unicode characters
any pointer 8 Address size
size_t 8 Unsigned; the type of sizeof and of .size()

The standard only guarantees minimums and ordering: char ≥ 8 bits, short and int ≥ 16, long ≥ 32, long long ≥ 64, and 1 == sizeof(char) ≤ sizeof(short) ≤ sizeof(int) ≤ sizeof(long) ≤ sizeof(long long). When the exact width matters, use <cstdint>: int8_t, int32_t, int64_t, uint64_t.

C++verified run
cout << sizeof(int) << ' ' << sizeof(long) << ' ' << sizeof(long long) << ' '
     << sizeof(double) << ' ' << sizeof(void*) << '\n';
cout << numeric_limits<int>::max() << '\n';
cout << numeric_limits<int>::min() << '\n';
cout << numeric_limits<long long>::max() << '\n';
cout << numeric_limits<unsigned>::max() << '\n';
cout << numeric_limits<double>::epsilon() << '\n';
cout << INT_MAX + 1LL << '\n';     // promoted to long long first: no overflow
Output
4 8 8 8 8
2147483647
-2147483648

Literals

C++verified run
auto a = 42;          // int
auto b = 42u;         // unsigned int
auto c = 42LL;        // long long
auto d = 0x2A;        // hexadecimal 42
auto e = 052;         // octal 42 — a leading 0 means octal!
auto f = 0b101010;    // binary 42 (C++14)
auto g = 1'000'000;   // digit separators (C++14)
auto h = 3.14f;       // float; 3.14 alone is a double
auto s = R"(C:\new\table)";   // raw string: no escapes
cout << a << ' ' << b << ' ' << c << ' ' << d << ' ' << e << ' ' << f << ' ' << g << '\n';
cout << h << ' ' << s << '\n';
Output
42 42 42 42 42 42 1000000
3.14 C:\new\table

Initialization: five spellings

C++verified run
int a = 5;      // copy-initialization
int b(5);       // direct-initialization
int c{5};       // list (brace) initialization — C++11, the "uniform" syntax
int d = {5};    // copy-list-initialization
int e{};        // value-initialization: zero
vector<int> v1(3, 7);   // three 7s  (parentheses: the size+value constructor)
vector<int> v2{3, 7};   // two elements 3 and 7  (braces prefer initializer_list)
cout << a << b << c << d << e << ' ' << v1.size() << ' ' << v2.size() << '\n';
Output
55550 3 2

Braces forbid narrowing conversions — which is the main reason to prefer them:

C++compile error
double price = 9.99;
int a = price;      // compiles: silently truncates to 9
int b{9.99};        // error: narrowing conversion from double to int
g++ says
error: narrowing conversion of '9.9900000000000002e+0' from 'double' to 'int' [-Wnarrowing]

g++ reports narrowing from a variable (int c{price};) only as a warning while clang rejects it; the standard says it's ill-formed either way, so treat the warning as an error.

PitfallUninitialized local variables

int x; inside a function holds an indeterminate value, and reading it is undefined behaviour (C++26 downgrades it to "erroneous behaviour", which still isn't something to rely on). Globals, static variables and namespace-scope variables are zero-initialized before anything else runs. Always initialize: int x = 0; or int x{};.

auto and decltype

C++verified run
int x = 10;
const int ci = x;
int& ref = x;
auto a = ci;          // int        — top-level const dropped
auto& b = ci;         // const int& — const kept when you take a reference
auto c = ref;         // int        — references dropped too
decltype(ci) d = 5;   // const int  — decltype keeps the declared type exactly
decltype((d)) e = d;  // const int& — (parenthesized) lvalue gives a reference
cout << is_same_v<decltype(a), int> << is_same_v<decltype(b), const int&>
     << is_same_v<decltype(c), int> << is_same_v<decltype(d), const int>
     << is_same_v<decltype(e), const int&> << '\n';
Output
11111
  • auto deduces like a template parameter: it drops references and top-level const. Write const auto& to avoid copies in loops over containers: for (const auto& s : names).
  • decltype(name) gives the declared type; decltype((expr)) gives a reference for lvalues.
  • Use auto when the type is obvious or unspeakable (iterators, lambdas); spell the type out when it documents intent.

Enumerations

C++verified run
enum Color { Red, Green, Blue };              // unscoped: names leak, converts to int
enum class Level : uint8_t { Low = 1, High = 5 };   // scoped, chosen underlying type
// in main:
Color c = Green;
int n = c;                                   // implicit conversion: allowed
Level l = Level::High;
int m = static_cast<int>(l);                 // enum class needs an explicit cast
cout << n << ' ' << m << ' ' << sizeof(Level) << '\n';
Output
1 5 1
enum enum class C++11
Names spill into the surrounding scope (Red) Names are scoped (Level::High)
Converts implicitly to int No implicit conversion; use static_cast
Two enums can't both have a None in one scope No clashes
Underlying type chosen by the compiler unless specified Defaults to int; can be specified

Group Operators Notes
Arithmetic + - * / % / on integers truncates toward zero; % takes the sign of the left operand

Bitwise & | ^ ~ << >> >> on negative signed values is arithmetic since C++20

cout << 7 / 2 << ' ' << -7 / 2 << ' ' << 7 % 3 << ' ' << -7 % 3 << ' ' << 7 % -3 << '\n';
cout << 7.0 / 2 << '\n';

Promotions, conversions and the signed/unsigned trap

  • Integral promotion: bool, char, short (and their unsigned versions) become int in arithmetic. 'a' + 1 is an int (98).
  • Usual arithmetic conversions: when operands differ, the "smaller" is converted to the "larger" type: int → long → long long → float → double. If one operand is unsigned and has the same rank as the signed one, the signed operand becomes unsigned.
C++verified run
cout << ('a' + 1) << ' ' << char('a' + 1) << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << (-1 < 1u) << '\n';      // -1 becomes 4294967295u
vector<int> v;                               // empty
cout << v.size() - 1 << '\n';                // size_t wraps around: huge number
for (int k = 0; k + 1 < (int)v.size(); ++k) {} // safe way to write "size() - 1" loops
unsigned u = 0;
--u;                                         // unsigned arithmetic wraps: well defined
cout << u << '\n';
Output
98 b
false
18446744073709551615
4294967295
PitfallOverflow happens before the assignment

long long x = 100000 * 100000; is still computed in int and overflows (signed overflow is undefined behaviour) before the result is stored. Make one operand wide first: 100000LL * 100000, or 1LL * a * b. This bug fails more coding-round test cases than any other.

Signed integers Unsigned integers
Overflow Undefined behaviour — the optimizer may assume it never happens Well defined: wraps modulo 2ⁿ
Use for Counts, indices you subtract from, anything that can go negative Bit masks, hashing, sizes from the STL

Floating point

C++verified run
double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
cout << setprecision(17) << a << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << (a == 0.3) << '\n';
const double EPS = 1e-9;
cout << (fabs(a - 0.3) < EPS) << '\n';
cout << setprecision(6) << 1.0 / 0 << ' ' << sqrt(-1.0) << '\n';   // inf and nan (glibc prints -nan); no crash
Output
0.30000000000000004
false
true
inf -nan
  • Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly, so compare with a tolerance.
  • Floating-point division by zero gives inf or nan; integer division by zero is undefined behaviour (usually a crash).
  • Printing: cout << fixed << setprecision(2) << x; prints exactly two decimals.

Bit manipulation essentials

C++verified run
int x = 44;                                   // 101100
cout << (x & 1) << '\n';                      // 0 → even
cout << (x & (x - 1)) << '\n';                // 40: lowest set bit cleared
cout << (x & -x) << '\n';                     // 4: lowest set bit alone
cout << (x | (1 << 0)) << '\n';               // 45: set bit 0
cout << (x ^ (1 << 2)) << '\n';               // 40: toggle bit 2
cout << ((x >> 3) & 1) << '\n';               // 1: is bit 3 set?
cout << __builtin_popcount(x) << ' ' << __builtin_ctz(x) << ' ' << __builtin_clz(x) << '\n';
cout << bitset<8>(x) << '\n';
int a = 5, b = 9;
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;                       // swap without a temporary
cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n';
Output
0
40
4
45
40
1
3 2 26
00101100
9 5

__builtin_popcount (count set bits), __builtin_ctz (trailing zeros) and __builtin_clz (leading zeros) are GCC/Clang built-ins; use the ll versions (__builtin_popcountll) for 64-bit values. C++20 adds portable versions in <bit>: std::popcount, std::countr_zero, std::countl_zero, std::has_single_bit.

Interview questions

QWhat are the sizes of int, long and pointers?

On 64-bit Linux: int 4 bytes, long 8, long long 8, pointers 8. On 64-bit Windows long is 4. The standard only fixes minimums (int ≥ 16 bits, long ≥ 32, long long ≥ 64) and that sizeof(char) is 1, so use int32_t/int64_t when width matters.

QWhat happens on integer overflow?

For signed types it is undefined behaviour — the compiler assumes it can't happen and may optimize accordingly (e.g. x + 1 > x becomes true). Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2ⁿ. In practice, use long long or check before multiplying.

QWhy does -1 < 1u evaluate to false?

The usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed -1 into unsigned, giving 4294967295, which is greater than 1. Mixing signed and unsigned in comparisons is a classic bug, especially with .size(), which returns unsigned size_t.

QWhy is v.size() - 1 dangerous?

size() returns an unsigned size_t. For an empty vector, 0 - 1 wraps to 18446744073709551615, so a loop for (i = 0; i < v.size() - 1; ++i) runs (almost) forever and reads out of bounds. Cast to int first or write i + 1 < v.size().

QWhat's the difference between int x(5), int x = 5 and int x{5}?

For an int, all store 5. Braces are list-initialization: they reject narrowing conversions (int x{3.7} is an error) and work uniformly for aggregates and containers. With classes, braces prefer an initializer_list constructor, so vector<int>(3, 7) and vector<int>{3, 7} mean different things.

QWhat value does an uninitialized local int have?

An indeterminate one — reading it is undefined behaviour (erroneous behaviour from C++26). Globals and statics are zero-initialized. int x{}; value-initializes to zero.

Qenum vs enum class?

enum class (C++11) is scoped — you write Color::Red — and has no implicit conversion to int, so different enums can't be mixed up or compared with numbers accidentally. Plain enum names leak into the enclosing scope and convert to int. Both can specify an underlying type (: uint8_t).

Q++i vs i++?

++i increments and returns the variable itself (an lvalue). i++ saves a copy of the old value, increments, and returns the copy. For int the compiler generates the same code when the result isn't used, but for iterators and class types i++ makes an extra copy, so prefer ++i.

QWhat does sizeof(i++) do to i?

Nothing. sizeof doesn't evaluate its operand (except for variable-length arrays, which aren't standard C++); it only inspects its type at compile time.

QWhy is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3?

0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have no exact binary representation, so each is rounded; the rounding errors don't cancel. Compare floating-point numbers with fabs(a - b) < eps, with an epsilon suited to the magnitudes involved.

QWhat does auto deduce for const int&?

Plain int: auto drops references and top-level const, like template argument deduction. auto& would give const int&, and decltype(auto) keeps the exact type.

QWhat is size_t?

An unsigned integer type big enough to hold the size of any object — 8 bytes on 64-bit systems. It's the type of sizeof and of the size() of every standard container.

QHow do integer / and % behave with negative numbers?

Since C++11, division truncates toward zero, so -7 / 2 == -3, and % satisfies (a / b) * b + a % b == a, so -7 % 2 == -1 — the remainder takes the sign of the dividend. For a non-negative modulo write ((a % m) + m) % m.

QIs char signed or unsigned?

Implementation-defined. On x86 with g++ it's signed; on ARM it's unsigned. char, signed char and unsigned char are three distinct types. Use unsigned char (or std::byte) for raw bytes.

QHow do you check if a number is a power of two?

n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 — a power of two has exactly one set bit, and n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. In C++20, std::has_single_bit(n) for unsigned n.

03if · switch · loops · C arrays · std::array · vector12 questions

Control Flow & Arrays

Branches and loops including the C++17 forms, switch fall-through, C arrays and why they decay to pointers, multidimensional arrays, std::array, and vector as the default.

Branches

C++verified run
map<string, int> stock{{"pen", 4}, {"ink", 0}};
// if with initializer (C++17): `it` is scoped to the if/else
if (auto it = stock.find("pen"); it != stock.end() && it->second > 0)
    cout << "pen in stock: " << it->second << '\n';
else
    cout << "no pens\n";

int marks = 72;
string grade = marks >= 90 ? "A" : marks >= 75 ? "B" : marks >= 60 ? "C" : "F";
cout << grade << '\n';
Output
pen in stock: 4
C
  • Any scalar converts to bool in a condition: zero, null pointers and false are false; everything else is true.
  • if (x = 5) assigns and is always true — compile with -Wall and the compiler warns. Some people write if (5 == x) to make the typo a compile error.
  • if constexpr C++17 picks a branch at compile time inside templates (section 16).

switch

C++verified run
for (int day : {1, 6, 7, 9}) {
    switch (day) {
        case 6:
        case 7:
            cout << day << ": weekend\n";
            break;
        case 1: {
            string note = "start of week";   // needs braces to declare a variable
            cout << day << ": " << note << '\n';
            [[fallthrough]];                  // C++17: says "falling through is intended"
        }
        case 2: case 3: case 4: case 5:
            cout << day << ": weekday\n";
            break;
        default:
            cout << day << ": invalid\n";
    }
}
Output
1: start of week
1: weekday
6: weekend
7: weekend
9: invalid
  • The expression must be an integer, char or enum type; case labels must be compile-time constants. You can't switch on a std::string.
  • Without break, execution falls through to the next case.
  • A variable declared under one case is in scope for the rest of the switch, so jumping past its initialization is an error — wrap the case in braces.
  • Compilers turn dense switches into a jump table (O(1)), which is why switch can beat a chain of ifs.

Loops

C++verified run
for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) cout << i << ' ';          // classic for
cout << '\n';
int n = 3;
while (n--) cout << n << ' ';                          // test, then body
cout << '\n';
int k = 10;
do { cout << k << ' '; } while (k < 5);                // body runs at least once
cout << '\n';
vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};
for (int& x : v) x *= 10;                              // range-for by reference: modifies
for (const auto& x : v) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';
map<string, int> age{{"ann", 31}, {"bob", 27}};
for (const auto& [name, a] : age) cout << name << '=' << a << ' ';   // structured bindings
cout << '\n';
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) {
    if (i % 2) continue;                               // skip odd numbers
    if (i > 6) break;                                  // leave the loop
    cout << i << ' ';
}
cout << '\n';
Output
0 1 2 
2 1 0 
10 
10 20 30 
ann=31 bob=27 
0 2 4 6
PitfallDon't modify a container's size inside a range-for

for (auto x : v) v.push_back(x); can reallocate the vector while the loop's hidden iterators still point into the old buffer — undefined behaviour. Use an index loop, or collect changes and apply them after the loop.

C arrays

C++verified run
int a[5] = {1, 2};                  // remaining elements are zero
int b[] = {4, 5, 6};                // size deduced: 3
cout << a[1] << a[2] << ' ' << size(b) << ' ' << sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) << '\n';
int grid[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};       // row-major in memory
cout << grid[1][2] << ' ' << *(*(grid + 1) + 2) << ' ' << sizeof(grid) << '\n';
char word[] = "hi";                 // 3 chars: 'h', 'i', '\0'
cout << sizeof(word) << '\n';
Output
20 3 5
6 6 24
3
  • Fixed size known at compile time; elements are contiguous.
  • No bounds checking: a[10] on a 5-element array compiles and is undefined behaviour.
  • Arrays can't be assigned or copied with =, and can't be returned from functions.
  • int arr[n]; with a run-time n (a variable-length array) is a C99 feature that g++ accepts as an extension — it is not standard C++ and can overflow the stack. Use vector<int> arr(n);.

Array-to-pointer decay

When an array is passed to a function, it decays to a pointer to its first element, and its size is lost.

C++verified run
void show(int arr[]) {               // really: void show(int* arr)
    cout << "inside: " << sizeof(arr) << '\n';      // size of a pointer
}
template <size_t N>
void show_ref(int (&arr)[N]) {       // reference to array: the size survives
    cout << "by reference: " << N << '\n';
}
// in main:
int data[10] = {};
cout << "outside: " << sizeof(data) << '\n';
show(data);
show_ref(data);
Output
outside: 40
inside: 8
by reference: 10

So functions that take C arrays also take the length: void sum(const int* a, int n). For 2D arrays, every dimension except the first must be given: void f(int m[][3], int rows).

std::array and std::vector

C array std::array<T, N> C++11 std::vector<T>
Size Fixed, compile time Fixed, compile time Dynamic
Storage Stack (if local) Stack (if local) — no heap Heap
Knows its size Only in scope (std::size) .size() .size()
Copy with = No Yes Yes
Decays to pointer Yes No No
Bounds-checked access No .at(i) .at(i)
Works with STL algorithms Via pointers Yes Yes
C++verified run
array<int, 4> a{3, 1, 4, 1};
sort(a.begin(), a.end());
array<int, 4> b = a;                       // copies
cout << b[0] << b[3] << ' ' << b.size() << '\n';

int rows = 2, cols = 3;
vector<vector<int>> g(rows, vector<int>(cols, 0));   // 2x3 grid of zeros
g[1][2] = 9;
for (auto& row : g) {
    for (int x : row) cout << x << ' ';
    cout << '\n';
}
try {
    cout << b.at(7);
} catch (const out_of_range& e) {
    cout << "out_of_range caught\n";
}
Output
14 4
0 0 0 
0 0 9 
out_of_range caught
TipDefault to vector

Use std::vector for anything whose size is decided at run time, std::array for small fixed sizes, and C arrays only when an interviewer or an API demands them. vector is contiguous like an array, so it's just as cache-friendly.

Interview questions

QWhat is array decay?

When a C array is used in most expressions — including being passed to a function — it converts to a pointer to its first element. The array's size is lost, so sizeof(arr) inside the function gives the pointer size (8), not the array size. Exceptions: sizeof, &arr, and binding to a reference to array don't decay.

QHow do you find the length of a C array?

sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]), or std::size(a) in C++17 — but only where the array hasn't decayed (in the scope where it's declared, or via a reference-to-array template parameter).

QWhy can't you switch on a string?

switch needs an integral or enum value and constant case labels, because it may compile to a jump table indexed by the value. Strings aren't integral. Use if/else, a map<string, function<...>>, or switch on an enum produced by parsing the string.

QWhat is fall-through in a switch?

Without break, control continues into the next case body. It's sometimes intended (grouping cases); C++17's [[fallthrough]]; documents that and silences the warning.

Qwhile vs do-while?

while tests the condition before each iteration, so the body may run zero times. do-while tests after, so the body always runs at least once — useful for menus and input validation.

QWhat is the difference between a C array, std::array and std::vector?

A C array has a fixed compile-time size, decays to a pointer, can't be copied or returned, and has no bounds checking. std::array wraps a fixed-size array with no overhead but behaves like a value: it knows its size, copies, and works with algorithms. std::vector is a resizable heap array that manages its own memory.

QAre variable-length arrays allowed in C++?

No. int a[n] with a run-time n is a C99 feature; g++ supports it as an extension, but it's not standard C++ and a big n overflows the stack. Use std::vector.

QHow are 2D arrays stored in memory?

Row-major: int g[2][3] stores g[0][0], g[0][1], g[0][2], g[1][0], … contiguously, and g[i][j] is at offset i * 3 + j. That's why looping over rows in the outer loop and columns in the inner loop is faster (sequential, cache-friendly access).

QWhat does for (auto x : v) vs for (auto& x : v) vs for (const auto& x : v) do?

The first copies each element (changes don't affect v; copies can be expensive). The second binds a reference, so you can modify elements. The third binds a const reference: no copies and no modification — the default for reading.

QWhat does int a[5] = {1}; contain?

{1, 0, 0, 0, 0}. When an aggregate has fewer initializers than elements, the rest are value-initialized (zero). int a[5]; as a local has indeterminate values; int a[5] = {}; is all zeros.

QHow does break differ from continue, and how do you leave nested loops?

break exits the innermost loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration of the innermost loop. To leave nested loops, use a flag, put the loops in a function and return, or (rarely) goto.

QWhy is i[a] the same as a[i]?

a[i] is defined as *(a + i), and addition is commutative, so i[a] is *(i + a) — the same element. It's a trick question; never write it.

04& · * · nullptr · const pointers · references13 questions

Pointers & References

What a pointer holds, pointer arithmetic, nullptr, the four combinations of const and pointers, void pointers, references and how they differ from pointers, and the classic pointer bugs.

What a pointer is

A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address. &x gives the address of x; *p follows the pointer to the object it points at (dereferencing).

C++verified run
int x = 42;
int* p = &x;              // p holds the address of x
cout << *p << '\n';       // 42: read through the pointer
*p = 7;                   // write through the pointer
cout << x << '\n';        // 7
int** pp = &p;            // pointer to pointer
**pp = 99;
cout << x << ' ' << sizeof(p) << ' ' << sizeof(pp) << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << (p == &x) << ' ' << (*pp == p) << '\n';
Output
42
7
99 8 8
true true
  • Every pointer is the same size on a platform (8 bytes on 64-bit), whatever it points to.
  • The pointed-to type tells the compiler how many bytes to read and how far p + 1 moves.
  • int* a, b; declares one pointer and one int. Write one declaration per line.

Pointer arithmetic

C++verified run
int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int* p = arr;                     // decays to &arr[0]
cout << *(p + 2) << ' ' << p[3] << '\n';       // p[i] is *(p + i)
int* q = &arr[4];
cout << q - p << '\n';            // 4 elements apart (type ptrdiff_t)
++p;                              // moves sizeof(int) = 4 bytes
cout << *p << '\n';
double d[2];
cout << (char*)(d + 1) - (char*)d << '\n';    // 8: one double is 8 bytes
Output
30 40
4
20
8
  • p + n moves n * sizeof(T) bytes. Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them.
  • Only arithmetic within one array (or one past its end) is defined. Comparing or subtracting pointers into different objects is undefined.

nullptr, NULL and 0

C++verified run
void f(int)   { cout << "f(int)\n"; }
void f(char*) { cout << "f(char*)\n"; }
// in main:
f(0);          // 0 is an int literal
f(nullptr);    // nullptr has type std::nullptr_t: converts only to pointers
int* p = nullptr;
if (!p) cout << "p is null\n";
Output
f(int)
f(char*)
p is null

NULL is a macro for 0 (or 0L), so f(NULL) picks f(int) or is ambiguous. nullptr C++11 is a real null-pointer constant that never converts to an integer. Always use nullptr.

const and pointers

Read the declaration right to left: const int* p is "p is a pointer to an int that is const".

Declaration Change the pointee (*p = …) Repoint (p = …) Read as
int* p Yes Yes pointer to int
const int* p (same as int const* p) No Yes pointer to const int
int* const p Yes No const pointer to int
const int* const p No No const pointer to const int
C++compile error
int a = 1, b = 2;
const int* p1 = &a;
p1 = &b;          // fine: the pointer itself isn't const
*p1 = 5;          // error: assignment of read-only location
int* const p2 = &a;
*p2 = 5;          // fine
p2 = &b;          // error: assignment of read-only variable 'p2'
g++ says
error: assignment of read-only location '* p1'
error: assignment of read-only variable 'p2'

void*

A void* can hold the address of any object, but you can't dereference it or do arithmetic on it until you cast it back to a real type. It's how C's malloc, memcpy and qsort stay generic. In C++, prefer templates; when you do need a void*, convert back with static_cast<T*>.

C++verified run
int n = 5;
void* vp = &n;
int* ip = static_cast<int*>(vp);
cout << *ip << '\n';
Output
5

References

A reference is another name (an alias) for an existing object.

C++verified run
int x = 10;
int& r = x;          // r IS x from now on
r = 20;              // assigns to x
cout << x << ' ' << boolalpha << (&r == &x) << '\n';   // same address
int y = 99;
r = y;               // does NOT reseat r: copies y's value into x
cout << x << '\n';
const int& tmp = 3 + 4;   // const reference to a temporary: lifetime extended
cout << tmp << '\n';
Output
20 true
99
7
  • Must be initialized when declared and can never be reseated to refer to something else.
  • There are no null references, no references to references, no arrays of references, and no reference arithmetic.
  • A const T& can bind to a temporary and extends its lifetime to the reference's scope; a plain T& can't bind to a temporary.
  • Under the hood a reference is usually implemented as a pointer, but the language treats it as the object itself.

Pointer vs reference

Pointer Reference
Can be null Yes (nullptr) No
Must be initialized No (but should be) Yes
Can be reseated Yes No
Syntax to use *p, p->member Like the object: r, r.member
Arithmetic Yes No
Own address Has its own (&p) &r gives the referent's address
Multiple levels int** No reference to reference
Use for Optional objects, reseating, arrays, ownership (smart pointers) Function parameters and return values that always refer to something

Passing to functions

C++verified run
void by_value(int a)      { a = 100; }
void by_pointer(int* a)   { if (a) *a = 100; }
void by_reference(int& a) { a = 100; }
// in main:
int x = 1, y = 1, z = 1;
by_value(x);
by_pointer(&y);
by_reference(z);
cout << x << ' ' << y << ' ' << z << '\n';
Output
1 100 100
  • By value: the function works on a copy. Cheap for small types (int, double, pointers, iterators).
  • By pointer: can modify the caller's object; can be nullptr to mean "no object".
  • By reference: can modify the caller's object; can't be null; cleaner syntax.
  • By const&: no copy, no modification — the default for strings, vectors and class objects you only read.

Classic pointer bugs

Bug What it is Prevention
Wild pointer Uninitialized pointer with a garbage address Initialize every pointer, even to nullptr
Null dereference *p when p == nullptr — usually a segfault Check before dereferencing; prefer references
Dangling pointer Points to memory that was freed or went out of scope Set to nullptr after delete; don't return addresses of locals; use smart pointers
Memory leak new without a matching delete RAII and smart pointers (section 14)
Double free delete twice on the same pointer Single ownership: unique_ptr
Buffer overflow Writing past the end of an array vector, .at(), sanitizers
C++compiles
int* make_bad() {
    int local = 5;
    return &local;      // dangling: local dies when the function returns
}
// g++ warns: address of local variable 'local' returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]
How to say itPointer or reference — which would you use?

"I use a reference whenever the thing must exist and I'm not going to reseat it — that's most function parameters, usually as const T&. I use a pointer when 'no object' is a valid value, when I need to reseat it, or when I'm walking through an array. And if the pointer owns memory, it should be a unique_ptr or shared_ptr, not a raw pointer."

Interview questions

QWhat is a pointer and what is its size?

A variable that holds the address of another object (or function). On a 64-bit system every data pointer is 8 bytes, regardless of the type it points to; the type only tells the compiler how to interpret the bytes at that address.

QDifference between a pointer and a reference?

A reference is an alias that must be bound at initialization, can't be null and can't be reseated; you use it with normal object syntax. A pointer is a separate object holding an address: it can be null, reassigned, incremented, and needs */-> to reach the object.

QWhat's the difference between const int* p, int* const p and const int* const p?

const int* p: you can't modify the int through p, but p can point elsewhere. int* const p: p always points to the same int, but the int can be changed through it. const int* const p: neither. Read right to left.

QWhy use nullptr instead of NULL?

NULL is an integer constant, so it can select an int overload instead of a pointer overload, or be ambiguous. nullptr has its own type, std::nullptr_t, which converts only to pointer types, so overload resolution does the right thing.

QWhat is a dangling pointer? Give two ways to create one.

A pointer to memory that is no longer valid. Created by returning the address of a local variable, by using a pointer after delete, or by keeping a pointer/iterator into a vector that later reallocates. Using it is undefined behaviour.

QWhat is a wild pointer?

A pointer that was never initialized, so it holds an arbitrary address. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. Always initialize pointers, at least to nullptr.

QWhat is a void* and what can't you do with it?

A pointer to an object of unknown type. Any object pointer converts to void* implicitly. You can't dereference it or do arithmetic on it; you must static_cast it back to the correct type first.

QCan a reference be null? Can you have an array of references?

No to both. A reference must be bound to a valid object; producing a "null reference" by dereferencing a null pointer is already undefined behaviour. Arrays (and pointers) of references aren't allowed because references aren't objects with their own storage; use std::reference_wrapper in containers.

QWhat does p + 1 mean for an int* and for a double*?

It points to the next element: 4 bytes further for int* and 8 bytes further for double*. Pointer arithmetic is always scaled by sizeof(T).

QWhy does const T& binding to a temporary work but T& doesn't?

Binding a non-const lvalue reference to a temporary would let you modify a value that is about to vanish, which is almost always a bug, so the language forbids it. A const T& may bind, and the temporary's lifetime is extended to match the reference. (C++11 added rvalue references, T&&, for binding temporaries you do want to modify — see section 10.)

QHow do you swap two variables using pointers and using references?

void swap(int* a, int* b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; } called as swap(&x, &y), or void swap(int& a, int& b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; } called as swap(x, y). In real code, std::swap(x, y).

QWhat happens if you dereference a null pointer?

Undefined behaviour. On most systems the zero page is unmapped, so the process gets a segmentation fault — but the compiler may also assume it never happens and remove nearby null checks.

QWhat is a function pointer?

A pointer that stores the address of a function: int (*op)(int, int) = add; op(2, 3);. Used for callbacks and dispatch tables. In modern C++, std::function or a template parameter is usually preferred (section 06).

05std::string · C strings · string_view · stringstream14 questions

Strings

C strings and their dangers, std::string operations and complexity, small string optimization, conversions, splitting with stringstream, character functions, and how C++ strings differ from Java's.

C strings

A C string is a char array ending with the null character '\0'. String literals have type const char[N], where N counts the terminator.

C++verified run
char name[10] = "Sai";                 // 'S','a','i','\0', then zeros
cout << strlen(name) << ' ' << sizeof(name) << '\n';   // 3 characters, 10 bytes
char buf[20];
strcpy(buf, name);                     // copy (no bounds check!)
strcat(buf, " Revanth");               // append (no bounds check!)
cout << buf << '\n';
cout << strcmp("apple", "banana") << ' ' << strcmp("b", "b") << '\n';   // <0, 0
const char* lit = "hello";             // literals are read-only
cout << lit[1] << ' ' << *(lit + 4) << '\n';
Output
3 10
Sai Revanth
-1 0
e o
Function Does Watch out
strlen(s) Counts characters before '\0' — O(n) Calling it in a loop condition makes the loop O(n²)
strcpy(dst, src) / strncpy Copy strcpy overflows dst if src is longer; strncpy may leave dst unterminated
strcat(dst, src) Append Same overflow risk
strcmp(a, b) Compare: negative, zero or positive a == b on char* compares addresses, not text
strchr, strstr Find a char / substring Return a pointer or nullptr
PitfallString literals are read-only

char* s = "hello"; is ill-formed in C++11 and later (g++ accepts it with a warning). Writing s[0] = 'H' through such a pointer is undefined behaviour — literals usually live in read-only memory, so it crashes. Use const char* s = "hello"; to point at a literal, or char s[] = "hello"; to get a modifiable copy.

std::string

std::string owns a heap (or inline) buffer, tracks its size, grows automatically, and cleans up in its destructor. Unlike Java, a C++ string is mutable and has value semantics: b = a copies the characters.

C++verified run
string s = "interview";
s += " prep";                          // append
s.push_back('!');
cout << s << " | size " << s.size() << '\n';
cout << s[0] << s.at(1) << ' ' << s.front() << s.back() << '\n';
cout << s.substr(0, 5) << '|' << s.substr(10) << '\n';   // substr(pos, LENGTH)
s.insert(0, ">> ");
s.erase(s.size() - 1);                 // drop the '!'
s.replace(3, 9, "C++");                // replace 9 chars starting at 3
cout << s << '\n';
string a = "abc", b = a;               // b is a separate copy
b[0] = 'X';
cout << a << ' ' << b << ' ' << boolalpha << (a < b) << ' ' << (a == "abc") << '\n';
Output
interview prep! | size 15
in i!
inter|prep!
>> C++ prep
abc Xbc false true

Searching

C++verified run
string text = "the cat sat on the mat";
cout << text.find("the") << ' ' << text.rfind("the") << '\n';
cout << text.find("at", 6) << '\n';               // search from index 6
cout << text.find_first_of("aeiou") << '\n';      // first vowel
size_t pos = text.find("dog");
if (pos == string::npos) cout << "not found\n";   // npos is the largest size_t
int count = 0;
for (size_t p = text.find("at"); p != string::npos; p = text.find("at", p + 1)) ++count;
cout << "\"at\" occurs " << count << " times\n";
cout << boolalpha << text.starts_with("the") << ' ' << text.ends_with("mat") << '\n';  // C++20
Output
0 15
9
2
not found
"at" occurs 3 times
true true

Operations and their cost

Operation Complexity Notes
s[i], s.at(i), size(), back() O(1) at throws out_of_range; [] doesn't check
s += t, push_back(c) Amortized O(len t) The buffer grows geometrically
s = s + t inside a loop O(n) per step Builds a new string each time; O(n²) overall — use +=
insert, erase in the middle O(n) Shifts the tail
substr(pos, len) O(len) Returns a copy
find(t) O(n·m) worst case Use KMP/Z for guaranteed linear (section 32)
==, <, compare O(n) Lexicographic
c_str(), data() O(1) Null-terminated const char* for C APIs

Small string optimization

Most implementations store short strings inside the string object itself, avoiding a heap allocation. In libstdc++ (g++), a std::string is 32 bytes and holds up to 15 characters inline.

C++verified run
string small = "hi";
string big(100, 'x');
cout << sizeof(string) << ' ' << small.capacity() << ' ' << big.capacity() << '\n';
Output
32 15 100

Conversions

C++verified run
int n = stoi("42");                  // also stol, stoll, stoul, stod
double d = stod("3.75");
string s = to_string(123) + "|" + to_string(2.5);
int digit = '7' - '0';               // char digit → int
char c = 'a' + 2;                    // int offset → char
cout << n + 1 << ' ' << d * 2 << ' ' << s << ' ' << digit << ' ' << c << '\n';
cout << stoi("  15abc") << '\n';     // leading spaces skipped, stops at the first non-digit
try {
    stoi("abc");
} catch (const invalid_argument&) {
    cout << "invalid_argument\n";
}
try {
    stoi("99999999999");
} catch (const out_of_range&) {
    cout << "out_of_range\n";
}
Output
43 7.5 123|2.500000 7 c
15
invalid_argument
out_of_range

std::from_chars / std::to_chars C++17 in <charconv> are the fastest conversions — no exceptions, no locale, no allocation.

Character functions (<cctype>)

Function True for
isalpha(c) / isdigit(c) / isalnum(c) Letters / digits / either
isspace(c) Space, tab, newline, …
isupper(c) / islower(c) Case tests
toupper(c) / tolower(c) Return the converted character (as int)
ispunct(c) Punctuation

Pass unsigned char values: calling them with a negative char (non-ASCII bytes) is undefined.

Splitting and parsing

C++verified run
string line = "  C++ is   fun  ";
stringstream ss(line);
string word;
vector<string> words;
while (ss >> word) words.push_back(word);          // splits on any whitespace
cout << words.size() << ": ";
for (auto& w : words) cout << '[' << w << ']';
cout << '\n';

string csv = "red,green,,blue";
stringstream cs(csv);
string item;
while (getline(cs, item, ',')) cout << '[' << item << ']';   // keeps empty fields
cout << '\n';

ostringstream out;
out << "x=" << 3 << ", y=" << 4.5;                 // build a string from pieces
cout << out.str() << '\n';
Output
3: [C++][is][fun]
[red][green][][blue]
x=3, y=4.5

Everyday string algorithms

C++verified run
string s = "Madam, I'm Adam";
string clean;
for (unsigned char ch : s)
    if (isalnum(ch)) clean += tolower(ch);
string rev(clean.rbegin(), clean.rend());
cout << clean << ' ' << boolalpha << (clean == rev) << '\n';   // palindrome check

string t = "hello world";
transform(t.begin(), t.end(), t.begin(), ::toupper);
cout << t << '\n';
t.erase(remove(t.begin(), t.end(), 'L'), t.end());            // remove all 'L'
cout << t << '\n';
string w = "listen", x = "silent";
sort(w.begin(), w.end());
sort(x.begin(), x.end());
cout << "anagram: " << (w == x) << '\n';
cout << count(s.begin(), s.end(), 'a') << '\n';               // occurrences of 'a'
Output
madamimadam true
HELLO WORLD
HEO WORD
anagram: true
3

std::string_view C++17

A string_view is a non-owning pointer + length into someone else's characters. Taking one never copies, and substr on it is O(1), so it's the best type for read-only string parameters.

C++verified run
size_t vowels(string_view sv) {          // accepts string, const char*, literals: no copy
    return count_if(sv.begin(), sv.end(), [](char c) {
        return string_view("aeiou").find(c) != string_view::npos;
    });
}
// in main:
string s = "programming";
cout << vowels(s) << ' ' << vowels("education") << ' ' << vowels(string_view(s).substr(0, 7)) << '\n';
Output
3 5 2
PitfallA string_view can dangle

It doesn't own the characters. Returning a string_view into a local string, or keeping one to a temporary (string_view v = s + "x";), leaves it pointing at freed memory. Use it for parameters, not for storing.

C++ strings vs Java strings

C++ std::string Java String
Mutable Yes No — every change creates a new object
a == b Compares characters Compares references
Assignment Copies the characters Copies the reference
String pool / interning No Yes
Builder type Not needed: += is amortized O(1) per char StringBuilder
Null-terminated Yes, for c_str() compatibility No

Interview questions

QWhat is the difference between a C string and std::string?

A C string is a raw char array terminated by '\0': you manage its memory, its length costs O(n) to compute, and nothing stops you writing past the end. std::string is a class that owns and resizes its buffer, stores its length, supports +, == and <, and frees memory automatically. c_str() gives a C string when an API needs one.

QWhy can't you compare C strings with ==?

== on two char* compares the pointers — whether they point to the same memory — not the text. Use strcmp(a, b) == 0, or convert to std::string.

QWhat is the small string optimization?

Short strings are stored in a buffer inside the std::string object itself instead of on the heap. In libstdc++ the object is 32 bytes and holds up to 15 characters inline, so creating and copying short strings never allocates.

QIs std::string copy-on-write?

Not since C++11. The standard's rules for iterator invalidation and const member functions effectively forbid copy-on-write, and libstdc++ dropped its COW string with the C++11 ABI. Copies are real copies (which SSO makes cheap for short strings).

QWhat does substr(2, 3) return?

Three characters starting at index 2. The second argument is a length, not an end index (unlike Java's substring(begin, end)). It returns a new string (O(len)); string_view::substr returns a view in O(1).

QWhat is string::npos?

A static const size_t equal to the largest size_t value (−1 converted to unsigned). find returns it when nothing matches, and as a length argument it means "until the end of the string".

QHow do you convert between int and string?

std::to_string(42) and std::stoi("42") (plus stol, stoll, stod). stoi throws invalid_argument if no number can be parsed and out_of_range if it doesn't fit. For speed and no exceptions, std::from_chars and std::to_chars.

QHow do you split a string by spaces, and by a delimiter?

Whitespace: put it in a stringstream and read with >> in a loop. A delimiter: while (getline(ss, part, ',')). Or loop with find and substr.

QWhy is s = s + c in a loop slow while s += c is fast?

s + c builds a brand-new string (copying all of s) every iteration, giving O(n²) total. s += c appends in place, and the buffer grows geometrically, so it's amortized O(1) per character.

QWhat is string_view and when shouldn't you use it?

A non-owning view: a pointer and a length into existing characters. It's ideal for read-only parameters because it accepts strings and literals without copying. Don't store it beyond the life of the characters it views — returning a view into a local or a temporary dangles. It's also not guaranteed to be null-terminated, so don't pass data() to C functions.

QWhy is modifying a string literal undefined behaviour?

Literals have type const char[N] and are usually placed in read-only memory and may be shared between identical literals. Writing to one through a non-const pointer is undefined and typically crashes.

Qs[i] vs s.at(i)?

s[i] doesn't check bounds (undefined behaviour if i >= size(), except s[size()] which gives '\0'). s.at(i) checks and throws std::out_of_range.

QHow would you reverse a string?

std::reverse(s.begin(), s.end()) in place, string r(s.rbegin(), s.rend()) for a copy, or two pointers swapping s[i] and s[n-1-i] up to the middle.

QHow do you count the frequency of each character?

For lowercase letters, an int freq[26] = {} indexed by c - 'a'; for any byte, an array<int, 256>; for arbitrary keys, an unordered_map<char, int>. The array versions are fastest.

06parameters · defaults · overloading · inline · function pointers · recursion14 questions

Functions, Overloading & Recursion

Declaring and returning, default arguments, overloading and how the compiler picks an overload, name mangling and extern "C", inline and constexpr functions, static locals, function pointers, and recursion with its costs.

Declaring, defining, returning

C++verified run
int add(int a, int b);                       // declaration (prototype)
auto mul(int a, int b) -> int { return a * b; }   // trailing return type
auto half(double x) { return x / 2; }        // return type deduced: double (C++14)
pair<int, int> min_max(const vector<int>& v) {    // return two values
    auto [lo, hi] = minmax_element(v.begin(), v.end());
    return {*lo, *hi};
}
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }      // definition
// in main:
cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << mul(4, 5) << ' ' << half(7) << '\n';
auto [mn, mx] = min_max({4, 9, 1, 7});       // structured bindings (C++17)
cout << mn << ' ' << mx << '\n';
Output
5 20 3.5
1 9
  • A function must be declared before it is called; the definition can come later or live in another file.
  • To return several values, return a struct, pair or tuple and unpack it with structured bindings.
  • Returning large objects by value is cheap: the compiler constructs them directly in the caller (return value optimization, section 10).
  • Never return a reference or pointer to a local variable — it dies when the function returns.
  • [[nodiscard]] C++17 on a function makes the compiler warn when a caller ignores the result.

Default arguments

C++verified run
void greet(const string& name, const string& greeting = "Hello", int times = 1) {
    for (int i = 0; i < times; ++i) cout << greeting << ", " << name << "! ";
    cout << '\n';
}
// in main:
greet("Sai");
greet("Sai", "Hi");
greet("Sai", "Hey", 2);
Output
Hello, Sai! 
Hi, Sai! 
Hey, Sai! Hey, Sai!
  • Defaults must be the trailing parameters: once one parameter has a default, all to its right need one too.
  • Specify them once, normally in the declaration in the header — not again in the definition.
  • Defaults are filled in at the call site, using the static type. A virtual function called through a base pointer uses the base class's default value even when the derived override runs — a classic puzzle (section 41).

Function overloading

Several functions may share a name if their parameter lists differ (number, types, or const/reference qualification). The return type alone isn't enough.

C++verified run
void print(int x)            { cout << "int " << x << '\n'; }
void print(double x)         { cout << "double " << x << '\n'; }
void print(const string& s)  { cout << "string " << s << '\n'; }
void print(const char* s)    { cout << "const char* " << s << '\n'; }
// in main:
print(5);
print(5.5);
print('A');              // char → int is a promotion: picks print(int)
print(5.5f);             // float → double is a promotion: picks print(double)
print("hi");             // exact match for const char*, beats converting to string
print(string("hi"));
Output
int 5
double 5.5
int 65
double 5.5
const char* hi
string hi

How the compiler ranks candidates for each argument:

  1. Exact match (including array-to-pointer and adding const).
  2. Promotion: char/short/bool → int, float → double.
  3. Standard conversion: int → double, double → int, int → long, derived pointer → base pointer.
  4. User-defined conversion: a converting constructor or conversion operator (const char* → std::string).
  5. Ellipsis (...).

If two candidates tie, the call is ambiguous and doesn't compile:

C++compile error
void f(long x)   {}
void f(double x) {}
// in main:
f(5);   // int → long and int → double are both conversions: ambiguous
g++ says
error: call of overloaded 'f(int)' is ambiguous

Name mangling and extern "C"

To let overloads coexist in one program, the compiler encodes the parameter types into the symbol name: print(int) becomes _Z5printi and print(double) becomes _Z5printd with g++. C has no overloading and no mangling, so to call a C library from C++ (or export a function to C), declare it extern "C":

C++compiles
extern "C" int c_style_add(int a, int b);    // keep the plain symbol name
extern "C" {
    #include <string.h>                       // C headers are already wrapped like this
}

inline and constexpr functions

  • inline originally asked the compiler to paste the body at the call site. Today compilers decide inlining on their own; the keyword's real meaning is "this definition may appear in several translation units", so you can define small functions in headers without breaking the One Definition Rule.
  • Member functions defined inside a class body are implicitly inline.
  • A constexpr function C++11 can run at compile time when its arguments are constants; consteval C++20 must run at compile time.
C++verified run
constexpr long long factorial(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * factorial(n - 1); }
// in main:
constexpr auto f10 = factorial(10);     // computed by the compiler
static_assert(f10 == 3628800);          // checked at compile time
int n = 5;
cout << f10 << ' ' << factorial(n) << '\n';   // also callable at run time
Output
3628800 120

static local variables

A static local is initialized once, the first time control passes its declaration, and keeps its value between calls. Since C++11 that first initialization is thread-safe.

C++verified run
int next_id() {
    static int counter = 0;     // lives for the whole program
    return ++counter;
}
// in main:
cout << next_id() << next_id() << next_id() << '\n';
Output
123

Function pointers and callbacks

C++verified run
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int sub(int a, int b) { return a - b; }
using BinOp = int (*)(int, int);          // or: typedef int (*BinOp)(int, int);
int apply(BinOp op, int x, int y) { return op(x, y); }
bool desc(int a, int b) { return a > b; }
// in main:
int (*fp)(int, int) = add;                // & is optional for functions
cout << fp(2, 3) << ' ' << apply(sub, 9, 4) << '\n';
BinOp table[] = {add, sub};               // dispatch table
cout << table[1](10, 3) << '\n';
vector<int> v{3, 1, 2};
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), desc);           // a function pointer as a comparator
for (int x : v) cout << x;
cout << '\n';
Output
5 5
7
321

Modern alternatives: pass a lambda (section 20), take the callable as a template parameter (zero overhead, can be inlined), or store it in a std::function when you need to keep callables of different types.

Recursion

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it hits a base case. Each call gets its own stack frame (parameters, locals, return address), so recursion depth is limited by the stack size — typically 8 MB on Linux, 1 MB on Windows.

C++verified run
long long fib_slow(int n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib_slow(n - 1) + fib_slow(n - 2); }   // O(2^n)

long long fib_memo(int n, vector<long long>& memo) {                                   // O(n)
    if (n < 2) return n;
    if (memo[n] != -1) return memo[n];
    return memo[n] = fib_memo(n - 1, memo) + fib_memo(n - 2, memo);
}

long long power(long long base, int exp) {      // fast exponentiation: O(log exp)
    if (exp == 0) return 1;
    long long half = power(base, exp / 2);
    return exp % 2 ? half * half * base : half * half;
}

void hanoi(int n, char from, char to, char via, int& moves) {
    if (n == 0) return;
    hanoi(n - 1, from, via, to, moves);
    ++moves;
    hanoi(n - 1, via, to, from, moves);
}
// in main:
vector<long long> memo(91, -1);
cout << fib_slow(20) << ' ' << fib_memo(90, memo) << '\n';
cout << power(3, 13) << '\n';
int moves = 0;
hanoi(10, 'A', 'C', 'B', moves);
cout << moves << " moves\n";      // 2^10 - 1
Output
6765 2880067194370816120
1594323
1023 moves
Recursion Iteration
Natural for Trees, graphs (DFS), divide and conquer, backtracking Linear scans, simple repetition
Memory O(depth) stack frames O(1) extra
Risk Stack overflow on deep input (e.g. a 10⁶-node linked list) —
Speed Call overhead per level Usually faster
TipTail calls

A call is a tail call when it's the last thing the function does (return f(n - 1, acc * n);). Compilers often turn tail recursion into a loop at -O2, but C++ doesn't guarantee it — don't rely on it for deep recursion.

Interview questions

QWhat is function overloading and how does the compiler choose?

Several functions with the same name but different parameter lists. At each call the compiler ranks candidates by how well each argument converts — exact match, then promotion, then standard conversion, then user-defined conversion — and picks the unique best one; if two are equally good, the call is ambiguous. It's compile-time (static) polymorphism.

QCan you overload on the return type alone?

No. The call f(x) doesn't mention the return type, so the compiler couldn't choose. Overloads must differ in their parameters (or in the const/ref qualifiers of member functions).

QWhat is name mangling?

The compiler encodes a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its linker symbol, so overloads get distinct names (_Z5printi, _Z5printd). extern "C" turns it off so C code can call the function, at the price of not being able to overload it.

QWhat are the rules for default arguments?

They must be the rightmost parameters, are given once (usually in the declaration), and are substituted at the call site based on the static type. For virtual functions, the default comes from the static type even if a derived override runs.

QWhat does inline mean today?

That the function (or variable, since C++17) may be defined in multiple translation units, as long as all definitions are identical — so it can live in a header. Whether a call is actually inlined is the optimizer's decision, with or without the keyword.

QInline function vs macro?

An inline function is type-checked, evaluates each argument once, respects scope and can be debugged. A macro is text substitution by the preprocessor: #define SQ(x) x*x gives SQ(a+1) = a+1*a+1, and SQ(i++) increments twice. Prefer inline/constexpr functions and templates.

QWhat is a static local variable?

A local variable with static storage duration: initialized once, on first use, and kept until the program ends. Its initialization is thread-safe since C++11, which is why the Meyers singleton (static Foo instance; in a function) works.

QPass by value vs reference vs pointer — when to use each?

By value for cheap types and when you need a copy anyway (it also enables move). By const& for read-only access to strings, containers and class objects. By & when the function must modify the argument. By pointer when "no object" (nullptr) is a valid input or for C-style APIs.

QWhat is a function pointer? Give a use case.

A variable that holds a function's address: int (*op)(int, int) = add;. Used for callbacks (qsort comparators, event handlers) and dispatch tables (ops[choice](a, b)). Lambdas without captures convert to function pointers.

QWhat is recursion, and what are its risks?

A function solving a problem by calling itself on smaller instances, stopping at a base case. Risks: stack overflow when the depth is large, exponential time when subproblems repeat (fix with memoization or bottom-up DP), and call overhead compared to loops.

QWhy is naive recursive Fibonacci slow, and how do you fix it?

fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), which recompute the same values again and again — about φⁿ calls, exponential time. Memoize results in an array (O(n) time), or iterate keeping the last two values (O(n) time, O(1) space).

QWhat is constexpr on a function?

It allows the function to be evaluated at compile time when called with constant arguments, so its result can be used where a constant is required (array sizes, template arguments, static_assert). Called with run-time values it runs normally.

QCan main be overloaded, called recursively, or declared inline/static?

No. The program can't call main itself (that's ill-formed in C++, unlike C), take its address, overload it, or declare it inline, static or constexpr.

QWhat are variadic functions?

Functions taking a variable number of arguments. The C style is int printf(const char*, ...) with va_list — no type safety. The C++ way is a variadic template, template <typename... Args> void log(Args&&... args), which is type-safe (section 16).

Classes, Objects & Constructors

Class vs struct, access control, every kind of constructor, initializer lists and initialization order, explicit, destructors and the order things are built and torn down, this, const members, static members and friends.

Class and object

A class is a user-defined type that bundles data (data members) with the functions that work on it (member functions). An object is an instance of a class, occupying memory.

C++verified run
class Rectangle {
private:                       // only members (and friends) can touch these
    double width = 0, height = 0;
public:                        // the interface
    Rectangle(double w, double h) : width(w), height(h) {}
    double area() const { return width * height; }   // const: doesn't modify
    void scale(double f);                            // declared here...
};
void Rectangle::scale(double f) { width *= f; height *= f; }   // ...defined outside with ::
// in main:
Rectangle r(3, 4);             // object on the stack
r.scale(2);
cout << r.area() << '\n';
Rectangle* p = new Rectangle(1, 2);   // object on the heap
cout << p->area() << '\n';
delete p;
Output
48
2

class vs struct

The only difference is the default access: members and base classes are private by default in a class and public in a struct. By convention, struct is used for plain data bundles with no invariants and class for types with private state and an interface.

Access specifier Accessible from the class itself From derived classes From outside
public Yes Yes Yes
protected Yes Yes No
private Yes No No

Access is checked per class, not per object: a member function can read the private members of another object of the same class (that's how copy constructors work).

Constructors

A constructor has the class's name and no return type; it runs when an object is created and puts it in a valid state.

C++verified run
class Student {
    string name;
    int roll;
    const int batch;                 // const member: must be set in the initializer list
    vector<int> marks;
public:
    Student() : Student("unknown", 0) {}                 // delegating constructor (C++11)
    Student(string n, int r, int b = 2027)               // parameterized, with a default
        : name(std::move(n)), roll(r), batch(b) {}        // member initializer list
    Student(const Student& other)                         // copy constructor
        : name(other.name + " (copy)"), roll(other.roll), batch(other.batch), marks(other.marks) {}
    void show() const { cout << name << ' ' << roll << ' ' << batch << '\n'; }
};
// in main:
Student a;                       // default constructor
Student b("Sai", 42);            // parameterized
Student c = b;                   // copy constructor (not assignment!)
Student d{b};                    // also copy construction
a.show(); b.show(); c.show(); d.show();
Output
unknown 0 2027
Sai 42 2027
Sai (copy) 42 2027
Sai (copy) 42 2027
Kind Signature Runs when
Default X() X a;, X a{};, new X, arrays of X
Parameterized X(int, string) X a(1, "s");
Copy X(const X&) X b = a;, X b(a);, pass/return by value (unless elided)
Move C++11 X(X&&) noexcept Initializing from a temporary or std::move(a)
Delegating C++11 X() : X(0, "") {} Forwards to another constructor of the same class
Converting Any non-explicit constructor callable with one argument Implicit conversions like X x = 5;
  • If you declare no constructors at all, the compiler generates a default constructor. Declaring any constructor removes it; write X() = default; to get it back.
  • X() = delete; (or any function = delete) forbids that operation explicitly.

The member initializer list

Members are initialized before the constructor body runs. Assigning in the body means default-construct first, then assign — two steps. The initializer list does it in one step and is required for:

  1. const members,
  2. reference members,
  3. members (and base classes) with no default constructor,
  4. base-class constructors that take arguments.
PitfallMembers are initialized in declaration order, not list order

The order in which you write the initializer list is ignored: members are always initialized in the order they're declared in the class. -Wall warns when the two orders differ (-Wreorder).

C++verified run
class Trap {
    int a;
    int b;
public:
    Trap(int x) : b(x), a(b * 2) {}    // a is initialized FIRST, from a garbage b
    void show() const { cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; }
};
class Fixed {
    int b;                              // declare b first...
    int a;
public:
    Fixed(int x) : b(x), a(b * 2) {}    // ...so b is ready when a uses it
    void show() const { cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; }
};
// in main:
Fixed(5).show();
Output
10 5

(The Trap version reads an uninitialized member, which is undefined behaviour — so it isn't run here.)

Default member initializers C++11

C++verified run
struct Config {
    int retries = 3;                  // used unless a constructor says otherwise
    double timeout{2.5};
    string mode = "fast";
    Config() = default;
