    explicit Config(int r) : retries(r) {}   // timeout and mode keep their defaults
};
// in main:
Config a, b(10);
cout << a.retries << ' ' << b.retries << ' ' << b.timeout << ' ' << b.mode << '\n';
Output
3 10 2.5 fast

explicit

A constructor callable with one argument doubles as an implicit conversion. explicit turns that off.

C++compile error
class Meters {
    double v;
public:
    explicit Meters(double x) : v(x) {}
};
void walk(Meters m) {}
// in main:
walk(Meters(5.0));   // fine: explicit construction
walk(5.0);           // error: no implicit conversion from double to Meters
g++ says
error: could not convert '5.0e+0' from 'double' to 'Meters'

Mark single-argument constructors explicit unless the conversion is genuinely natural (like string from const char*).

The most vexing parse

C++compiles
struct Widget { int v = 0; };
// in main:
Widget w1;       // an object, default-initialized
Widget w2{};     // an object, value-initialized
Widget w3();     // NOT an object: declares a function returning Widget!

Destructors

A destructor ~X() runs automatically when an object's lifetime ends: at the end of its scope for locals, at delete for heap objects, at program exit for statics. It takes no parameters, returns nothing, and a class has exactly one. Its job is to release what the object owns — memory, files, locks.

C++verified run
struct Tracer {
    string name;
    Tracer(string n) : name(n) { cout << "construct " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Tracer() { cout << "destroy " << name << '\n'; }
};
struct Holder {
    Tracer first{"member1"};
    Tracer second{"member2"};
    Holder()  { cout << "Holder body\n"; }
    ~Holder() { cout << "~Holder body\n"; }
};
Tracer global("global");
// in main:
cout << "main starts\n";
{
    Tracer a("a");
    Tracer b("b");
    Holder h;
}                                // destroyed here, in reverse order
Tracer* heap = new Tracer("heap");
delete heap;                     // destroyed only when you delete it
cout << "main ends\n";
Output
construct global
main starts
construct a
construct b
construct member1
construct member2
Holder body
~Holder body
destroy member2
destroy member1
destroy b
destroy a
construct heap
destroy heap
main ends
destroy global

Order rules: members are constructed in declaration order before the constructor body; the destructor body runs first, then members are destroyed in reverse order. Local objects are destroyed in the reverse order of construction. Globals are constructed before main and destroyed after it.

The this pointer

Inside a non-static member function, this points to the object the function was called on (type X*, or const X* in a const member function). Uses: disambiguating members from parameters, returning *this for chaining, passing the object to other functions.

C++verified run
class Counter {
    int count = 0;
public:
    Counter& add(int count) {        // parameter shadows the member
        this->count += count;        // this-> selects the member
        return *this;                // return a reference to self for chaining
    }
    int get() const { return count; }
};
// in main:
Counter c;
cout << c.add(5).add(10).add(1).get() << '\n';
Output
16

const member functions and mutable

A member function marked const promises not to modify the object; it's the only kind you can call on a const object or through a const&. A mutable member can still be changed inside const functions — used for caches, counters and mutexes that don't affect the object's visible state.

C++verified run
class Doc {
    string text;
    mutable int reads = 0;                     // bookkeeping, not "real" state
public:
    Doc(string t) : text(std::move(t)) {}
    const string& get() const { ++reads; return text; }
    int read_count() const { return reads; }
};
// in main:
const Doc d("notes");
d.get(); d.get();
cout << d.get() << ' ' << d.read_count() << '\n';
Output
notes 3

Static members

A static data member belongs to the class, not to any object: one copy shared by all instances. A static member function has no this, so it can only touch static members directly; call it as X::f().

C++verified run
class Account {
    static int created;                 // declaration
    inline static double rate = 7.5;    // C++17: define in the class with inline
    int id;
public:
    Account() : id(++created) {}
    static int total() { return created; }   // no this pointer
    int get_id() const { return id; }
    static double get_rate() { return rate; }
};
int Account::created = 0;               // definition (pre-C++17 style) in one .cpp file
// in main:
Account a, b, c;
cout << Account::total() << ' ' << c.get_id() << ' ' << Account::get_rate() << '\n';
cout << sizeof(Account) << '\n';        // static members don't add to object size
Output
3 3 7.5
4

Friends

A friend function or class may access a class's private and protected members. Friendship is granted by the class (not taken), and it is not inherited, not transitive and not mutual.

C++verified run
class Box {
    double secret = 42;
    friend void inspect(const Box& b);      // a friend function
    friend class Auditor;                   // every member of Auditor is a friend
};
void inspect(const Box& b) { cout << "inspect: " << b.secret << '\n'; }
class Auditor {
public:
    double read(const Box& b) const { return b.secret; }
};
// in main:
Box b;
inspect(b);
cout << Auditor().read(b) << '\n';
Output
inspect: 42
42

The most common legitimate friend is operator<< for printing (section 11).

Size of objects

C++verified run
struct Empty {};
struct OneChar { char c; };
struct Mixed { char c; int i; char d; };      // padding added for alignment
struct Packed { int i; char c; char d; };     // same members, better order
struct WithFunc { int x; void f() {} };       // functions don't take space in objects
cout << sizeof(Empty) << ' ' << sizeof(OneChar) << ' ' << sizeof(Mixed) << ' '
     << sizeof(Packed) << ' ' << sizeof(WithFunc) << '\n';
Output
1 1 12 8 4
  • An empty class has size 1, so two distinct objects always have distinct addresses.
  • Member functions live in the code segment, once per class; they don't increase object size. A virtual function adds one hidden pointer (section 09).
  • The compiler inserts padding so each member is aligned; ordering members from largest to smallest minimizes it (section 13).

Interview questions

QWhat is the difference between a class and an object?

A class is a blueprint — a type describing data and behaviour. An object is an instance of that type occupying memory, with its own copy of the non-static data members. class Car is the class; Car mine; is an object.

QWhat is the difference between class and struct in C++?

Only the default access level: class members and base classes default to private, struct ones to public. Both can have constructors, virtual functions, inheritance and templates. Conventionally struct is used for passive data.

QWhat is a constructor? Can it be private, virtual, or return a value?

A special member function that initializes an object; it has the class name and no return type. It can be private (singletons, factory functions, non-instantiable classes). It can't be virtual — when it runs, the object's dynamic type isn't established yet; use a virtual clone() instead. It can't return a value, but it can throw an exception to report failure.

QWhy use a member initializer list instead of assignment in the constructor body?

Members are initialized before the body runs, so assigning in the body means default-constructing and then assigning — two operations. The initializer list initializes directly. It's mandatory for const members, reference members, members or bases without a default constructor, and base-class constructors with arguments.

QIn what order are members initialized?

In the order they're declared in the class, regardless of the order in the initializer list. Base classes are initialized before members (in the order they're listed in the class's base list). Destruction is the exact reverse.

QWhen does the compiler generate a default constructor?

Only if the class declares no constructors at all, and only if every member and base can be default-constructed. Declaring any constructor (even a copy constructor) suppresses it; X() = default; brings it back.

QWhat does explicit do?

It stops a constructor (or conversion operator) from being used for implicit conversions and copy-initialization. With explicit Meters(double), walk(5.0) and Meters m = 5.0; don't compile, but Meters m(5.0) does. It prevents surprising silent conversions.

QWhat is a delegating constructor?

A constructor that calls another constructor of the same class in its initializer list: Student() : Student("unknown", 0) {}. It removes duplicated initialization code. Available since C++11.

QWhat is a destructor? When is it called?

A member function ~X() that releases the object's resources. It's called automatically when a local goes out of scope, when delete is called on a heap object, when a temporary's full expression ends, and at program exit for static objects. It takes no arguments, can't be overloaded, and should not throw.

QCan a destructor be private? Can it be overloaded?

It can be private — then the object can't be created on the stack (its destructor must be accessible at scope end), which is a way to force heap allocation with a destroy() member. It can't be overloaded: there's exactly one destructor with no parameters.

QWhat is the this pointer?

A hidden parameter of every non-static member function pointing to the object it was called on. Its type is X* (const X* inside a const member function). Static member functions don't have one.

QWhat is a static data member and a static member function?

A static data member is shared by all objects of the class — one copy, stored outside the objects. A static member function belongs to the class rather than an object, has no this, can access only static members directly, and is called as X::f().

QWhat is a friend function? Doesn't it break encapsulation?

A non-member function that the class grants access to its private members. It's part of the class's interface, declared by the class itself, so it's controlled access rather than a breach — typical for operator<< and symmetric operators. Overusing friends does weaken encapsulation.

QWhat is a const member function?

One that promises not to modify the object's (non-mutable) members; this is a pointer to const inside it. Only const member functions can be called on const objects, const references and const pointers.

QWhat is mutable?

A member marked mutable can be modified even inside const member functions. Use it for things that don't change the object's logical state: caches, access counters, mutexes.

QWhat is the size of an empty class, and why?

1 byte. Every object must have a unique address, so it can't be zero-sized. (As a base class, an empty class can take zero bytes — the empty base optimization.)

QWhat is the most vexing parse?

Widget w(); looks like creating an object but is parsed as declaring a function w that returns a Widget. Write Widget w; or Widget w{};.

QCopy constructor vs assignment operator — which runs in X b = a;?

The copy constructor: b is being created. Assignment runs only when the target already exists: X b; b = a;.

08encapsulation · abstraction · inheritance · polymorphism16 questions

The Four Pillars of OOP

The four pillars with C++ mechanisms and real-life examples, inheritance access modes and types, name hiding, the diamond problem and virtual inheritance, compile-time vs run-time polymorphism, upcasting and object slicing.

The four pillars at a glance

Pillar Idea C++ mechanism Real-life example
Encapsulation Bundle data with the code that guards it; hide the internals Classes, private/protected, member functions An ATM: you can't touch the cash, only use the buttons
Abstraction Show what an object does, hide how Abstract classes, pure virtual functions, headers vs source files Driving a car with a steering wheel and pedals, not the engine
Inheritance Build a new class from an existing one (IS-A) class Derived : public Base A savings account is an account
Polymorphism One interface, many behaviours Overloading and templates (compile time); virtual functions (run time) "Pay" works for card, UPI and cash

Encapsulation

Keep data private and expose operations that keep the object valid (its invariants). Nobody outside can put a BankAccount into an impossible state.

C++verified run
class BankAccount {
    string owner;
    double balance = 0;                       // hidden: can't be set to -500 from outside
public:
    explicit BankAccount(string name) : owner(std::move(name)) {}
    void deposit(double amt) {
        if (amt <= 0) throw invalid_argument("deposit must be positive");
        balance += amt;
    }
    bool withdraw(double amt) {
        if (amt <= 0 || amt > balance) return false;   // invariant: balance >= 0
        balance -= amt;
        return true;
    }
    double get_balance() const { return balance; }      // read-only access
};
// in main:
BankAccount acc("Sai");
acc.deposit(1000);
cout << boolalpha << acc.withdraw(300) << ' ' << acc.withdraw(5000) << ' ' << acc.get_balance() << '\n';
Output
true false 700

Benefits: the class controls every change (validation, logging, thread safety), and the internal representation can change without touching callers.

Abstraction

An abstract class declares an interface with pure virtual functions (= 0) and can't be instantiated. Concrete classes implement it; client code depends only on the interface.

C++verified run
class Shape {                                  // abstract: has a pure virtual function
public:
    virtual double area() const = 0;
    virtual string name() const = 0;
    virtual ~Shape() = default;                // always virtual in a polymorphic base
    void describe() const { cout << name() << " with area " << area() << '\n'; }
};
class Circle : public Shape {
    double r;
public:
    explicit Circle(double r) : r(r) {}
    double area() const override { return 3.14159 * r * r; }
    string name() const override { return "circle"; }
};
class Square : public Shape {
    double s;
public:
    explicit Square(double s) : s(s) {}
    double area() const override { return s * s; }
    string name() const override { return "square"; }
};
// in main:
vector<unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
shapes.push_back(make_unique<Circle>(1));
shapes.push_back(make_unique<Square>(3));
for (const auto& s : shapes) s->describe();    // the caller never needs the concrete type
Output
circle with area 3.14159
square with area 9
Encapsulation Abstraction
Hides data and implementation details Hides complexity behind a simple interface
About how data is protected About what is exposed
Implemented with access specifiers Implemented with abstract classes / interfaces
Works inside one class Works at the design level, across classes

C++ has no interface keyword: an "interface" is an abstract class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor.

Inheritance

C++verified run
class Employee {
protected:                       // visible to derived classes, hidden from outsiders
    string name;
    double base_pay;
public:
    Employee(string n, double pay) : name(std::move(n)), base_pay(pay) {
        cout << "Employee(" << name << ")\n";
    }
    ~Employee() { cout << "~Employee\n"; }
    double pay() const { return base_pay; }
};
class Manager : public Employee {
    double bonus;
public:
    Manager(string n, double pay, double b)
        : Employee(std::move(n), pay), bonus(b) {    // base constructor runs first
        cout << "Manager\n";
    }
    ~Manager() { cout << "~Manager\n"; }
    double total() const { return base_pay + bonus; }   // uses a protected member
};
// in main:
Manager m("Anu", 50000, 10000);
cout << m.pay() << ' ' << m.total() << '\n';
Output
Employee(Anu)
Manager
50000 60000
~Manager
~Employee

Construction goes base → members → derived body; destruction is the reverse: derived body → members → base.

Inheritance access modes

The access mode caps how inherited members appear in the derived class:

Base member public inheritance protected inheritance private inheritance
public public protected private
protected protected protected private
private not accessible not accessible not accessible
  • public inheritance models IS-A and is what you want 95% of the time. Only with public inheritance can a Derived* convert implicitly to Base* outside the class.
  • private inheritance means "implemented in terms of" — usually better replaced by composition.
  • Private members are inherited (they take space in the derived object) but aren't accessible.

What isn't inherited

Constructors (unless you write using Base::Base; C++11), the destructor, the copy/move assignment operators, and friendships. The derived class gets its own compiler-generated versions, which call the base versions.

Types of inheritance

Type Shape
Single B : A
Multilevel C : B, B : A
Multiple C : A, B
Hierarchical B : A, C : A
Hybrid A mix — e.g. the diamond: B : A, C : A, D : B, C

Name hiding

A member in the derived class hides every base member with the same name, regardless of parameters — overloads aren't merged across scopes.

C++compile error
struct Base {
    void f(int)    { cout << "Base::f(int)\n"; }
    void f(double) { cout << "Base::f(double)\n"; }
};
struct Derived : Base {
    void f(string) { cout << "Derived::f(string)\n"; }   // hides BOTH Base::f overloads
};
// in main:
Derived d;
d.f("text");
d.f(5);        // error: Base::f(int) is hidden
g++ says
error: cannot convert 'int' to 'std::string' {aka 'std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>'}

Fix it by bringing the base overloads into scope:

C++verified run
struct Base {
    void f(int)    { cout << "Base::f(int)\n"; }
    void f(double) { cout << "Base::f(double)\n"; }
};
struct Derived : Base {
    using Base::f;                                       // un-hide
    void f(string) { cout << "Derived::f(string)\n"; }
};
// in main:
Derived d;
d.f("text");
d.f(5);
d.f(2.5);
Output
Derived::f(string)
Base::f(int)
Base::f(double)

IS-A vs HAS-A: prefer composition

  • IS-A (inheritance): a Manager is an Employee. Use it when the derived class can stand in anywhere the base is expected (the Liskov substitution principle).
  • HAS-A (composition): a Car has an Engine member. More flexible: you can swap parts, hide their interface, and avoid deep fragile hierarchies.
  • Rule of thumb: favour composition over inheritance unless you need polymorphism through a base interface.

Multiple inheritance and the diamond problem

C++verified run
struct Device {
    int id;
    Device(int i) : id(i) { cout << "Device(" << i << ")\n"; }
};
struct Printer : virtual Device {            // virtual inheritance
    Printer() : Device(1) { cout << "Printer\n"; }
};
struct Scanner : virtual Device {
    Scanner() : Device(2) { cout << "Scanner\n"; }
};
struct Copier : Printer, Scanner {
    Copier() : Device(3) { cout << "Copier\n"; }   // the MOST DERIVED class builds the virtual base
};
// in main:
Copier c;
cout << "id = " << c.id << '\n';             // one shared Device: no ambiguity
Output
Device(3)
Printer
Scanner
Copier
id = 3
  • Without virtual, a Copier would contain two Device subobjects, and c.id would be ambiguous (you'd need c.Printer::id).
  • With virtual inheritance there's one shared Device, and it's initialized by the most derived class — the Device(1) and Device(2) calls in Printer and Scanner are ignored.
  • Cost: the compiler adds hidden pointers/offsets to find the shared base, so objects get bigger and access slightly slower.

Polymorphism

Compile-time (static) Run-time (dynamic)
Mechanisms Function overloading, operator overloading, templates Virtual functions through base pointers/references
Decided By the compiler, from static types At run time, from the object's dynamic type
Also called Early binding Late binding
Cost None at run time (can be inlined) One indirect call through the vtable
Flexibility Types fixed at compile time New derived classes work without recompiling callers
C++verified run
struct Payment {
    virtual void pay(double amt) const { cout << "generic payment " << amt << '\n'; }
    virtual ~Payment() = default;
};
struct Card : Payment {
    void pay(double amt) const override { cout << "card payment " << amt << '\n'; }
};
struct Upi : Payment {
    void pay(double amt) const override { cout << "UPI payment " << amt << '\n'; }
};
void checkout(const Payment& p) { p.pay(499); }    // works for every present and future type
// in main:
Card c; Upi u;
checkout(c);
checkout(u);
Payment sliced = c;                                // copies only the Payment part!
sliced.pay(1);
Output
card payment 499
UPI payment 499
generic payment 1

Upcasting, downcasting and object slicing

  • Upcasting (derived → base pointer or reference) is implicit and safe.
  • Downcasting (base → derived) needs a cast: dynamic_cast checks at run time, static_cast doesn't (section 09).
  • Object slicing: assigning or passing a derived object by value to a base object copies only the base part. The derived data and the virtual behaviour are "sliced off" — the last line above prints "generic payment". Always pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer.

Interview questions

QWhat are the four pillars of OOP? Explain each with an example.

Encapsulation — data and methods bundled with private data (a BankAccount whose balance changes only through deposit/withdraw). Abstraction — exposing what an object does while hiding how (a Shape interface with area()). Inheritance — deriving a class from another to reuse and extend it (Manager : Employee). Polymorphism — the same call behaving differently by type (checkout(payment) for card or UPI).

QDifference between encapsulation and abstraction?

Encapsulation is about hiding data and protecting invariants inside a class, via access specifiers. Abstraction is about hiding complexity behind an interface, via abstract classes and well-chosen public functions. Encapsulation is one way to achieve abstraction.

QWhat is an abstract class? Can you create its object? Can it have a constructor?

A class with at least one pure virtual function (virtual f() = 0;). You can't instantiate it, but you can have pointers and references to it. It can have constructors (called when building derived objects), data members, and non-virtual functions.

QHow does C++ implement interfaces?

With abstract classes that have only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor. A class "implements" several interfaces by inheriting from several of them (multiple inheritance of interfaces is safe because they have no data).

QExplain public, protected and private inheritance.

They cap the access of inherited members: public keeps public as public and protected as protected; protected turns both into protected; private turns both into private. Base private members are never accessible. Only public inheritance lets outside code treat a Derived as a Base.

QWhat is the diamond problem and how does C++ solve it?

When D inherits from B and C, which both inherit from A, D contains two A subobjects, so names from A are ambiguous and A's state is duplicated. Declaring the inheritance virtual (B : virtual A, C : virtual A) makes B and C share one A; the most derived class constructs it.

QWhy doesn't Java have the diamond problem for classes?

Java allows single class inheritance only; multiple inheritance is for interfaces, which have no instance fields. Since Java 8, default methods can still conflict, and the class must override to resolve it. C++ allows multiple inheritance of classes with data, hence virtual inheritance.

QCompile-time vs run-time polymorphism?

Compile-time: function/operator overloading and templates, resolved from static types, zero run-time cost. Run-time: virtual functions called through a base pointer or reference, resolved from the dynamic type via the vtable, enabling code that works with types written later.

QWhat is object slicing?

Copying a derived object into a base object by value: only the base subobject is copied, so derived members are lost and virtual calls on the copy use the base version. It happens with Base b = derived;, pass-by-value parameters and vector<Base>. Use references, pointers or vector<unique_ptr<Base>>.

QWhat is name hiding?

A name declared in a derived class hides all members with that name in the base, even ones with different parameter lists, because lookup stops at the first scope that has the name. using Base::f; brings the base overloads back.

QIs a constructor inherited? Is a destructor? Friend functions?

None of them are inherited by default. A derived class can inherit constructors explicitly with using Base::Base;. The derived class always gets its own destructor, which calls the base destructor automatically. Friendship isn't inherited.

QWhat is the order of constructor and destructor calls in inheritance?

Construction: virtual bases first, then direct bases in declaration order, then members in declaration order, then the derived constructor body. Destruction is exactly the reverse.

QComposition vs inheritance — when to use which?

Use inheritance for a true IS-A relationship where the derived type should be usable through the base interface. Use composition (HAS-A) to reuse functionality: it keeps coupling low, hides the part's interface, and allows swapping implementations at run time. Default to composition.

QCan a derived class access private members of its base?

Not directly. Private members are inherited (they're part of the derived object's memory) but only the base's own members and friends can access them. Derived classes use protected members or the base's public/protected functions.

QWhat is multiple inheritance? What are its problems?

A class with more than one direct base: class C : public A, public B. Problems: ambiguity when both bases have a member with the same name (resolve with A::f()), the diamond problem, and more complex object layout and casts. It's safest when extra bases are pure interfaces.

QWhat is upcasting and downcasting?

Upcasting converts a derived pointer/reference to a base one; it's implicit and always safe. Downcasting goes the other way and needs an explicit cast: dynamic_cast verifies the dynamic type (returning nullptr or throwing bad_cast on failure); static_cast trusts you, and a wrong guess is undefined behaviour.

09virtual · override · final · vptr · dynamic_cast · typeid16 questions

Virtual Functions, vtables & RTTI

How a virtual call is dispatched through the vptr and vtable, override and final, why base destructors must be virtual, virtual calls inside constructors, default arguments, the cost of virtual, the clone idiom, and RTTI.

Static vs dynamic binding

C++verified run
struct Animal {
    void eat() const { cout << "Animal eats\n"; }               // non-virtual
    virtual void speak() const { cout << "...\n"; }             // virtual
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
};
struct Dog : Animal {
    void eat() const { cout << "Dog eats\n"; }                  // hides, doesn't override
    void speak() const override { cout << "Woof\n"; }
};
// in main:
Dog d;
Animal* p = &d;
Animal& r = d;
p->eat();      // static binding: decided by the pointer's type (Animal)
p->speak();    // dynamic binding: decided by the object's type (Dog)
r.speak();
d.eat();
Output
Animal eats
Woof
Woof
Dog eats
  • A non-virtual call is bound at compile time from the static type of the pointer or reference.
  • A virtual call made through a pointer or reference is bound at run time from the dynamic type of the object.
  • A virtual call on an object by value (d.speak()) is already known at compile time — no dispatch needed.
  • Once a function is virtual in a base, it is virtual in every derived class, with or without the keyword.

How it works: vptr and vtable

  • For every class with virtual functions, the compiler builds one vtable: a static array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function.
  • Every object of such a class carries a hidden vptr (normally its first 8 bytes) pointing to its class's vtable. The constructor sets it.
  • A virtual call compiles to: read the vptr, index the vtable, call indirectly. A derived class's vtable copies the base's slots and replaces those it overrides.
  • The standard doesn't mention vtables — they're how every major compiler implements the rules.
C++verified run
struct Plain    { double x; void f() {} };
struct Virtual  { double x; virtual void f() {} virtual ~Virtual() = default; };
struct TwoVirts { double x; virtual void f() {} virtual void g() {} virtual ~TwoVirts() = default; };
cout << sizeof(Plain) << ' ' << sizeof(Virtual) << ' ' << sizeof(TwoVirts) << '\n';
Output
8 16 16

Adding virtual functions adds one pointer per object (not one per function); the vtables themselves are shared per class.

override and final C++11

override asks the compiler to check that a function really overrides a base virtual. Without it, a tiny signature difference silently creates a new function instead.

C++compile error
struct Base {
    virtual double area() const { return 0; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};
struct Circle : Base {
    double area() override { return 3.14; }   // missing const: different signature
};
g++ says
error: 'double Circle::area()' marked 'override', but does not override

final stops further overriding (on a function) or inheritance (on a class):

C++compile error
struct Base { virtual void run() {} virtual ~Base() = default; };
struct Mid : Base { void run() final {} };
struct Leaf final : Mid {};
struct Oops : Leaf {};          // error: cannot derive from 'final' base
g++ says
error: cannot derive from 'final' base 'Leaf' in derived type 'Oops'

final also lets the compiler devirtualize calls — call the function directly and even inline it.

Virtual destructors

If you delete a derived object through a base pointer and the base destructor is not virtual, only the base destructor runs — the behaviour is undefined (in practice the derived part leaks). Rule: a class with any virtual function, or meant to be used as a base through pointers, needs a virtual destructor.

C++verified run
struct Base {
    Base()  { cout << "Base()\n"; }
    virtual ~Base() { cout << "~Base()\n"; }      // remove 'virtual' and ~Derived never runs
};
struct Derived : Base {
    int* data = new int[100];
    Derived()  { cout << "Derived()\n"; }
    ~Derived() override { delete[] data; cout << "~Derived() freed buffer\n"; }
};
// in main:
Base* p = new Derived;
delete p;               // virtual: ~Derived, then ~Base
Output
Base()
Derived()
~Derived() freed buffer
~Base()

A base that is never deleted polymorphically can instead make its destructor protected and non-virtual.

Pure virtual functions and abstract classes

C++verified run
class Plugin {
public:
    virtual string id() const = 0;            // pure virtual
    virtual ~Plugin() = 0;                    // pure virtual destructor...
};
Plugin::~Plugin() { cout << "~Plugin\n"; }    // ...still needs a body: derived destructors call it
class Logger : public Plugin {
public:
    string id() const override { return "logger"; }
    ~Logger() override { cout << "~Logger\n"; }
};
// in main:
unique_ptr<Plugin> p = make_unique<Logger>();
cout << p->id() << '\n';
Output
logger
~Logger
~Plugin
  • A class with at least one pure virtual function is abstract: no objects of it can be created.
  • A derived class that doesn't override all pure virtuals is abstract too.
  • A pure virtual function may have a definition, callable as Base::f(). A pure virtual destructor must have one.

Virtual calls inside constructors and destructors

While the Base constructor runs, the Derived part doesn't exist yet, so the object's dynamic type is Base; virtual calls go to Base's version. The same happens in reverse during destruction.

C++verified run
struct Base {
    Base() { hello(); }                        // calls Base::hello, NOT Derived::hello
    virtual void hello() const { cout << "hello from Base\n"; }
    void later() const { hello(); }            // normal virtual dispatch
    virtual ~Base() { hello(); }               // Base::hello again
};
struct Derived : Base {
    void hello() const override { cout << "hello from Derived\n"; }
};
// in main:
Derived d;
d.later();
Output
hello from Base
hello from Derived
hello from Base

Calling a pure virtual function from a constructor or destructor is undefined behaviour (g++ aborts with "pure virtual method called").

Default arguments are bound statically

C++verified run
struct Base {
    virtual void show(int x = 1) const { cout << "Base " << x << '\n'; }
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};
struct Derived : Base {
    void show(int x = 2) const override { cout << "Derived " << x << '\n'; }
};
// in main:
Derived d;
Base& b = d;
b.show();      // runs Derived::show with Base's default: 1
d.show();
Output
Derived 1
Derived 2

The function is chosen at run time, but the default argument is filled in at compile time from the static type. Never give an override a different default.

Can these be virtual?

Virtual? Why
Constructor No No object (and no vptr) exists yet to dispatch on; use a virtual clone() or a factory
Destructor Yes, and should be in polymorphic bases So delete base_ptr destroys the whole object
Static member function No No object, no this, nothing to dispatch on
Friend function No (it isn't a member) Can call a virtual member to get the effect
Inline function Yes Inlined only when the call is resolved statically
Private function Yes Overriding ignores access; the Non-Virtual Interface pattern uses this
Template member function No The vtable would need a slot for every possible instantiation

The virtual constructor idiom: clone()

C++verified run
struct Shape {
    virtual unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;
    virtual string name() const = 0;
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
};
struct Circle : Shape {
    double r = 2;
    unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const override { return make_unique<Circle>(*this); }
    string name() const override { return "circle r=" + to_string(int(r)); }
};
// in main:
unique_ptr<Shape> original = make_unique<Circle>();
unique_ptr<Shape> copy = original->clone();   // copies the right dynamic type
cout << copy->name() << '\n';
Output
circle r=2

With raw pointers, an override may return a pointer to the derived type (Circle* clone() const override) — a covariant return type.

RTTI: typeid and dynamic_cast

Run-time type information lets you ask an object's dynamic type. It only works on polymorphic types (classes with at least one virtual function).

C++verified run
struct Vehicle { virtual ~Vehicle() = default; };
struct Car : Vehicle { void honk() const { cout << "beep\n"; } };
struct Bike : Vehicle {};
// in main:
vector<unique_ptr<Vehicle>> garage;
garage.push_back(make_unique<Car>());
garage.push_back(make_unique<Bike>());
for (auto& v : garage) {
    if (auto* c = dynamic_cast<Car*>(v.get()))     // nullptr if v isn't a Car
        c->honk();
    else
        cout << "not a car\n";
    cout << boolalpha << (typeid(*v) == typeid(Car)) << '\n';
}
Bike b;
Vehicle& ref = b;
try {
    Car& c = dynamic_cast<Car&>(ref);              // references can't be null: it throws
    c.honk();
} catch (const bad_cast&) {
    cout << "bad_cast\n";
}
Output
beep
true
not a car
false
bad_cast
  • dynamic_cast<T*> returns nullptr on failure; dynamic_cast<T&> throws std::bad_cast.
  • It walks the class hierarchy at run time, so it's slower than static_cast. Needing it often is a design smell: a virtual function usually does the job better.
  • typeid(x).name() is implementation-defined (g++ prints mangled names like 3Car); compare type_info objects instead.
  • -fno-rtti disables RTTI (common in games and embedded code) — then dynamic_cast and typeid on polymorphic types don't compile.

Cost of virtual functions

  1. Space: one vptr per object (8 bytes), one vtable per class.
  2. Time: an extra memory load and an indirect call; the CPU's branch predictor usually guesses the target well.
  3. Lost optimizations: a call through a vtable can't be inlined unless the compiler can prove the dynamic type (final, local objects, whole-program optimization).

For hot inner loops, alternatives are templates (static polymorphism, e.g. CRTP in section 27) or std::variant with std::visit (section 22).

Interview questions

QWhat is a virtual function?

A member function declared with virtual whose call, made through a base-class pointer or reference, is resolved at run time according to the dynamic type of the object. It's how C++ implements run-time polymorphism.

QHow are virtual functions implemented?

Each polymorphic class gets a vtable — an array of pointers to its virtual function implementations. Each object stores a hidden vptr to its class's vtable, set by the constructor. A virtual call loads the vptr, reads the right slot and calls through it.

QHow many vtables and vptrs are there?

One vtable per polymorphic class (shared by all its objects), and one vptr per object (more with multiple inheritance — one per polymorphic base subobject). The vptr is usually at offset 0.

QWhy must a base class destructor be virtual?

If you delete a derived object through a base pointer and the destructor isn't virtual, behaviour is undefined — typically only the base destructor runs and the derived part's resources leak. A virtual destructor makes delete dispatch to the derived destructor, which then calls the base one.

QCan a constructor be virtual?

No. To make a virtual call you need an object whose vptr is set — and that's exactly what the constructor creates. Also, at construction you already know the exact type you're building. Use a virtual clone() or a factory function.

QWhat happens when you call a virtual function from a constructor?

It calls the version of the class whose constructor is running, not the most derived override, because the derived part hasn't been constructed yet (the vptr points to the current class's vtable). The same applies in destructors. Calling a pure virtual this way is undefined.

QWhat is a pure virtual function? Can it have a body?

A virtual function declared = 0, which makes the class abstract and forces concrete derived classes to override it. It can have a body, callable explicitly as Base::f(); a pure virtual destructor must have one.

QWhat do override and final do?

override makes the compiler verify that the function overrides a base virtual function with the same signature — catching typos and const mismatches. final on a virtual function forbids overriding it further; on a class, forbids deriving from it. Both are C++11.

QWhich default argument is used when calling a virtual function through a base reference?

The base class's. Default arguments are substituted at compile time from the static type, while the function body is chosen at run time. So the derived function runs with the base default.

QWhat is the cost of a virtual function?

A vptr per object (8 bytes), a vtable per class, an extra load and indirect branch per call, and usually no inlining. In most code it's negligible; in tight loops over millions of objects it can matter.

QWhat is RTTI? What are typeid and dynamic_cast?

Run-time type information about polymorphic objects. typeid(expr) returns a std::type_info describing the dynamic type. dynamic_cast safely converts pointers/references within a hierarchy, checking the dynamic type at run time and returning nullptr (pointers) or throwing bad_cast (references) on failure.

Qdynamic_cast vs static_cast for downcasting?

dynamic_cast checks at run time and fails safely, but needs a polymorphic type and costs a hierarchy walk. static_cast does no check: it's free, but if the object isn't really of the target type the result is undefined behaviour. Use static_cast only when you know the type for sure.

QCan a static function be virtual? Can a virtual function be private?

Static: no — it has no object to dispatch on. Private: yes; access control is checked at the call site using the static type, but overriding works regardless. The Non-Virtual Interface pattern relies on this: public non-virtual function calls a private virtual hook.

QWhat is a covariant return type?

An override may return a pointer or reference to a class derived from the base version's return type: Base* clone() can be overridden as Derived* clone(). It doesn't apply to smart pointers, which are unrelated class types.

QWhat is the difference between overloading and overriding?

Overloading: same name, different parameters, in the same scope; resolved at compile time. Overriding: a derived class redefines a base virtual function with the same signature; resolved at run time through the vtable.

QWhat is the size of an object with virtual functions?

Its data members plus one vptr (8 bytes on 64-bit), rounded up for alignment. A class with only a double member is 8 bytes; add any number of virtual functions and it becomes 16.

10copy constructor · operator= · lvalues · rvalues · std::move · RVO · forwarding18 questions

Copy, Move & the Rule of 0/3/5

The six special member functions and when the compiler writes them, shallow vs deep copy, copy-and-swap, lvalues and rvalues, move semantics, why moves must be noexcept, copy elision, perfect forwarding, and the rules of three, five and zero.

The six special member functions

Function Signature for class X Compiler generates it when…
Default constructor X() You declare no constructor at all
Destructor ~X() You don't declare one
Copy constructor X(const X&) You don't declare one and declare no move operation
Copy assignment X& operator=(const X&) Same as copy constructor
Move constructor C++11 X(X&&) noexcept You declare none of: copy constructor, copy assignment, move assignment, destructor
Move assignment C++11 X& operator=(X&&) noexcept Same as move constructor

The generated versions work member by member: copy each member, move each member, destroy each member. That's perfect when every member manages itself (string, vector, unique_ptr) and wrong when a member is a raw owning pointer.

RememberThe generation rules in one line each

Declare a destructor or a copy operation → no implicit moves (moves silently become copies). Declare a move operation → the copy operations are deleted. Declare any constructor → no implicit default constructor.

Shallow vs deep copy

A class owning a raw pointer gets a shallow copy by default: both objects hold the same address, and both destructors delete[] it — a double free.

C++verified run
class Buffer {
    char* data;
    size_t len;
public:
    explicit Buffer(const char* s) : data(new char[strlen(s) + 1]), len(strlen(s)) {
        strcpy(data, s);
    }
    Buffer(const Buffer& other)                    // DEEP copy: allocate and copy the bytes
        : data(new char[other.len + 1]), len(other.len) {
        strcpy(data, other.data);
        cout << "deep copy\n";
    }
    Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& other) {       // copy assignment
        if (this != &other) {                      // guard against self-assignment
            char* fresh = new char[other.len + 1]; // allocate first: if new throws, *this is untouched
            strcpy(fresh, other.data);
            delete[] data;
            data = fresh;
            len = other.len;
        }
        cout << "copy assign\n";
        return *this;
    }
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data; }
    void set(size_t i, char c) { data[i] = c; }
    const char* str() const { return data; }
};
// in main:
Buffer a("hello");
Buffer b = a;          // copy constructor
b.set(0, 'J');
Buffer c("x");
c = a;                 // copy assignment
c = c;                 // self-assignment is harmless
cout << a.str() << ' ' << b.str() << ' ' << c.str() << '\n';
Output
deep copy
copy assign
copy assign
hello Jello hello

Delete the copy constructor and assignment above and the program crashes with a double free — AddressSanitizer reports it immediately.

Why the copy constructor takes const X&

C++compile error
struct X {
    X() = default;
    X(X other) {}      // by value: copying the argument would need... the copy constructor
};
g++ says
error: invalid constructor; you probably meant 'X (const X&)'

By value it would recurse forever, so the language forbids it. By reference avoids the copy, and const lets you copy from const objects and temporaries.

Copy-and-swap

A simpler, exception-safe way to write assignment: take the argument by value (the copy happens there), then swap.

C++verified run
class Text {
    char* p;
public:
    Text(const char* s = "") : p(new char[strlen(s) + 1]) { strcpy(p, s); }
    Text(const Text& o) : Text(o.p ? o.p : "") {}
    Text(Text&& o) noexcept : p(exchange(o.p, nullptr)) {}
    ~Text() { delete[] p; }
    friend void swap(Text& a, Text& b) noexcept { std::swap(a.p, b.p); }
    Text& operator=(Text other) noexcept {   // copy (or move) made when the argument is passed
        swap(*this, other);                  // take its contents
        return *this;                        // other's destructor frees our old buffer
    }
    const char* get() const { return p ? p : "(empty)"; }
};
// in main:
Text a("alpha"), b("beta");
a = b;                   // copy-assigns
a = a;                   // self-assignment: works without a check
Text c;
c = std::move(b);        // move-assigns through the same operator
cout << a.get() << ' ' << b.get() << ' ' << c.get() << '\n';
Output
beta (empty) beta

It gives the strong exception guarantee (if copying throws, *this is untouched), handles self-assignment, and one operator serves both copy and move assignment.

lvalues and rvalues

  • An lvalue has an identity you can take the address of: a variable, *p, a[i], a function returning T&.
  • An rvalue is a temporary about to vanish: a literal, a + b, a function returning by value, std::move(x).
  • C++11 splits rvalues into prvalues (pure temporaries) and xvalues ("expiring" objects, like std::move(x)).
C++verified run
void take(int& x)        { cout << "lvalue ref\n"; }
void take(const int& x)  { cout << "const lvalue ref\n"; }
void take(int&& x)       { cout << "rvalue ref\n"; }
int make() { return 7; }
// in main:
int a = 1;
const int c = 2;
take(a);              // lvalue
take(c);              // const lvalue
take(10);             // literal: rvalue
take(make());         // returned by value: rvalue
take(a + 1);          // expression result: rvalue
take(std::move(a));   // cast to rvalue
int&& r = 5;
take(r);              // a NAMED rvalue reference is itself an lvalue!
Output
lvalue ref
const lvalue ref
rvalue ref
rvalue ref
rvalue ref
rvalue ref
lvalue ref

Move semantics

Copying a vector of a million elements allocates and copies a million elements. Moving it just takes over the pointer, size and capacity — three word-sized copies — and leaves the source empty. A move constructor X(X&&) steals resources from an rvalue that is about to die anyway.

C++verified run
class Image {
    int* pixels;
    size_t n;
public:
    explicit Image(size_t count) : pixels(new int[count]()), n(count) {}
    Image(const Image& o) : pixels(new int[o.n]), n(o.n) {        // copy: O(n)
        copy(o.pixels, o.pixels + n, pixels);
        cout << "copied " << n << " pixels\n";
    }
    Image(Image&& o) noexcept : pixels(o.pixels), n(o.n) {        // move: O(1)
        o.pixels = nullptr;                                       // leave the source empty
        o.n = 0;
        cout << "moved\n";
    }
    Image& operator=(Image&& o) noexcept {
        if (this != &o) {
            delete[] pixels;
            pixels = exchange(o.pixels, nullptr);
            n = exchange(o.n, 0);
        }
        cout << "move-assigned\n";
        return *this;
    }
    Image& operator=(const Image&) = delete;                      // keep the example short
    ~Image() { delete[] pixels; }
    size_t size() const { return n; }
};
// in main:
Image a(1'000'000);
Image b = a;               // copy
Image c = std::move(a);    // move: a is now empty
Image d(10);
d = std::move(b);          // move assignment
cout << a.size() << ' ' << b.size() << ' ' << c.size() << ' ' << d.size() << '\n';
Output
copied 1000000 pixels
moved
move-assigned
0 0 1000000 1000000

std::move doesn't move

std::move(x) is just static_cast<T&&>(x): it marks x as movable so overload resolution picks the move constructor or move assignment. If the type has no move operations, or x is const, the copy happens instead.

PitfallMoving from a const object copies

const string s = "..."; string t = std::move(s); compiles but copies: std::move(s) is a const string&&, which can't bind to string&&, so the copy constructor (const string&) is chosen. Don't make objects const if you plan to move from them.

A moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state: you may destroy it or assign a new value to it, but don't assume its contents (standard containers are in practice empty).

Why moves should be noexcept

When a vector grows, it must transfer its elements to a new buffer without breaking its strong exception guarantee. It only moves them if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies (std::move_if_noexcept).

C++verified run
struct Safe {
    Safe() = default;
    Safe(const Safe&) { cout << "copy "; }
    Safe(Safe&&) noexcept { cout << "move "; }
};
struct Unsafe {
    Unsafe() = default;
    Unsafe(const Unsafe&) { cout << "copy "; }
    Unsafe(Unsafe&&) { cout << "move "; }           // may throw (as far as vector knows)
};
// in main:
vector<Safe> a;
a.reserve(2); a.emplace_back(); a.emplace_back();
a.emplace_back();                                   // reallocation: existing elements are MOVED
cout << '\n';
vector<Unsafe> b;
b.reserve(2); b.emplace_back(); b.emplace_back();
b.emplace_back();                                   // reallocation: existing elements are COPIED
cout << '\n';
Output
move move 
copy copy

Copy elision: RVO and NRVO

C++verified run
struct Tracer {
    Tracer() { cout << "construct\n"; }
    Tracer(const Tracer&) { cout << "copy\n"; }
    Tracer(Tracer&&) noexcept { cout << "move\n"; }
};
Tracer rvo()  { return Tracer(); }          // returns a prvalue: elision GUARANTEED (C++17)
Tracer nrvo() { Tracer t; return t; }       // named: elision allowed, done by g++ in practice
Tracer forced() { Tracer t; return std::move(t); }   // blocks NRVO: forces a move
// in main:
cout << "-- rvo\n";    Tracer a = rvo();
cout << "-- nrvo\n";   Tracer b = nrvo();
cout << "-- forced\n"; Tracer c = forced();
Output
-- rvo
construct
-- nrvo
construct
-- forced
construct
move
  • RVO: when a function returns a temporary (a prvalue), C++17 guarantees the object is built directly in the caller's storage — no copy, no move, and copy/move constructors needn't even exist.
  • NRVO: returning a named local can also be elided; compilers do it whenever every return statement returns the same local, but it isn't guaranteed. If it isn't elided, the return is treated as a move automatically.
  • So never write return std::move(local); — it disables NRVO (g++ warns with -Wpessimizing-move).
C++verified run
struct Pinned {
    Pinned() = default;
    Pinned(const Pinned&) = delete;
    Pinned(Pinned&&) = delete;
};
Pinned make() { return Pinned{}; }   // OK in C++17: nothing is copied or moved
// in main:
Pinned p = make();
cout << "guaranteed elision works even for non-movable types\n";
Output
guaranteed elision works even for non-movable types

The rules of three, five and zero

  • Rule of three (C++98): if a class needs a user-written destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it almost certainly needs all three — it's managing a resource.
  • Rule of five (C++11): add the move constructor and move assignment, or the class will copy where it could move.
  • Rule of zero: best of all, write none of them. Hold resources in members that already manage themselves, and the compiler-generated versions are correct, exception-safe and move-enabled.
C++verified run
class Document {                               // rule of zero
    string title;
    vector<string> lines;
    unique_ptr<int[]> scratch = make_unique<int[]>(16);   // move-only member
public:
    explicit Document(string t) : title(std::move(t)) {}
    void add(string line) { lines.push_back(std::move(line)); }
    size_t count() const { return lines.size(); }
};
// in main:
Document d("notes");
d.add("first");
Document moved = std::move(d);                 // generated move constructor: just works
cout << moved.count() << ' ' << d.count() << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << is_copy_constructible_v<Document> << ' '
     << is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<Document> << '\n';
Output
1 0
false true

Document isn't copyable because unique_ptr isn't — the compiler deletes the copy constructor for you. To make any class non-copyable on purpose: X(const X&) = delete; X& operator=(const X&) = delete;.

Perfect forwarding

In a template, T&& with T deduced is a forwarding reference (also called a universal reference): it binds to anything. Reference collapsing decides the result — if either side is &, the result is &:

T deduced as T&& becomes
int& (lvalue passed) int& && → int&
int (rvalue passed) int&&

std::forward<T>(arg) casts back to an rvalue only if an rvalue was passed, so the callee sees the original value category.

C++verified run
void sink(const string& s) { cout << "copied: " << s << '\n'; }
void sink(string&& s)      { cout << "moved: " << s << '\n'; }

template <typename T>
void relay(T&& arg) {                 // forwarding reference
    sink(std::forward<T>(arg));       // keeps lvalue as lvalue, rvalue as rvalue
}
template <typename T, typename... Args>
unique_ptr<T> build(Args&&... args) { // how make_unique is written
    return unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
}
// in main:
string name = "Sai";
relay(name);                          // lvalue
relay(string("temp"));                // rvalue
relay(std::move(name));               // rvalue
auto p = build<pair<string, int>>("age", 21);
cout << p->first << '=' << p->second << '\n';
Output
copied: Sai
moved: temp
moved: Sai
age=21

std::move unconditionally casts to an rvalue; std::forward conditionally casts, only when the original argument was an rvalue. Use move on things you own and are done with, forward on forwarding references.

Interview questions

QWhat is a copy constructor and when is it called?

A constructor X(const X&) that creates a new object as a copy of an existing one. It's called for X b = a; and X b(a);, when passing an object by value, when returning by value if the copy isn't elided, and when a container copies elements.

QWhy is the copy constructor's parameter a reference? Why const?

If it took the object by value, passing the argument would itself need a copy — infinite recursion — so it's ill-formed. const allows copying from const objects and temporaries and promises not to modify the source.

QWhat is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy?

A shallow copy copies member values as they are, so two objects end up sharing the same heap memory through copied pointers — leading to double frees and aliasing bugs. A deep copy allocates new memory and copies the pointed-to data, so each object owns its own. The default copy is shallow; write a deep copy (or use RAII members) when a class owns raw memory.

QWhen is the copy constructor called and when is the assignment operator called?

The copy constructor runs when a new object is being created from an existing one (X b = a;). Copy assignment runs when an existing object is given a new value (b = a;). The = sign in a declaration is initialization, not assignment.

QHow do you handle self-assignment?

Either check if (this != &other) at the top, or use copy-and-swap, where self-assignment is naturally safe. Without care, delete[] data followed by copying from other.data would read freed memory when other is *this.

QWhat is the copy-and-swap idiom?

Implement assignment as X& operator=(X other) { swap(*this, other); return *this; }. The by-value parameter makes the copy (or move); swapping is noexcept; the old contents are freed when other is destroyed. It's exception-safe (strong guarantee), handles self-assignment, and serves as both copy and move assignment.

QWhat is the rule of three / five / zero?

Three: a class that needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment usually needs all three. Five: in C++11 also the move constructor and move assignment. Zero: prefer designing classes that need none of them, by owning resources through members like vector, string and unique_ptr.

QWhat are lvalues and rvalues?

An lvalue refers to an object with identity that persists beyond the expression — you can take its address (x, *p, v[0]). An rvalue is a temporary or a value about to expire (42, a + b, f() returning by value, std::move(x)). Lvalue references T& bind to lvalues; rvalue references T&& bind to rvalues; const T& binds to both.

QWhat is move semantics and why is it faster?

Transferring ownership of resources from an object that's about to be discarded instead of duplicating them. Moving a vector copies three pointers and nulls the source's, O(1), instead of allocating and copying every element, O(n). It also enables move-only types like unique_ptr and thread.

QWhat does std::move do?

Nothing at run time: it's an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference, static_cast<T&&>(x). It lets overload resolution pick a move constructor or move assignment. The actual moving is done by those functions — and if none exists, the copy is used.

QWhat state is an object in after it has been moved from?

Valid but unspecified: its invariants hold, so it can be destroyed or assigned to, but you shouldn't rely on its value. Standard library types define some cases (a moved-from unique_ptr is null); a moved-from vector or string is empty in all major implementations.

QWhy should a move constructor be noexcept?

Because containers use move_if_noexcept: when vector reallocates, it moves elements only if the move can't throw — otherwise a throw halfway would leave both buffers partly moved and break its strong exception guarantee — so it copies instead. A non-noexcept move constructor silently turns every reallocation into copies.

QWhat is RVO? What changed in C++17?

Return value optimization: the compiler constructs a function's return value directly in the caller's object, skipping the copy/move. C++17 made it mandatory for prvalues (return X(args);), so it works even for types that can't be copied or moved. Named RVO (X x; ...; return x;) is still optional but universally done; if it isn't, the return falls back to a move.

QShould you write return std::move(local);?

No. It turns the return expression into an xvalue, which disables NRVO and forces a move constructor call. Plain return local; gets NRVO or, failing that, an implicit move — and by-value parameters are implicitly moved on return too. std::move in a return statement only makes sense for something that isn't a local, such as moving a data member out of an object you're finished with.

QWhat is perfect forwarding?

Passing arguments from a function template to another function while preserving whether each was an lvalue or an rvalue (and its constness), using a forwarding reference T&& and std::forward<T>(arg). It's how make_unique, emplace_back and std::thread pass your arguments on without extra copies.

QWhat is the difference between an rvalue reference and a forwarding reference?

string&& or vector<int>&& with a concrete type is an rvalue reference: it binds only rvalues. T&& where T is a deduced template parameter (or auto&&) is a forwarding reference: it binds anything, and T encodes whether an lvalue or rvalue was passed.

Qstd::move vs std::forward?

move always casts to an rvalue — use it when you're done with an object you own. forward<T> casts to an rvalue only if the original argument was an rvalue — use it only on forwarding references inside templates.

QHow do you make a class non-copyable, or move-only?

Delete the copy operations: X(const X&) = delete; X& operator=(const X&) = delete;. To keep it movable, also declare (or default) the move constructor and move assignment. unique_ptr, thread, fstream and mutex (not even movable) are examples.

11member vs friend · << >> · <=> · ++ · [] · () · conversions12 questions

Operator Overloading

The rules of operator overloading, which operators can't be overloaded, member vs non-member operators, a complete Fraction class, prefix and postfix ++, subscript, function-call and conversion operators, and C++20's spaceship operator.

The rules

  • An overloaded operator is a function named operator@: Fraction operator+(const Fraction&, const Fraction&).
  • At least one operand must be a class or enum type — you can't redefine int + int.
  • You can't invent new operators, change precedence, associativity or the number of operands.
  • &&, || and , can be overloaded but then lose short-circuiting/sequencing — don't.
  • Overloads should do what the operator obviously means; + that subtracts is legal and terrible.
Can't be overloaded
:: scope resolution
. and .* member access
?: conditional
sizeof, alignof, typeid compile-time / type operators
static_cast and the other named casts
#, ## preprocessor operators
Must be member functions
= assignment
[] subscript
() function call
-> member access through pointer
conversion operators operator bool(), operator double()

Member or non-member?

  • Member: the left operand is always an object of your class. Use for =, [], (), ->, compound assignment (+=), and unary operators.
  • Non-member (often a friend): when the left operand isn't your class — cout << f (left is ostream) or 2 * f (left is int) — and for symmetric binary operators, so implicit conversions work on both sides.
  • Idiom: implement += as a member, then + as a non-member that copies and uses +=.

A complete example: Fraction

C++verified run
class Fraction {
    long long num, den;
    void normalize() {
        if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; }
        long long g = gcd(llabs(num), den);
        if (g) { num /= g; den /= g; }
    }
public:
    Fraction(long long n = 0, long long d = 1) : num(n), den(d) {   // implicit from int: 2 → 2/1
        if (d == 0) throw invalid_argument("zero denominator");
        normalize();
    }
    Fraction& operator+=(const Fraction& o) {          // compound: member, returns *this
        num = num * o.den + o.num * den;
        den *= o.den;
        normalize();
        return *this;
    }
    Fraction& operator*=(const Fraction& o) { num *= o.num; den *= o.den; normalize(); return *this; }
    Fraction operator-() const { return Fraction(-num, den); }     // unary minus
    Fraction& operator++() { num += den; return *this; }           // prefix ++f
    Fraction operator++(int) { Fraction old = *this; ++*this; return old; }   // postfix f++
    explicit operator double() const { return double(num) / den; }  // conversion, explicit

    friend Fraction operator+(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a += b; }   // symmetric
    friend Fraction operator*(Fraction a, const Fraction& b) { return a *= b; }
    friend bool operator==(const Fraction&, const Fraction&) = default;          // C++20
    friend auto operator<=>(const Fraction& a, const Fraction& b) {               // C++20
        return a.num * b.den <=> b.num * a.den;
    }
    friend ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const Fraction& f) {   // left operand is ostream
        return os << f.num << '/' << f.den;
    }
    friend istream& operator>>(istream& is, Fraction& f) {
        char slash;
        long long n, d;
        if (is >> n >> slash >> d) f = Fraction(n, d);
        return is;
    }
};
// in main:
Fraction a(1, 2), b(1, 3);
cout << a + b << ' ' << a * b << ' ' << -a << '\n';
cout << 2 + a << ' ' << a + 2 << '\n';            // works both ways: non-member +
Fraction c(3, 4);
cout << c++ << ' ' << c << ' ' << ++c << '\n';    // postfix returns the old value
cout << boolalpha << (a < b) << ' ' << (a == Fraction(2, 4)) << ' ' << (a != b) << '\n';
cout << static_cast<double>(b) << '\n';
stringstream in("5/10");
Fraction d;
in >> d;
cout << d << '\n';
Output
5/6 1/6 -1/2
5/2 5/2
3/4 7/4 11/4
false true true
0.333333
1/2

Points interviewers look for:

  • operator<< returns the stream by reference so calls chain (cout << a << b), and takes the object by const&.
  • Prefix ++ returns *this by reference; postfix takes a dummy int parameter and returns the old value by value — which is why ++it can be cheaper than it++.
  • Compound assignment returns *this by reference; binary + returns a new object by value.
  • explicit operator double() means double x = f; doesn't compile but static_cast<double>(f) does.

The spaceship operator <=> C++20

One three-way comparison gives you <, <=, >, >=; a defaulted == gives you !=. Defaulting both compares members in declaration order, lexicographically.

C++verified run
struct Version {
    int major, minor, patch;
    auto operator<=>(const Version&) const = default;   // also generates ==
};
// in main:
vector<Version> vs{{1, 2, 3}, {1, 10, 0}, {0, 9, 9}};
sort(vs.begin(), vs.end());
for (auto& v : vs) cout << v.major << '.' << v.minor << '.' << v.patch << ' ';
cout << '\n' << boolalpha << (Version{1, 2, 3} == Version{1, 2, 3}) << ' '
     << (Version{2, 0, 0} > Version{1, 99, 99}) << '\n';
Output
0.9.9 1.2.3 1.10.0 
true true

<=> returns std::strong_ordering (less, equal, greater) for types like int, std::weak_ordering when equivalent values may differ, and std::partial_ordering when some values are unordered (floating-point NaN).

Subscript, function call and smart access

C++verified run
class Matrix {
    size_t rows, cols;
    vector<double> cells;
public:
    Matrix(size_t r, size_t c) : rows(r), cols(c), cells(r * c) {}
    double& operator()(size_t r, size_t c) { return cells[r * cols + c]; }        // m(1, 2) = 5
    double operator()(size_t r, size_t c) const { return cells[r * cols + c]; }
};
class SafeArray {
    vector<int> v;
public:
    explicit SafeArray(size_t n) : v(n) {}
    int& operator[](size_t i) {                        // non-const: allows a[i] = x
        if (i >= v.size()) throw out_of_range("index " + to_string(i));
        return v[i];
    }
    const int& operator[](size_t i) const { return v.at(i); }   // const objects: read-only
};
struct GreaterThan {                                   // a functor: object with operator()
    int limit;
    bool operator()(int x) const { return x > limit; }
};
// in main:
Matrix m(2, 3);
m(1, 2) = 5.5;
cout << m(1, 2) << '\n';
SafeArray a(3);
a[0] = 42;
cout << a[0] << '\n';
try { a[5] = 1; } catch (const out_of_range& e) { cout << "caught " << e.what() << '\n'; }
vector<int> v{3, 8, 1, 9, 4};
cout << count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), GreaterThan{3}) << '\n';
Output
5.5
42
caught index 5
3

Function objects (functors) carry state and are easily inlined, which is why the STL takes comparators and predicates as objects — lambdas are just a shorter way to write them (section 20).

Canonical signatures

Operator Canonical form
Copy assignment X& operator=(const X&)
Move assignment X& operator=(X&&) noexcept
Compound (+=) X& operator+=(const X&) — member
Binary (+) X operator+(X lhs, const X& rhs) — non-member, return lhs += rhs;
Equality bool operator==(const X&) const (or = default in C++20)
Three-way auto operator<=>(const X&) const = default
Stream out / in ostream& operator<<(ostream&, const X&) / istream& operator>>(istream&, X&)
Prefix / postfix ++ X& operator++() / X operator++(int)
Subscript T& operator[](size_t) plus const T& operator[](size_t) const
Conversion explicit operator bool() const

Interview questions

QWhat is operator overloading? Is it compile-time or run-time polymorphism?

Giving operators custom meaning for user-defined types by writing functions named operator+, operator<<, etc. Overload resolution picks the right one at compile time, so it's compile-time polymorphism (unless the operator function itself is virtual).

QWhich operators can't be overloaded?

::, ., .*, ?:, sizeof, alignof, typeid, the named casts, and the preprocessor's # and ##.

QWhy is operator<< usually a non-member friend?

Its left operand is the ostream, not your class, so it can't be a member of your class (it would have to be a member of ostream). It's made a friend when it needs private members. It returns ostream& so output can chain.

QWhen should a binary operator be a member and when a non-member?

Non-member when the left operand may not be your type (2 * f, cout << f) or when you want implicit conversions on both operands — a member operator+ would accept f + 2 but not 2 + f. Members for =, [], (), ->, conversions (required) and for compound assignment and unary operators.

QHow do you distinguish prefix and postfix ++?

Postfix takes a dummy int parameter: X operator++(int). Prefix is X& operator++(). Postfix copies the old value, increments, and returns the copy by value; prefix increments and returns *this by reference.

QWhy does operator= return X&?

To allow chaining (a = b = c, which is a = (b = c)) and to match built-in types' behaviour. Returning by value would make an unnecessary copy.

QWhat is a functor?

An object of a class that overloads operator(), so it can be called like a function. Unlike a function pointer it can hold state (GreaterThan{3}) and its call is easily inlined. STL comparators and predicates are typically functors or lambdas.

QWhat is a conversion operator, and why make it explicit?

A member like operator double() const that converts an object to another type. Non-explicit conversions happen silently in arithmetic, comparisons and overload resolution, causing surprises; explicit requires a cast. explicit operator bool() is still used automatically in if (x) and while (x) contexts.

QWhat does C++20's <=> do?

It's the three-way comparison: a <=> b returns an ordering that says less, equal or greater. Defining (or defaulting) <=> lets the compiler rewrite <, <=, > and >= in terms of it, and a defaulted == gives !=, so one or two declarations replace six operators.

QWhy should you avoid overloading &&, || and ,?

The built-in versions guarantee short-circuit evaluation and left-to-right sequencing. Overloaded versions are ordinary function calls, so both operands are always evaluated, which surprises everyone reading the code.

QCan you overload operators for built-in types only?

No. At least one operand must be a user-defined type (class or enum); int operator+(int, int) isn't allowed.

QWhy provide both const and non-const operator[]?

The non-const version returns T& so a[i] = x works on modifiable objects. The const version returns const T& (or T) so const objects can still be read but not written.

12const · constexpr · static · extern · volatile · mutable · the four casts15 questions

const, static, Casts & Other Keywords

Const-correctness, const vs constexpr vs consteval vs constinit, the four meanings of static, linkage and extern, volatile, the four C++ casts and the C-style cast, attributes, and storage durations.

const everywhere

C++verified run
class Inventory {
    vector<int> items{5, 3, 8};
public:
    int total() const {                       // const member: callable on const objects
        return accumulate(items.begin(), items.end(), 0);
    }
    int& at(size_t i) { return items[i]; }               // non-const overload: writable
    const int& at(size_t i) const { return items[i]; }   // const overload: read-only
};
void report(const Inventory& inv) {           // const&: no copy, no modification
    cout << inv.total() << ' ' << inv.at(0) << '\n';     // picks the const at()
}
// in main:
Inventory inv;
inv.at(0) = 10;                               // picks the non-const at()
report(inv);
const int limit = 100;                        // a constant
const int* p = &limit;                        // pointer to const (section 04)
cout << *p << '\n';
Output
21 10
100
  • Const-correctness: mark everything that shouldn't change as const — parameters taken by reference, member functions that only read, local values. The compiler then enforces it, and const objects can only call const member functions.
  • const participates in overloading for member functions (at() above) and for reference parameters.
  • Returning a const value (const string f()) is pointless and blocks moves; return by plain value.

const vs constexpr vs consteval vs constinit

Keyword Means Example
const Can't be modified after initialization; the value may be known only at run time const int n = read();
constexpr C++11 Value (or function result) can be computed at compile time; a constexpr variable must be constexpr int N = 1 << 10;
consteval C++20 Function must be evaluated at compile time ("immediate function") consteval int sq(int x) { return x * x; }
constinit C++20 A static/thread-local variable must be initialized at compile time, but stays mutable constinit int counter = 0;
C++verified run
constexpr int cube(int x) { return x * x * x; }
consteval int square_ct(int x) { return x * x; }
constinit int hits = 0;                      // static storage, compile-time init, still mutable
// in main:
constexpr int a = cube(3);                   // compile time
int n = 4;
int b = cube(n);                             // run time: same function
int arr[square_ct(3)];                       // array size must be a constant
hits++;
cout << a << ' ' << b << ' ' << size(arr) << ' ' << hits << '\n';
Output
27 64 9 1

The four meanings of static

Where Meaning
Local variable in a function Static storage duration: initialized once (thread-safely), keeps its value between calls
Global variable or free function Internal linkage: visible only in this translation unit (prefer an unnamed namespace)
Data member of a class One copy shared by all objects of the class
Member function of a class Belongs to the class: no this, called as X::f()
C++verified run
static int file_private = 1;            // internal linkage: other .cpp files can't see it
namespace {                             // unnamed namespace: the modern equivalent
    int also_private = 2;
}
int calls() {
    static int n = 0;                   // static local
    return ++n;
}
struct Widget {
    static inline int created = 0;      // static data member (C++17 inline definition)
    Widget() { ++created; }
    static int count() { return created; }   // static member function
};
// in main:
calls(); calls();
Widget w1, w2, w3;
cout << file_private + also_private << ' ' << calls() << ' ' << Widget::count() << '\n';
Output
3 3 3

Linkage and extern

  • External linkage: the name can be used from other translation units (non-static functions and globals by default).
  • Internal linkage: only this translation unit (static globals, anything in an unnamed namespace, const globals by default).
  • No linkage: local variables.
  • extern int g; declares a global defined in another file; exactly one .cpp file must contain the definition int g = 0;. Since C++17, inline int g = 0; in a header is another way to share one variable.

volatile

volatile tells the compiler that every read and write of a variable is observable and must actually happen — it can't be cached in a register or optimized away. It's for memory-mapped hardware registers and signal handlers.

Pitfallvolatile is not for threads

volatile gives no atomicity and no ordering between threads; a volatile int incremented by two threads is still a data race (undefined behaviour). Use std::atomic or a mutex (sections 23–24). Java's volatile is a different thing.

The four C++ casts

Cast Use for Checked
static_cast<T>(x) Well-defined conversions: numeric types, void* back to T*, upcasts, downcasts you know are right, enums At compile time only
dynamic_cast<T>(x) Safe downcasts and cross-casts in polymorphic hierarchies At run time: nullptr or bad_cast on failure
const_cast<T>(x) Adding or removing const/volatile — e.g. calling an old API that forgot const No; writing to a really-const object through it is UB
reinterpret_cast<T>(x) Reinterpreting bits: pointer ↔ integer, unrelated pointer types No; platform-specific, often UB to use
C++verified run
double d = 9.99;
int i = static_cast<int>(d);                     // 9: truncates
enum class Color { Red, Green };
int g = static_cast<int>(Color::Green);
struct Base { virtual ~Base() = default; };
struct Derived : Base { int extra = 7; };
Base* bp = new Derived;
Derived* dp = static_cast<Derived*>(bp);         // OK only because it really IS a Derived
Derived* checked = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(bp);   // verified at run time
cout << i << ' ' << g << ' ' << dp->extra << ' ' << (checked == dp) << '\n';
delete bp;

const int secret = 42;
const int* cp = &secret;
int* writable = const_cast<int*>(cp);            // compiles — but writing *writable is UB
cout << *writable << '\n';

int value = 0x41424344;
char* bytes = reinterpret_cast<char*>(&value);   // look at the raw bytes
cout << bytes[0] << bytes[1] << bytes[2] << bytes[3] << '\n';   // little-endian: DCBA
uintptr_t addr = reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(&value);
cout << boolalpha << (addr != 0) << '\n';
Output
9 1 7 1
42
DCBA
true

C-style casts (T)x try const_cast, then static_cast, then static_cast + const_cast, then reinterpret_cast, then that plus const_cast — taking the first that compiles. So one innocent-looking (Derived*)p can silently become a reinterpret_cast. They're hard to search for, too. Prefer the named casts.

Attributes

Attribute Meaning
[[nodiscard]] C++17 Warn if the return value is ignored (e.g. vector::empty, error codes)
[[maybe_unused]] C++17 Silence "unused" warnings
[[fallthrough]] C++17 Intentional fall-through in a switch
[[likely]] / [[unlikely]] C++20 Branch-probability hints
[[noreturn]] C++11 The function never returns (std::exit, std::terminate)
[[deprecated("why")]] C++14 Warn on use
[[no_unique_address]] C++20 An empty member may take no space

Storage durations

Duration Objects Lifetime
Automatic Local variables, parameters Block entry to block exit
Static Globals, namespace-scope, static locals and members Program start (or first use, for static locals) to program end
Thread thread_local variables The thread's lifetime
Dynamic Objects from new new to delete
