Interview questions

QWhat is const-correctness?

Using const consistently for everything that shouldn't change — reference parameters, member functions that only read, objects that are never modified — so the compiler enforces read-only access and documents intent. It also matters for usability: a non-const member function can't be called on a const&.

QDifference between const and constexpr?

const means read-only after initialization; the value may come from run time. constexpr means the value is a compile-time constant (for variables) or the function can be evaluated at compile time. Every constexpr variable is implicitly const, but not the other way round.

QWhat does static mean in each context?

Static local: one instance kept across calls, initialized on first use. Static global or function: internal linkage, visible only in its file. Static data member: shared by all objects of the class. Static member function: no this, operates at class level.

QWhat is the difference between a global variable and a static global variable?

A plain global has external linkage — other translation units can use it via extern. A static global has internal linkage — it's private to its file, and another file can define its own variable with the same name without conflict.

QWhat does extern do?

It declares a variable (or function) without defining it, saying the definition is in some other translation unit. extern "C" additionally gives C linkage (no name mangling).

QExplain the four C++ casts.

static_cast for ordinary, compile-time-checked conversions (numeric, up/down the hierarchy when you know the type, void*). dynamic_cast for run-time-checked downcasts on polymorphic types. const_cast to add or remove const/volatile. reinterpret_cast for low-level bit reinterpretation between unrelated pointer types or pointers and integers.

QWhy prefer C++ casts over C-style casts?

C-style casts silently pick whichever of the C++ casts compiles, including dangerous reinterpret_casts and const_casts you didn't intend. Named casts state intent, are restricted to their purpose, and are easy to search for in code review.

QIs it safe to modify a variable after const_casting away its constness?

Only if the original object wasn't declared const. Casting away const from a reference to a non-const object and writing is fine; writing to an object that was defined const is undefined behaviour (it may sit in read-only memory, or the compiler may have folded its value into the code).

QWhat does volatile do? Can it be used for thread synchronization?

It forces every access to happen as written — no caching in registers, no elimination of "redundant" reads or writes — for hardware registers and signal handlers. It does not make operations atomic or order them across threads, so it's useless for synchronization; use std::atomic.

QWhat is mutable and where is it used?

It lets a member be modified inside const member functions. Used for state that doesn't affect the object's logical value: caches, memoized results, access counters, and mutexes locked inside const getters.

Qtypedef vs using?

Both create type aliases. using Name = Type; reads more naturally (especially for function pointers) and, unlike typedef, can be templated: template <class T> using Vec = vector<T>;.

QWhat is constinit?

A C++20 specifier for variables with static or thread storage duration that requires them to be initialized at compile time (avoiding the static initialization order problem) while leaving them modifiable, unlike constexpr.

QWhat is the difference between internal and external linkage?

A name with external linkage refers to the same entity across all translation units in the program; with internal linkage, each translation unit has its own private entity. Functions and non-const globals have external linkage by default; static and unnamed-namespace members have internal linkage.

QWhat is an unnamed (anonymous) namespace?

namespace { ... } — everything inside it has internal linkage and is unique to the translation unit. It's the modern replacement for static globals and also works for classes and types.

QWhat is the static initialization order fiasco?

Globals in different translation units are initialized in an unspecified order, so a global constructor that uses another file's global may see it uninitialized. Fixes: replace the global with a function returning a static local (initialized on first use), or use constinit/constexpr initialization.

Part 4Memory & Errors
13stack · heap · segments · new/delete · alignment · UB15 questions

Memory Layout, new/delete & Undefined Behaviour

Where every kind of object lives in a running process, stack vs heap, what new and delete really do, new vs malloc, placement new, leaks and how to find them, alignment and padding, and the undefined behaviour every C++ programmer must recognise.

The memory layout of a process

Segment Holds Lifetime
.text Machine code; read-only and shared between processes Whole program
.rodata String literals, const globals Whole program
.data Globals and statics with a non-zero initializer Whole program
.bss Globals and statics that are zero or uninitialized (take no space in the file) Whole program
Heap Everything from new / malloc Until delete / free
Stack Local variables, parameters, return addresses, saved registers Until the function returns

Stack vs heap

Stack Heap
Allocation Move the stack pointer: practically free Allocator searches free lists: slower, may call the OS
Freed Automatically at scope exit Manually (delete) or by RAII owners
Size Small: ~8 MB per thread on Linux, 1 MB on Windows Large: limited by RAM and address space
Fragmentation None Possible over time
Access pattern Hot in cache, contiguous Can be scattered
Thread Each thread has its own stack Shared by all threads
Failure Stack overflow → crash (segfault) std::bad_alloc thrown
PitfallBig arrays on the stack crash

int dp[10000000]; inside main needs 40 MB of stack and crashes with a segmentation fault before your first line runs. Make it a global (it goes in .bss), static, or a vector<int> dp(10000000); (heap). The same goes for very deep recursion — 10⁶ levels of DFS will overflow the default stack.

new and delete

new T(args) does two things: calls operator new(sizeof(T)) to get raw memory, then runs T's constructor on it. delete p runs the destructor, then calls operator delete to release the memory.

C++verified run
struct Node {
    int val;
    Node(int v) : val(v) { cout << "Node(" << v << ")\n"; }
    ~Node() { cout << "~Node(" << val << ")\n"; }
};
// in main:
Node* one = new Node(1);                 // single object
delete one;
Node* many = new Node[2]{Node(7), Node(8)};   // array: constructors for each element
delete[] many;                           // array form: destructors for each element
int* zeros = new int[5]();               // () value-initializes: all zero
int* junk = new int[5];                  // indeterminate values
cout << zeros[4] << '\n';
delete[] zeros;
delete[] junk;
int* safe = new (nothrow) int[10];       // returns nullptr instead of throwing
cout << boolalpha << (safe != nullptr) << '\n';
delete[] safe;
try {
    size_t huge = size_t(1) << 60;
    char* p = new char[huge];            // far more than the machine has
    p[0] = 'x';                          // (use it, so the optimizer can't drop the new)
    cout << p[0];
    delete[] p;
} catch (const bad_alloc& e) {
    cout << "bad_alloc caught\n";
}
Output
Node(1)
~Node(1)
Node(7)
Node(8)
~Node(8)
~Node(7)
0
true
bad_alloc caught
  • new pairs with delete, new[] with delete[]. Mixing them is undefined behaviour: delete on an array runs one destructor and passes the wrong pointer back to the allocator.
  • delete nullptr is a safe no-op, so no need to check before deleting.
  • Plain new throws std::bad_alloc on failure; it never returns nullptr (unless you use new (nothrow)).

new vs malloc

new / delete malloc / free
Is An operator (overloadable per class) A C library function
Calls constructor / destructor Yes No — raw bytes only
Size Computed from the type You pass bytes: malloc(n * sizeof(T))
Returns Typed pointer T* void* (needs a cast in C++)
On failure Throws bad_alloc Returns NULL
Resize No (use vector) realloc
Mixing Never free what new gave you, or delete what malloc gave you

Placement new

Placement new constructs an object in memory you already have, without allocating. You must call the destructor yourself. It's how vector, optional and memory pools construct elements in pre-allocated storage.

C++verified run
alignas(string) unsigned char storage[sizeof(string)];   // raw, correctly aligned bytes
string* s = new (storage) string("built in place");      // construct there: no allocation
cout << *s << '\n';
s->~string();                                            // explicit destructor call
Output
built in place

Leaks, dangling pointers and how to find them

Bug Example Detector
Memory leak new with no delete, or an early return/exception skipping the delete Valgrind, LeakSanitizer (-fsanitize=address)
Use after free Reading through a pointer after delete AddressSanitizer
Double free delete p; delete p; AddressSanitizer, glibc aborts
Mismatched free delete on new[] memory, free on new memory AddressSanitizer
Buffer overflow a[n] on an n-element array AddressSanitizer, vector::at
Uninitialized read Reading int x; before assigning Valgrind, MemorySanitizer, -Wall
Shell
g++ -g -fsanitize=address,undefined app.cpp && ./a.out    # fast, catches most bugs as they happen
valgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out                          # slower, no recompiling needed

The cure for most of these is not to write delete at all: let vector, string and smart pointers own memory (section 14).

Alignment and padding

Each type has an alignment: its address must be a multiple of it (int 4, double 8). The compiler inserts padding between members and at the end so every member is aligned and arrays of the struct stay aligned.

C++verified run
struct Bad  { char a; double b; char c; };     // 1 + 7 pad + 8 + 1 + 7 pad = 24
struct Good { double b; char a; char c; };     // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6 pad = 16
struct alignas(64) CacheLine { int counter; }; // force 64-byte alignment
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct Packed { char a; double b; char c; };   // no padding: 10 bytes, slow unaligned access
#pragma pack(pop)
// in main:
cout << sizeof(Bad) << ' ' << sizeof(Good) << ' ' << alignof(double) << ' '
     << sizeof(CacheLine) << ' ' << sizeof(Packed) << '\n';
cout << offsetof(Bad, b) << ' ' << offsetof(Good, a) << '\n';
Output
24 16 8 64 10
8 8

Order members from largest alignment to smallest to minimize padding. alignas(64) keeps hot per-thread counters on separate cache lines (avoiding false sharing, section 24).

Undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined

Kind Meaning Example
Undefined behaviour No requirements at all: crash, wrong output, or "works" a[10] on int a[5], signed overflow
Unspecified One of several allowed outcomes; needn't be documented Order of evaluating function arguments f(g(), h())
Implementation-defined The compiler picks and documents it sizeof(long), whether char is signed

The UB you must recognise

Undefined behaviour Example
Out-of-bounds access v[v.size()], arr[-1]
Dereferencing null, dangling or wild pointers *p after delete p
Signed integer overflow INT_MAX + 1
Reading an uninitialized variable int x; cout << x;
Modifying a variable twice without sequencing i = i++ + ++i;
Division by zero (integers) x / 0
Shifting by ≥ the bit width or by a negative amount 1 << 32 for a 32-bit int
Data race Two threads, one writing, no synchronization
Mismatched new/delete[] delete on new int[10]
Modifying a string literal or a const object char* s = (char*)"hi"; s[0] = 'H';
Returning a reference to a local int& f() { int x; return x; }
Calling a pure virtual function during construction Through a helper called from the base constructor
Violating strict aliasing Reading a float through an int*
Flowing off the end of a non-void function Missing return
How to say itWhy does undefined behaviour matter so much in C++?

"Because the optimizer is allowed to assume it never happens. If I write if (x + 1 < x) to detect overflow on a signed x, the compiler can delete the check, since overflow is UB. So UB isn't just 'might crash' — it can make correct-looking code do something completely different at -O2. I build with -fsanitize=address,undefined in testing to catch it."

Interview questions

QExplain the memory layout of a C++ program.

From low to high addresses: .text (code), .rodata (literals and constants), .data (initialized globals/statics), .bss (zero-initialized globals/statics), the heap growing upward, shared libraries and mappings, free space, then the stack growing downward, and kernel space at the top.

QStack vs heap?

The stack holds function frames: allocation is a pointer bump, memory is freed automatically when the function returns, but it's small (megabytes) and per-thread. The heap holds dynamically allocated objects: it's large and shared by threads, but allocation is slower, lifetime is manual (or RAII-managed), and it can fragment.

QWhat does new do internally? And delete?

new T(args) calls operator new(sizeof(T)) to allocate raw memory (throwing bad_alloc on failure) and then calls T's constructor on it. delete p calls the destructor, then operator delete to free the memory. The array forms do the same for each element and store the element count to know how many destructors to run.

QDifference between new and malloc?

new is a type-aware operator that allocates and constructs, returns T*, throws bad_alloc on failure, and can be overloaded per class. malloc is a C function that only allocates raw bytes, returns void*, and returns NULL on failure; it calls no constructor. Pair new/delete and malloc/free — never mix them.

QWhat happens if you delete memory allocated with new[]?

Undefined behaviour. Typically only the first element's destructor runs and the pointer passed to the allocator is wrong (it doesn't account for the hidden element count), so the heap gets corrupted or the program aborts.

QWhat is a memory leak? How do you avoid and detect it?

Memory that is allocated and never freed, usually because every pointer to it was lost. Avoid it with RAII — containers and smart pointers — so no code path forgets a delete, including early returns and exceptions. Detect it with Valgrind or LeakSanitizer.

QWhat is placement new?

A form of new that constructs an object at an address you provide, without allocating: new (buf) T(args). You must call the destructor explicitly (p->~T()) and manage the buffer. Containers and pools use it to separate allocation from construction.

QWhat is a segmentation fault?

The OS's response when a process accesses memory it isn't allowed to — an unmapped address (null or wild pointer), a write to read-only memory (string literals, code), or running off the end of the stack. The process gets the SIGSEGV signal and is killed.

QWhat causes a stack overflow?

Using more stack than the thread was given: unbounded or very deep recursion, or large local arrays. The result is a segfault. Fixes: iterate instead of recursing, move big data to the heap (vector) or static storage, or increase the stack size.

QWhat is structure padding? How can you reduce it?

The compiler inserts unused bytes between members (and at the end) so every member sits at an address that's a multiple of its alignment. struct {char; double; char;} is 24 bytes. Ordering members by decreasing alignment reduces it (16 bytes here); #pragma pack removes it at the cost of slow or illegal unaligned accesses.

QWhat is undefined behaviour? Give examples.

Behaviour for which the standard imposes no requirements. Examples: out-of-bounds access, using a freed or null pointer, signed overflow, reading uninitialized variables, unsequenced modifications like i = i++ + ++i, data races, and mismatched new[]/delete. The program may do anything, and the optimizer assumes it never happens.

QUndefined vs unspecified vs implementation-defined behaviour?

Undefined: no rules at all. Unspecified: one of a set of valid outcomes, not necessarily documented and possibly different each time (order of evaluating function arguments). Implementation-defined: like unspecified, but each compiler must document its choice (sizeof(int), signedness of char).

QWhere are string literals, static variables and local variables stored?

String literals in the read-only .rodata segment. Static and global variables in .data (non-zero initializer) or .bss (zero/no initializer). Local variables on the stack (or in registers). Objects created with new on the heap.

QIs delete nullptr safe? What about deleting twice?

Deleting a null pointer is a guaranteed no-op. Deleting the same non-null pointer twice is undefined behaviour (heap corruption, often an abort). Setting a raw pointer to nullptr after delete makes a second delete harmless — but the real fix is single ownership with unique_ptr.

QHow can you prevent objects of a class from being created on the heap, or on the stack?

Not on the heap: declare operator new (and operator new[]) as deleted or private. Not on the stack: make the destructor private (or protected) and provide a static factory plus a destroy() member, so only heap creation is possible.

14RAII · unique_ptr · shared_ptr · weak_ptr · make_shared16 questions

RAII & Smart Pointers

RAII as the core C++ idea, unique_ptr for single ownership, shared_ptr and its control block, weak_ptr for breaking cycles, custom deleters, enable_shared_from_this, and the mistakes interviewers ask about.

RAII: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization

Tie every resource — memory, a file, a socket, a lock — to the lifetime of an object: acquire it in the constructor, release it in the destructor. Because destructors run automatically when objects go out of scope, including when an exception unwinds the stack, the resource can't leak.

C++verified run
class File {                                      // a tiny RAII wrapper over C's FILE*
    FILE* f;
public:
    File(const char* path, const char* mode) : f(fopen(path, mode)) {
        if (!f) throw runtime_error("cannot open file");
        cout << "opened\n";
    }
    ~File() { fclose(f); cout << "closed\n"; }
    File(const File&) = delete;                   // owning: no copies
    File& operator=(const File&) = delete;
    void write(const string& s) { fputs(s.c_str(), f); }
};
void work() {
    File log("raii_demo.txt", "w");
    log.write("hello\n");
    throw runtime_error("something failed");      // the destructor still closes the file
}
// in main:
try { work(); } catch (const exception& e) { cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
Output
opened
closed
caught: something failed

The standard library is RAII all the way down: vector and string own memory, fstream owns a file, lock_guard owns a mutex lock, thread/jthread own a thread, smart pointers own heap objects. If you write delete in application code, you're probably missing an RAII type.

Choosing a smart pointer

unique_ptr<T> shared_ptr<T> weak_ptr<T>
Ownership Exclusive: one owner Shared: the last owner deletes None: observes a shared_ptr
Copyable No — move-only Yes (bumps the count) Yes
Size (64-bit) 8 bytes (with a stateless deleter) 16 bytes: object pointer + control-block pointer 16 bytes
Overhead None vs a raw pointer Atomic reference counting, a control block Same control block
Create with make_unique<T>(args) C++14 make_shared<T>(args) From a shared_ptr
Use for The default for any owning pointer Genuinely shared lifetime (caches, graphs, async callbacks) Breaking cycles, caches, observers

unique_ptr

C++verified run
struct Engine {
    int hp;
    Engine(int h) : hp(h) { cout << "Engine " << hp << " built\n"; }
    ~Engine() { cout << "Engine " << hp << " destroyed\n"; }
};
unique_ptr<Engine> factory(int hp) { return make_unique<Engine>(hp); }   // ownership out
void inspect(const Engine& e) { cout << "inspecting " << e.hp << '\n'; } // non-owning use
void consume(unique_ptr<Engine> e) { cout << "consumed " << e->hp << '\n'; }   // takes ownership
// in main:
auto a = factory(100);
inspect(*a);
unique_ptr<Engine> b = std::move(a);         // transfer: a becomes null
cout << boolalpha << (a == nullptr) << '\n';
consume(std::move(b));                       // destroyed at the end of consume
auto c = make_unique<Engine>(300);
c.reset(new Engine(400));                    // destroys 300, now owns 400
Engine* raw = c.release();                   // gives up ownership: we must delete
delete raw;
auto arr = make_unique<int[]>(5);            // array form calls delete[]
arr[2] = 7;
cout << arr[2] << ' ' << sizeof(unique_ptr<Engine>) << '\n';
Output
Engine 100 built
inspecting 100
true
consumed 100
Engine 100 destroyed
Engine 300 built
Engine 400 built
Engine 300 destroyed
Engine 400 destroyed
7 8
  • get() returns the raw pointer without giving up ownership; release() gives it up and returns it; reset(p) deletes the current object and takes p.
  • Pass unique_ptr by value (with std::move) to transfer ownership; pass T&/T* to functions that only use the object.
  • A unique_ptr<Derived> converts to unique_ptr<Base> — the base needs a virtual destructor.

Custom deleters

C++verified run
auto closer = [](FILE* f) { if (f) { fclose(f); cout << "fclose called\n"; } };
// in main:
{
    unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(closer)> f(fopen("deleter_demo.txt", "w"), closer);
    fputs("data", f.get());
}                                                    // fclose runs here
shared_ptr<int> counted(new int(5), [](int* p) { cout << "custom delete\n"; delete p; });
Output
fclose called
custom delete

shared_ptr

A shared_ptr keeps a control block with a strong count (how many shared_ptrs own the object) and a weak count. Copying increments the strong count; destroying or resetting decrements it; at zero the object is destroyed.

C++verified run
struct Session {
    string user;
    Session(string u) : user(std::move(u)) { cout << "open " << user << '\n'; }
    ~Session() { cout << "close " << user << '\n'; }
};
// in main:
shared_ptr<Session> s1 = make_shared<Session>("sai");
cout << s1.use_count() << '\n';                  // 1
{
    shared_ptr<Session> s2 = s1;                 // copy: shared ownership
    auto s3 = s2;
    cout << s1.use_count() << '\n';              // 3
}                                                // s2, s3 gone
cout << s1.use_count() << '\n';                  // 1
weak_ptr<Session> w = s1;                        // observes, doesn't own
if (auto locked = w.lock()) cout << "still alive: " << locked->user << '\n';
s1.reset();                                      // last owner: object destroyed now
cout << boolalpha << w.expired() << '\n';
cout << sizeof(shared_ptr<Session>) << '\n';
Output
open sai
1
3
1
still alive: sai
close sai
true
16

Why make_shared (and make_unique)

  1. One allocation for the object and its control block instead of two — faster and more cache-friendly.
  2. Exception safety: in f(shared_ptr<A>(new A), g()), before C++17 the compiler could run new A, then g() (which throws), and leak the A. f(make_shared<A>(), g()) can't leak.
  3. You never write new, so there's nothing to pair with delete.

One trade-off: with make_shared, the object's memory can't be returned until the last weak_ptr is also gone, because it shares the allocation with the control block.

Thread safety

The reference count is updated atomically, so different threads may copy and destroy their own shared_ptrs to the same object safely. The object itself is not protected — concurrent writes to it still need a mutex — and one shared_ptr instance modified from two threads is a data race (use std::atomic<shared_ptr<T>> C++20).

weak_ptr and reference cycles

Two objects holding shared_ptrs to each other keep each other's count above zero forever — a leak that reference counting can't see. Make one direction a weak_ptr.

C++verified run
struct Child;
struct Parent {
    shared_ptr<Child> child;
    ~Parent() { cout << "~Parent\n"; }
};
struct Child {
    weak_ptr<Parent> parent;          // weak: back-pointer doesn't own (shared_ptr here would leak)
    ~Child() { cout << "~Child\n"; }
};
// in main:
{
    auto p = make_shared<Parent>();
    auto c = make_shared<Child>();
    p->child = c;
    c->parent = p;
    cout << "parent owners: " << p.use_count() << ", child owners: " << c.use_count() << '\n';
}
cout << "scope left\n";
Output
parent owners: 1, child owners: 2
~Parent
~Child
scope left

Typical uses of weak_ptr: child → parent back-pointers in trees, observer lists, and caches that shouldn't keep entries alive.

enable_shared_from_this

Inside a member function, shared_ptr<T>(this) creates a second, independent control block — the object will be deleted twice. To get a shared_ptr to yourself, inherit from enable_shared_from_this and call shared_from_this().

C++verified run
struct Task : enable_shared_from_this<Task> {
    shared_ptr<Task> self() { return shared_from_this(); }   // shares the existing control block
};
// in main:
auto t = make_shared<Task>();
auto again = t->self();
cout << t.use_count() << '\n';     // 2: one control block
Output
2

shared_from_this() only works if the object is already owned by a shared_ptr; on a stack object it throws bad_weak_ptr.

Mistakes to avoid

Mistake Why it's wrong Do instead
shared_ptr<T> a(raw), b(raw); Two control blocks for one object: double delete Create one owner, copy it; or use make_shared
shared_ptr<T>(this) Same: a second control block enable_shared_from_this
Cycles of shared_ptr Never freed weak_ptr for back-references
delete p.get(); The smart pointer will delete again Let the owner delete; reset()
shared_ptr everywhere "to be safe" Hides ownership, costs atomic operations unique_ptr by default
Passing shared_ptr by value to every function Atomic increment + decrement per call Pass T& or const shared_ptr<T>& unless the callee keeps a copy
unique_ptr<T> for an array from new T[n] Calls delete instead of delete[] unique_ptr<T[]> or vector<T>
auto_ptr Copy silently transferred ownership; removed in C++17 unique_ptr

Interview questions

QWhat is RAII?

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: owning every resource through an object whose constructor acquires it and whose destructor releases it. Because destructors run deterministically at scope exit — even during exception unwinding — resources can't leak. vector, fstream, lock_guard and smart pointers are RAII types.

QWhat are smart pointers? Name them.

Class templates that own a heap object and delete it automatically. unique_ptr (exclusive, move-only ownership), shared_ptr (shared ownership with reference counting), and weak_ptr (a non-owning observer of a shared_ptr-managed object). auto_ptr was deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17.

Qunique_ptr vs shared_ptr?

unique_ptr has a single owner, can only be moved, and costs nothing over a raw pointer. shared_ptr allows many owners via an atomically updated reference count in a separately allocated control block; it's 16 bytes and slower to copy. Default to unique_ptr; use shared_ptr only when lifetime truly is shared.

QWhy can't you copy a unique_ptr?

Two copies would both believe they own the object and both delete it. Its copy constructor and copy assignment are deleted; ownership can only be transferred with std::move, which leaves the source null.

QHow does shared_ptr work internally?

It holds two pointers: one to the object, one to a control block containing the strong (owner) count, the weak count, and the deleter/allocator. Copies increment the strong count atomically; destructors decrement it; when it hits zero the deleter destroys the object, and when the weak count also hits zero the control block is freed.

QWhat is weak_ptr and why is it needed?

A non-owning reference to an object managed by shared_ptr. It doesn't affect the strong count, so it doesn't keep the object alive. It's needed to break reference cycles (which would otherwise leak) and to observe objects that may disappear. lock() returns a shared_ptr that's empty if the object is gone.

QWhat is a circular reference and how do you fix it?

Two (or more) objects owning each other via shared_ptr — their counts can never reach zero, so they leak. Fix it by making one link (usually child → parent or observer → subject) a weak_ptr.

QWhy prefer make_shared over shared_ptr<T>(new T)?

It performs a single allocation for object and control block (faster, better locality), avoids writing new, and is exception-safe in function arguments. Downsides: no custom deleter, and the memory isn't released until all weak_ptrs are gone.

QIs shared_ptr thread-safe?

The control block's reference counting is: separate shared_ptr instances can be copied and destroyed in different threads. Access to the pointed-to object is not synchronized, and concurrent modification of the same shared_ptr instance is a data race unless you use std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> (C++20).

QWhat is enable_shared_from_this?

A base class that lets an object already owned by shared_ptr obtain another shared_ptr to itself via shared_from_this(), sharing the existing control block. Writing shared_ptr<T>(this) instead would create a second control block and a double delete.

QWhat is a custom deleter? Give an example.

A callable the smart pointer invokes instead of delete: e.g. unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> f(fopen(...), &fclose); closes a C file handle. For unique_ptr the deleter is part of the type; for shared_ptr it's stored in the control block.

QHow do you pass smart pointers to functions?

If the function just uses the object: pass T& or T* (or const T&). If it takes ownership: unique_ptr<T> by value (caller uses std::move). If it shares ownership: shared_ptr<T> by value. If it might share: const shared_ptr<T>&. Avoid passing shared_ptr by value when no ownership is kept — it's an atomic increment and decrement for nothing.

QWhat was wrong with auto_ptr?

Copying an auto_ptr silently transferred ownership and nulled the source, so it couldn't safely go in containers or be passed around like a value. unique_ptr makes the transfer explicit with std::move and forbids copies.

QWhat happens if you create two shared_ptrs from the same raw pointer?

Each gets its own control block with count 1, so the object is deleted twice — undefined behaviour. Always create the first shared_ptr directly from new (or make_shared) and copy that one.

QWhat is the size of unique_ptr and shared_ptr?

unique_ptr<T> with the default (or any stateless) deleter is the size of a raw pointer, 8 bytes. shared_ptr<T> and weak_ptr<T> are two pointers, 16 bytes, plus the control block on the heap.

QCan a smart pointer manage an array?

Yes: unique_ptr<T[]> (and make_unique<T[]>(n)) uses delete[] and provides operator[]; shared_ptr<T[]> works since C++17. Usually a vector<T> is the better choice.

15try · catch · throw · noexcept · exception safety15 questions

Exception Handling

Throwing and catching, the standard exception hierarchy, custom exceptions, stack unwinding, exceptions in constructors and destructors, noexcept, the exception-safety guarantees, and when to use error codes, optional or expected instead.

The basics

C++verified run
double divide(double a, double b) {
    if (b == 0) throw invalid_argument("division by zero");   // throw an object
    return a / b;
}
// in main:
try {
    cout << divide(10, 4) << '\n';
    cout << divide(1, 0) << '\n';             // throws: the rest of the try block is skipped
    cout << "never printed\n";
} catch (const invalid_argument& e) {         // catch by const reference
    cout << "invalid_argument: " << e.what() << '\n';
} catch (const exception& e) {                // any other standard exception
    cout << "exception: " << e.what() << '\n';
} catch (...) {                               // anything at all
    cout << "unknown\n";
}
cout << "program continues\n";
Output
2.5
invalid_argument: division by zero
program continues
  • You can throw any type (throw 42; works), but throw objects derived from std::exception so callers can catch them uniformly and call what().
  • Catch by const&: catching by value copies the exception and slices derived exceptions to the base type.
  • Handlers are tried in order, and the first match wins — put derived classes before their bases. g++ warns when a handler can never be reached.
  • An exception nobody catches calls std::terminate, which aborts the program.

The standard exception hierarchy

Exception Thrown by / for
exception Base of everything; virtual const char* what() const noexcept
logic_error Bugs detectable before running:
↳ invalid_argument stoi("abc")
↳ out_of_range vector::at, string::at, stoi("99999999999")
↳ length_error string or vector beyond max_size()
↳ domain_error Math domain errors (rarely used)
runtime_error Problems only detectable at run time:
↳ overflow_error, underflow_error, range_error Arithmetic, e.g. bitset::to_ulong overflow
↳ system_error OS errors, e.g. std::thread creation failure
bad_alloc new failed
bad_cast dynamic_cast to a reference failed
bad_typeid typeid(*p) with a null p
bad_function_call Calling an empty std::function
bad_optional_access / bad_variant_access optional::value() when empty, get<T> on the wrong alternative
bad_weak_ptr shared_from_this() without an owner

Custom exceptions

C++verified run
class InsufficientFunds : public runtime_error {
    double shortfall_;
public:
    explicit InsufficientFunds(double s)
        : runtime_error("insufficient funds: short by " + to_string(int(s))), shortfall_(s) {}
    double shortfall() const noexcept { return shortfall_; }
};
void withdraw(double balance, double amount) {
    if (amount > balance) throw InsufficientFunds(amount - balance);
    cout << "withdrew " << amount << '\n';
}
// in main:
try {
    withdraw(500, 200);
    withdraw(500, 800);
} catch (const InsufficientFunds& e) {
    cout << e.what() << " (" << e.shortfall() << ")\n";
}
Output
withdrew 200
insufficient funds: short by 300 (300)

Derive from runtime_error or logic_error (they store the message for you) rather than from bare exception.

Rethrowing

C++verified run
void layer() {
    try {
        throw out_of_range("index 9");
    } catch (const exception& e) {
        cout << "layer logs: " << e.what() << '\n';
        throw;                       // rethrows the ORIGINAL object, type preserved
        // throw e;                  // would throw a sliced copy of type std::exception
    }
}
// in main:
try { layer(); }
catch (const out_of_range& e) { cout << "main got out_of_range: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
Output
layer logs: index 9
main got out_of_range: index 9

Stack unwinding

When an exception propagates out of a function, every fully constructed local object in each frame being left is destroyed, in reverse order. This is why RAII works: destructors release resources even on the error path.

C++verified run
struct Guard {
    string name;
    Guard(string n) : name(std::move(n)) { cout << "acquire " << name << '\n'; }
    ~Guard() { cout << "release " << name << '\n'; }
};
void inner() {
    Guard g("inner-lock");
    throw runtime_error("disk full");
}
void outer() {
    Guard g("outer-file");
    inner();
    cout << "not reached\n";
}
// in main:
try { outer(); } catch (const exception& e) { cout << "handled: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
Output
acquire outer-file
acquire inner-lock
release inner-lock
release outer-file
handled: disk full

Raw new without RAII is exactly what unwinding can't clean up: a new before the throw and a delete after it leaks.

Exceptions in constructors

Throwing is the way for a constructor to report failure. If a constructor throws, the object never existed: its destructor does not run, but every member and base class that was already constructed is destroyed.

C++verified run
struct Part {
    string n;
    Part(string s) : n(std::move(s)) { cout << "Part " << n << '\n'; }
    ~Part() { cout << "~Part " << n << '\n'; }
};
struct Machine {
    Part a{"A"};
    Part b{"B"};
    int* raw;
    Machine() : raw(new int[10]) {
        cout << "Machine body\n";
        delete[] raw;                          // we must clean raw ourselves before throwing...
        throw runtime_error("calibration failed");
    }
    ~Machine() { cout << "~Machine (never runs here)\n"; delete[] raw; }
};
// in main:
try { Machine m; } catch (const exception& e) { cout << "caught: " << e.what() << '\n'; }
Output
Part A
Part B
Machine body
~Part B
~Part A
caught: calibration failed

The raw pointer shows the trap: a raw owning member isn't destroyed automatically. Had it been a unique_ptr<int[]> or vector<int>, the cleanup would be automatic.

A function-try-block lets a constructor catch exceptions from its initializer list (to log or translate them; it always rethrows):

C++verified run
struct Config {
    int port;
    Config(const string& s) try : port(stoi(s)) {
        cout << "port " << port << '\n';
    } catch (const exception& e) {
        cout << "bad config: " << e.what() << '\n';   // rethrown automatically at the end
    }
};
// in main:
try { Config c("8080"); Config d("eighty"); } catch (...) { cout << "construction failed\n"; }
Output
port 8080
bad config: stoi
construction failed

Exceptions in destructors

Destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11. If an exception escapes one, std::terminate is called. And if a destructor throws during stack unwinding (while another exception is in flight), it's terminate regardless. Never let exceptions escape a destructor — catch and log inside it.

noexcept

C++verified run
void safe() noexcept {}
void risky() {}
template <typename T>
void info() { cout << boolalpha << noexcept(T(declval<T>())) << ' '; }   // noexcept as an operator
// in main:
cout << noexcept(safe()) << ' ' << noexcept(risky()) << '\n';
info<string>();           // string's move constructor is noexcept
info<vector<int>>();
cout << '\n';
Output
1 0
true true
  • As a specifier, noexcept promises the function won't throw. If it does, std::terminate is called — no unwinding guarantees.
  • As an operator, noexcept(expr) asks at compile time whether expr can throw.
  • Mark move constructors, move assignments, swap, and destructors noexcept: containers check it to decide whether moving is safe (section 10).

Exception-safety guarantees

Guarantee Promise Example
No-throw Never throws Destructors, swap, move operations, vector::pop_back
Strong If it throws, state is rolled back as if nothing happened (commit or rollback) vector::push_back (with a noexcept move or copyable type), copy-and-swap assignment
Basic If it throws, no leaks and invariants hold, but state may have changed Most operations; e.g. inserting a range into a vector
None Anything can happen Code with raw new/delete and no care

Techniques: RAII for every resource, do the work on a copy then swap it in (strong guarantee), and order statements so nothing can throw after you've modified state.

Exceptions vs error codes vs optional/expected

Exceptions Error codes / bool std::optional<T> C++17 std::expected<T, E> C++23
Can be ignored silently No Yes (unless [[nodiscard]]) Less likely Less likely
Cost on success ~Zero (table-based "zero-cost" model) A branch A branch A branch
Cost on failure High (microseconds) Low Low Low
Carries error details Yes, any type A code No (just "no value") Yes
Works in constructors and operators Yes No No No
Good for Rare, serious failures far from where they're handled Hot paths, C APIs, -fno-exceptions code "Not found" results Expected failures with a reason

Some codebases (games, embedded, Google's style guide historically) compile with -fno-exceptions; then new failure aborts, and errors travel as return values.

Interview questions

QHow does exception handling work in C++?

Code that may fail goes in a try block; failure is signalled with throw expr; the runtime unwinds the stack — destroying local objects in each exited frame — until it finds a catch clause whose type matches, which then runs. If none matches, std::terminate ends the program.

QWhy catch exceptions by reference?

Catching by value copies the exception object and slices derived exceptions down to the caught type, losing their extra data and their overridden what(). Catching by const& avoids the copy and preserves the dynamic type.

QWhat is stack unwinding?

The process of leaving functions while an exception propagates: for each frame between the throw and the matching catch, all fully constructed automatic objects are destroyed in reverse order of construction. It's what makes RAII cleanup automatic on error paths.

QWhat happens if a constructor throws?

The object is considered never constructed, so its destructor won't run. Already constructed members and base subobjects are destroyed, and the memory from new (if the object was heap-allocated) is freed. Resources held by raw pointers acquired in the constructor body leak unless cleaned up — use RAII members.

QCan a destructor throw?

It shouldn't. Destructors are noexcept by default, so a throw calls std::terminate; and a throw during unwinding terminates even if the destructor is marked noexcept(false). Handle errors inside the destructor or provide an explicit close() that can throw.

QWhat does noexcept do and why does it matter?

It declares that a function won't throw; if it does, the program terminates. It lets the compiler skip unwinding bookkeeping and lets libraries choose faster paths — notably vector moves elements on reallocation only if the move constructor is noexcept.

Qthrow; vs throw e; inside a catch block?

throw; rethrows the original exception object with its full dynamic type. throw e; throws a new copy of e as its static type — if e is a const exception& referring to an out_of_range, the copy is a sliced std::exception.

QWhat are the exception-safety guarantees?

No-throw: the operation never throws. Strong: if it throws, the program state is unchanged (commit-or-rollback). Basic: if it throws, nothing leaks and invariants hold, but the state may differ. Every function should offer at least the basic guarantee.

QWhat is catch (...)?

A handler that catches any exception of any type. You can't inspect the object (except via std::current_exception), so it's used to log and rethrow, to translate exceptions at module boundaries, or in main as a last resort.

QIn what order should catch blocks be written?

Most derived first, most general last (catch (...) at the very end). The first matching handler wins, so a catch (const exception&) placed before catch (const out_of_range&) would swallow it — the compiler warns about the unreachable handler.

QWhat is the difference between logic_error and runtime_error?

logic_error represents errors in the program's logic that could in principle be prevented by checking preconditions (invalid arguments, out-of-range indices). runtime_error represents conditions only detectable at run time (overflow, system failures, external input problems).

QWhat happens when an exception isn't caught?

std::terminate is called, which by default calls std::abort. Whether the stack is unwound first is implementation-defined, so destructors may not run.

QExceptions or error codes — which would you use?

Exceptions for rare, serious failures that must not be ignored and are handled far from where they occur, and for failures in constructors and operators. Error codes, optional or expected for expected failures on hot paths (parsing, lookups), in code built without exceptions, and across C boundaries.

QWhat is a function-try-block?

A try that wraps a whole function body including a constructor's member initializer list: X() try : m(f()) { ... } catch (...) { ... }. In a constructor, it can log or translate exceptions from member initialization, but the exception is always rethrown when the handler ends.

QAre exceptions slow?

On the success path, modern compilers use table-based unwinding, so a try block costs essentially nothing. Throwing is expensive — allocating the exception, searching tables, unwinding frames — typically microseconds. So exceptions shouldn't be used for normal control flow.

Templates & Concepts

Function and class templates, deduction and CTAD, non-type parameters, full and partial specialization, why templates live in headers, variadic templates and fold expressions, type traits and if constexpr, SFINAE, and C++20 concepts.

Why templates

A template is a recipe the compiler uses to generate code for each set of types you use it with. std::vector<int> and std::vector<string> are two separate classes stamped out from one template — that's compile-time (static) polymorphism: no virtual calls, full inlining, full type checking.

C++verified run
template <typename T>                        // 'class T' means the same
T biggest(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

template <typename T, typename U>
auto add(T a, U b) { return a + b; }         // return type deduced from the expression
// in main:
cout << biggest(3, 9) << ' ' << biggest(2.5, 1.5) << ' ' << biggest<string>("pear", "apple") << '\n';
cout << add(2, 3.5) << '\n';                 // T = int, U = double
// biggest(3, 4.5);                          // error: T deduced as both int and double
cout << biggest<double>(3, 4.5) << '\n';     // explicit argument fixes it
Output
9 2.5 pear
5.5
4.5
  • Deduction: the compiler infers T from the arguments; it doesn't apply conversions while deducing, so biggest(3, 4.5) fails.
  • Instantiation: each distinct T produces a separate function in the binary (possible "code bloat").
  • A non-template function beats a template on an exact tie; a more specialized template beats a less specialized one.
  • C++20 abbreviated templates: auto twice(auto x) { return x * 2; } is a template.

Class templates

C++verified run
template <typename T, size_t Capacity = 8>       // a type and a non-type parameter (with default)
class FixedStack {
    array<T, Capacity> data{};
    size_t top_ = 0;
public:
    bool push(const T& v) {
        if (top_ == Capacity) return false;
        data[top_++] = v;
        return true;
    }
    T pop();                                      // defined outside below
    bool empty() const { return top_ == 0; }
    static constexpr size_t capacity() { return Capacity; }
};
template <typename T, size_t Capacity>
T FixedStack<T, Capacity>::pop() { return data[--top_]; }
// in main:
FixedStack<string, 3> s;
s.push("a"); s.push("b"); s.push("c");
cout << boolalpha << s.push("d") << ' ' << s.pop() << s.pop() << ' ' << FixedStack<int>::capacity() << '\n';
pair p(1, 2.5);                                  // CTAD (C++17): pair<int, double> deduced
vector v{1, 2, 3};                               // vector<int>
cout << p.second << ' ' << v.size() << '\n';
Output
false cb 8
2.5 3
  • Non-type template parameters are compile-time values: integers, enums, pointers, and since C++20 floating-point and simple class types. std::array<int, 5> and std::bitset<64> use them.
  • Class template argument deduction (CTAD) C++17 lets you write pair p(1, 2.5) and vector v{1, 2, 3}.

Why templates go in headers

The compiler can only generate FixedStack<string, 3> where it sees the full template definition. If the definition sits in a .cpp file, other translation units see only declarations, the code is never instantiated, and you get linker errors. So template definitions go in headers (or you explicitly instantiate the types you need in the .cpp: template class FixedStack<int>;).

Specialization

C++verified run
template <typename T>
struct TypeName { static string get() { return "unknown"; } };          // primary template

template <>
struct TypeName<int> { static string get() { return "int"; } };         // FULL specialization

template <typename T>
struct TypeName<T*> {                                                   // PARTIAL specialization
    static string get() { return TypeName<T>::get() + "*"; }
};
template <typename T>
struct TypeName<vector<T>> {
    static string get() { return "vector<" + TypeName<T>::get() + ">"; }
};
// in main:
cout << TypeName<int>::get() << ' ' << TypeName<int**>::get() << ' '
     << TypeName<vector<int*>>::get() << ' ' << TypeName<double>::get() << '\n';
Output
int int** vector<int*> unknown
  • Full specialization gives a completely custom implementation for one exact set of arguments (vector<bool> is a famous one).
  • Partial specialization covers a family of arguments (all pointers, all vectors). Only class templates (and variable templates) can be partially specialized; for functions, overload instead.

Variadic templates and fold expressions

C++verified run
template <typename... Args>                          // a parameter pack
auto sum(Args... args) { return (args + ... + 0); }  // fold expression (C++17)

template <typename... Args>
void print_all(const Args&... args) {
    ((cout << args << ' '), ...);                    // comma fold: one print per argument
    cout << "| " << sizeof...(Args) << " args\n";    // number of arguments
}

void print_rec() { cout << '\n'; }                   // pre-C++17 style: recursion
template <typename T, typename... Rest>
void print_rec(const T& first, const Rest&... rest) {
    cout << first << ';';
    print_rec(rest...);                              // peel one argument per call
}
// in main:
cout << sum(1, 2, 3, 4.5) << ' ' << sum() << '\n';
print_all("id", 7, 2.5, 'x');
print_rec(1, "two", 3.0);
Output
10.5 0
id 7 2.5 x | 4 args
1;two;3;

Variadic templates are how make_unique, emplace_back, std::tuple and std::format accept any number of arguments of any types.

Type traits and if constexpr

<type_traits> answers questions about types at compile time. if constexpr C++17 discards the branch that isn't taken, so it may contain code that wouldn't compile for that type.

C++verified run
template <typename T>
string describe(const T& value) {
    if constexpr (is_integral_v<T>)
        return "integer, doubled = " + to_string(value * 2);
    else if constexpr (is_floating_point_v<T>)
        return "floating, halved = " + to_string(value / 2);
    else
        return "something else: " + string(value);   // only compiled for types where this works
}
// in main:
cout << describe(21) << '\n' << describe(5.0) << '\n' << describe("text") << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << is_same_v<int, int32_t> << ' ' << is_pointer_v<int*> << ' '
     << is_base_of_v<exception, runtime_error> << '\n';
using T = conditional_t<(sizeof(long) == 8), long, long long>;   // compile-time if for types
cout << sizeof(T) << '\n';
Output
integer, doubled = 42
floating, halved = 2.500000
something else: text
true true true
8

SFINAE

Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: when substituting template arguments into a declaration produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed from the candidate set instead of causing an error. enable_if uses it to switch overloads on and off — the pre-C++20 way to constrain templates.

C++verified run
template <typename T, enable_if_t<is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>
string kind(T) { return "integral"; }

template <typename T, enable_if_t<!is_integral_v<T>, int> = 0>
string kind(T) { return "not integral"; }
// in main:
cout << kind(42) << ' ' << kind(4.2) << '\n';
Output
integral not integral

Concepts C++20

A concept is a named compile-time predicate on types. It replaces most SFINAE with readable constraints and gives short, clear error messages.

C++verified run
template <typename T>
concept Numeric = integral<T> || floating_point<T>;

template <typename T>
concept Shape = requires(const T& s) {          // what a type must support
    { s.area() } -> convertible_to<double>;
    { s.name() } -> convertible_to<string>;
};

template <Numeric T>                             // constrained template parameter
T square(T x) { return x * x; }

void report(const Shape auto& s) {               // constrained abbreviated template
    cout << s.name() << ": " << s.area() << '\n';
}
struct Square { double side; double area() const { return side * side; } string name() const { return "square"; } };

template <typename T>
    requires (sizeof(T) <= 8)                    // a requires-clause
void small_only(T) { cout << "small type\n"; }
// in main:
cout << square(7) << ' ' << square(1.5) << '\n';
report(Square{3});
small_only(42);
// square("x");     // error: the constraint Numeric<const char*> is not satisfied
Output
49 2.25
square: 9
small type
C++compile error
template <typename T>
concept Numeric = integral<T> || floating_point<T>;
template <Numeric T>
T square(T x) { return x * x; }
// in main:
square(string("no"));
g++ says
error: no matching function for call to 'square(std::string)'
note: constraints not satisfied

Common standard concepts: integral, floating_point, same_as, derived_from, convertible_to, equality_comparable, totally_ordered, invocable, predicate, ranges::range, random_access_iterator.

Templates vs Java generics vs macros

C++ templates Java generics Macros
Mechanism Code generated per type at compile time Type erasure: one class, casts inserted Text substitution
Primitive types vector<int> directly Need boxing (List<Integer>) Anything
Run-time cost None; can inline Casts, boxing None
Binary size Can grow (one copy per type) One copy Grows
Non-type parameters Yes (array<int, 5>) No —
Type-checked Yes (and constrained with concepts) Yes No
Specialization Yes No —

Interview questions

QWhat are templates and why are they useful?

A way to write code parameterized by types (and values) that the compiler instantiates for each concrete type used. They give generic containers and algorithms (the whole STL) with full type safety and no run-time overhead — compile-time polymorphism.

QFunction template vs class template?

A function template generates functions (template <class T> T max(T, T)), and its arguments are usually deduced from the call. A class template generates classes (template <class T> class Stack), whose arguments are given explicitly or deduced by CTAD from constructor arguments.

QWhy must template definitions usually be in header files?

The compiler instantiates a template where it's used, which requires the complete definition to be visible in that translation unit. If the definition is in another .cpp, nothing gets instantiated and the linker reports undefined references. The alternative is explicit instantiation for a fixed set of types.

QWhat is template specialization? Partial vs full?

Full specialization provides a separate implementation for one exact set of template arguments (template <> struct Hash<string>). Partial specialization provides one for a pattern of arguments (template <class T> struct Hash<T*>). Classes can be partially specialized; function templates can only be fully specialized, so overloading is used instead.

QWhat is a non-type template parameter?

A template parameter that's a compile-time value rather than a type: template <int N> struct Buffer { char data[N]; };. std::array<T, N> and std::bitset<N> use them. Since C++20 they can also be floating-point values and some class types.

QWhat are variadic templates?

Templates that accept any number of template arguments via a parameter pack (typename... Args). The pack is expanded with args..., counted with sizeof...(Args), and reduced with fold expressions like (args + ...) in C++17. They power make_unique, emplace, tuple and std::format.

QWhat is SFINAE?

Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: if substituting template arguments into a function template's signature produces an invalid type or expression, that template is dropped from overload resolution instead of causing a compile error. std::enable_if uses it to enable overloads only for types meeting a condition.

QWhat are concepts? What problem do they solve?

Named compile-time requirements on template arguments (C++20), like std::integral or a custom Shape requiring area(). They document intent, select overloads, and replace pages of instantiation errors with a short message saying which constraint failed. They're a readable replacement for SFINAE.

QWhat does if constexpr do?

It evaluates its condition at compile time and discards the branch not taken, so the discarded branch needn't compile for the current template arguments. It replaces many uses of tag dispatch and SFINAE inside function bodies.

QWhat is CTAD?

Class Template Argument Deduction (C++17): the compiler deduces a class template's arguments from the constructor call, so pair p(1, 2.0) gives pair<int, double> and lock_guard lk(m) deduces the mutex type. Deduction guides can customize it.

QWhat is the difference between typename and class in a template parameter list?

None in template <class T> vs template <typename T>. But typename has a second job: inside templates, it tells the compiler that a dependent name is a type, as in typename T::value_type x;.

QTemplates vs virtual functions — when to use which?

Templates resolve the type at compile time: fastest, inlinable, but every type must be known when compiling, and each instantiation adds code. Virtual functions resolve at run time: one compiled interface that works with types added later, and heterogeneous containers of base pointers, at the cost of an indirect call.

QWhat is template metaprogramming?

Using templates to perform computation at compile time — e.g. computing factorials through recursive template instantiation, or selecting types with traits. Modern C++ prefers constexpr functions, if constexpr and concepts, which do the same with ordinary-looking code.

QHow do C++ templates differ from Java generics?

C++ instantiates separate code for each type at compile time, supports primitives, non-type parameters and specialization, and has no run-time cost. Java uses type erasure: one compiled class with Object and inserted casts, so no primitives (boxing instead), no new T(), and no specialization.

QCan a virtual function be a template?

No. A member function template can't be virtual, because the vtable must have a fixed number of slots and a template could have unboundedly many instantiations. A class template can, however, have virtual functions.

17vector · deque · list · set · map · unordered_* · stack · queue · priority_queue16 questions

STL Containers

The parts of the STL, every container with its data structure and complexities, the map operator[] trap, custom comparators and hashes, the container adaptors including min-heaps, pair and tuple, and how to choose.

The STL in one picture

The Standard Template Library has four parts that work together:

  • Containers hold data (vector, map, …).
  • Iterators are generalized pointers that walk containers (section 19).
  • Algorithms (sort, find, accumulate, …) work on iterator ranges, not on containers, so one sort serves every random-access container.
  • Function objects (comparators, predicates, lambdas) customize algorithms and containers.

Every container at a glance

Container Structure Access Insert/erase Find Ordered Notes
vector Dynamic array O(1) random O(1)* back, O(n) elsewhere O(n) No The default choice
deque Blocks of arrays O(1) random O(1) front and back, O(n) middle O(n) No Not contiguous
list Doubly linked list O(n) O(1) anywhere (with an iterator) O(n) No splice in O(1); no random access
forward_list Singly linked list O(n) O(1) after a position O(n) No Smallest node
array Fixed C array O(1) — O(n) No Size in the type
set / multiset Red-black tree — O(log n) O(log n) Yes Unique / duplicate keys
map / multimap Red-black tree O(log n) by key O(log n) O(log n) Yes, by key lower_bound, range queries
unordered_set / unordered_map Hash table O(1) avg by key O(1) avg, O(n) worst O(1) avg, O(n) worst No Needs hash and ==
stack Adaptor over deque top only O(1) push/pop — — LIFO
queue Adaptor over deque front/back O(1) push/pop — — FIFO
priority_queue Binary heap in a vector top O(1) O(log n) push/pop — Heap order Max-heap by default

* amortized

Sequence containers

C++verified run
vector<int> v{5, 2, 8};
v.push_back(1);                     // [5,2,8,1]
v.emplace_back(9);                  // constructs in place
v.insert(v.begin() + 1, 7);         // [5,7,2,8,1,9]   O(n)
v.erase(v.begin());                 // [7,2,8,1,9]     O(n)
v.pop_back();                       // [7,2,8,1]
cout << v.front() << ' ' << v.back() << ' ' << v.size() << '\n';

deque<int> d{2, 3};
d.push_front(1);                    // O(1) at both ends
d.push_back(4);
cout << d[0] << d[3] << '\n';

list<int> l{1, 2, 3};
auto it = next(l.begin());          // points at 2
l.insert(it, 10);                   // O(1): [1,10,2,3]
l.remove(3);                        // removes every 3
list<int> other{7, 8};
l.splice(l.end(), other);           // O(1): moves nodes, other becomes empty
for (int x : l) cout << x << ' ';
cout << "| other " << other.size() << '\n';
Output
7 1 4
14
1 10 2 7 8 | other 0

Ordered associative containers: set and map

Keys are kept sorted (by < unless you give a comparator), in a balanced binary search tree (red-black tree) — so every operation is O(log n) and iteration visits keys in order.

C++verified run
set<int> s{5, 1, 4, 1, 3};          // duplicates dropped: {1,3,4,5}
s.insert(2);
s.erase(4);
cout << s.count(3) << ' ' << boolalpha << s.contains(9) << '\n';   // contains: C++20
auto lb = s.lower_bound(3);         // first element >= 3
auto ub = s.upper_bound(3);         // first element > 3
cout << *lb << ' ' << *ub << ' ' << *s.begin() << ' ' << *s.rbegin() << '\n';   // min and max

multiset<int> ms{2, 2, 2, 7};
ms.erase(ms.find(2));               // erase ONE copy (ms.erase(2) would erase all three)
cout << ms.count(2) << '\n';

map<string, int> score;
score["sai"] = 90;                  // insert or overwrite
score["anu"] += 5;                  // missing key: value-initialized to 0, then += 5
score.insert({"ravi", 70});         // does nothing if the key exists
score.emplace("kiran", 88);
for (const auto& [name, marks] : score) cout << name << ':' << marks << ' ';
cout << '\n';
if (auto f = score.find("ravi"); f != score.end()) cout << "ravi has " << f->second << '\n';
cout << score.size() << '\n';
Output
1 false
3 5 1 5
2
anu:5 kiran:88 ravi:70 sai:90 
ravi has 70
4
Pitfallmap[key] inserts when the key is missing

if (m["x"] == 0) silently adds "x" with a default value — the map grows, and it can't be used on a const map. To test membership use find, count or contains; to read without inserting use at (throws if missing) or find.

Insert method If the key already exists
m[k] = v Overwrites
m.insert({k, v}) / m.emplace(k, v) Leaves the old value; returns {iterator, false}
m.try_emplace(k, args...) C++17 Leaves it, and doesn't even construct the value
m.insert_or_assign(k, v) C++17 Overwrites; tells you which happened

Custom ordering

C++verified run
struct Student { string name; int marks; };
struct ByMarksDesc {
    bool operator()(const Student& a, const Student& b) const {
        if (a.marks != b.marks) return a.marks > b.marks;   // higher marks first
        return a.name < b.name;                              // tie-break by name
    }
};
// in main:
set<Student, ByMarksDesc> ranking{{"anu", 88}, {"sai", 95}, {"ravi", 88}};
for (auto& s : ranking) cout << s.name << ' ';
cout << '\n';
map<string, int, greater<string>> rev{{"a", 1}, {"c", 3}, {"b", 2}};   // keys in descending order
for (auto& [k, v] : rev) cout << k;
cout << '\n';
Output
sai anu ravi 
cba

The comparator must be a strict weak ordering — use </>, never <=; two keys are treated as equal when neither is "less" than the other.

Erasing while iterating

C++verified run
map<int, string> m{{1, "a"}, {2, "b"}, {3, "c"}, {4, "d"}};
for (auto it = m.begin(); it != m.end(); ) {
    if (it->first % 2 == 0) it = m.erase(it);   // erase returns the next valid iterator
    else ++it;
}
for (auto& [k, v] : m) cout << k << v << ' ';
cout << '\n';
Output
1a 3c

Unordered containers: hash tables

C++verified run
unordered_map<string, int> freq;
for (string w : {"to", "be", "or", "not", "to", "be"}) ++freq[w];
cout << freq["to"] << ' ' << freq["be"] << ' ' << freq.size() << '\n';

unordered_set<int> seen;
vector<int> nums{4, 1, 4, 2, 1};
for (int x : nums)
    if (!seen.insert(x).second) cout << "duplicate " << x << '\n';   // insert returns {it, inserted?}

struct PairHash {                                     // pair<int,int> has no std::hash
    size_t operator()(const pair<int, int>& p) const {
        return hash<long long>()(((long long)p.first << 32) ^ (unsigned)p.second);
    }
};
unordered_map<pair<int, int>, string, PairHash> grid;
grid[{2, 3}] = "tree";
cout << grid[{2, 3}] << '\n';
Output
2 2 4
duplicate 4
duplicate 1
tree
  • Average O(1) lookup, but worst case O(n) when many keys collide.
  • No ordering: iteration order is unpredictable and changes after rehashing.
  • Keys need std::hash<K> and ==. pair, tuple and your structs need a custom hash — or use map instead.
  • Call reserve(n) when you know the size, to avoid repeated rehashing.

Container adaptors

C++verified run
stack<int> st;
st.push(1); st.push(2); st.push(3);
cout << st.top() << ' ';            // 3: LIFO
st.pop();
cout << st.top() << ' ' << st.size() << '\n';

queue<string> q;
q.push("first"); q.push("second");
cout << q.front() << ' ' << q.back() << '\n';    // FIFO
q.pop();

priority_queue<int> maxh;                        // max-heap: largest on top
for (int x : {3, 9, 1, 7}) maxh.push(x);
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minh{greater<int>(), {3, 9, 1, 7}};   // min-heap
cout << maxh.top() << ' ' << minh.top() << '\n';

auto cmp = [](const pair<int, string>& a, const pair<int, string>& b) {
    return a.first > b.first;                    // "a comes AFTER b" → smallest first
};
priority_queue<pair<int, string>, vector<pair<int, string>>, decltype(cmp)> tasks(cmp);
tasks.push({3, "write"}); tasks.push({1, "plan"}); tasks.push({2, "code"});
while (!tasks.empty()) { cout << tasks.top().second << ' '; tasks.pop(); }
cout << '\n';
Output
3 2 2
first second
9 1
plan code write
RememberThe priority_queue comparator is "backwards"

The comparator answers "should a be below b?". With the default less<T> the largest element ends on top (max-heap); with greater<T> the smallest does (min-heap). For pairs, the default compares .first then .second, so priority_queue<pair<int,int>> pops the biggest first.

Adaptors have no iterators: you can only touch the top/front/back. pop() returns void — read top() first.

pair and tuple

C++verified run
pair<string, int> p = {"age", 21};
auto p2 = make_pair(3, 4.5);
cout << p.first << ' ' << p2.second << '\n';
tuple<int, string, double> t{1, "x", 2.5};
cout << get<1>(t) << ' ' << get<double>(t) << '\n';
auto [id, tag, val] = t;                         // structured bindings
int a; string b;
tie(a, b, ignore) = t;                           // unpack into existing variables
cout << id << tag << val << ' ' << a << b << '\n';
cout << boolalpha << (make_pair(1, 9) < make_pair(2, 0)) << '\n';   // lexicographic comparison
Output
age 4.5
x 2.5
1x2.5 1x
true

Choosing a container

You need Use
A list of items, index access, append at the end vector
Fast insert/remove at both ends deque
Lots of inserts/erases in the middle with stable iterators, splicing list
Unique sorted keys, min/max, "next greater key", ranges set / map
Fastest key lookup, no order needed unordered_set / unordered_map
Duplicate keys multiset / multimap / unordered_multimap
LIFO / FIFO stack / queue
Repeatedly get the min or max priority_queue
Fixed size known at compile time array
A set of bits bitset<N> or vector<bool>

Interview questions

QWhat are the components of the STL?

Containers (data structures), iterators (generalized pointers into containers), algorithms (generic functions working on iterator ranges) and function objects (callables that customize them), plus allocators that control memory. Algorithms are decoupled from containers through iterators.

QDifference between vector and list?

vector is a contiguous dynamic array: O(1) random access, cache-friendly, amortized O(1) push_back, but O(n) insertion in the middle, and reallocation invalidates iterators. list is a doubly linked list: O(1) insertion/erasure anywhere given an iterator, stable iterators, splice, but no random access, poor cache behaviour and ~16 bytes of pointers per node. In practice vector usually wins even for middle inserts on small data.

QDifference between vector and deque?

Both offer random access. deque adds O(1) push_front, and growing never moves existing elements (references stay valid on push at the ends). But it isn't contiguous — you can't pass &d[0] to a C API — and indexing costs an extra indirection.

Qmap vs unordered_map?

map is a red-black tree: keys sorted, O(log n) operations, ordered iteration, lower_bound, needs only <. unordered_map is a hash table: O(1) average but O(n) worst case, no order, needs a hash function and ==, and uses more memory. Use map for ordering or range queries and guaranteed log time; unordered_map for raw lookup speed.

Qset vs multiset vs unordered_set?

set stores unique keys in sorted order (O(log n)). multiset allows duplicates (erase(key) removes all copies; erase(find(key)) removes one). unordered_set stores unique keys in a hash table with O(1) average operations and no ordering.

QWhat does map::operator[] do if the key doesn't exist?

It inserts the key with a value-initialized mapped value (0, empty string) and returns a reference to it. So reading with [] modifies the map, and [] can't be used on a const map. Use find, count, contains or at to read.

QHow is priority_queue implemented? How do you make a min-heap?

As a binary heap stored in a vector, using push_heap/pop_heap: top O(1), push/pop O(log n). It's a max-heap with less<T>; for a min-heap use priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>> or push negated values.

QWhat are container adaptors?

stack, queue and priority_queue: wrappers that restrict an underlying container (deque by default, vector for priority_queue) to a specific interface. They have no iterators.

QHow do you use a custom key type in map and in unordered_map?

For map: define operator< for the type or pass a comparator type as the third template argument. For unordered_map: provide a hash functor (or specialize std::hash) and operator==.

Qinsert vs emplace vs operator[] for a map?

m[k] = v default-constructs the value if missing, then assigns — and always overwrites. insert({k, v}) builds a pair first and does nothing if the key exists. emplace(k, v) constructs the element in place (but may construct it even if the key exists); try_emplace doesn't construct anything when the key is present.

QHow do you remove elements from a map while iterating?

Use the iterator returned by erase: it = m.erase(it); in the matching branch and ++it otherwise. Or C++20's std::erase_if(m, pred). Erasing it and then incrementing it is undefined behaviour.

QWhat is the time complexity of lower_bound on a set vs on a vector?

Both O(log n) when used correctly: s.lower_bound(x) (member function) on a set, std::lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) on a sorted vector. Calling std::lower_bound on a set's iterators is O(n), because they're not random access.

QWhy does stack::pop() return void?

For exception safety: returning the popped element by value would require a copy after it's been removed; if that copy threw, the element would be lost. Separating top() (read) from pop() (remove) avoids the problem.

QWhen would you use list over vector?

When you need iterators and references that stay valid across insertions and erasures, O(1) splicing of sequences between lists, or very large elements that are expensive to move — e.g. an LRU cache's recency list. Otherwise vector's cache-friendliness usually wins.

QWhat is a bitset?

A fixed-size sequence of N bits (bitset<64>) with bitwise operators, count(), test(), set(), flip() and conversion to string/integer. It packs bits efficiently and is popular for subset DP and sieve-style problems.

QWhich containers keep elements sorted?

set, multiset, map and multimap (and C++23's flat_set/flat_map). priority_queue keeps only heap order: the top is the maximum, but the rest isn't sorted.
