vector, map & unordered_map Internals

How vector grows and why push_back is amortized O(1), reserve vs resize, vector<bool>, iterator invalidation rules, the red-black tree behind map, the bucket array behind unordered_map, rehashing and anti-hash attacks, and the heap inside priority_queue.

vector: three pointers and geometric growth

A vector object is just three pointers — begin, end (one past the last element) and end of storage — so sizeof(vector<T>) is 24 bytes whatever it holds. The elements live in one heap block.

When push_back finds size() == capacity(), the vector reallocates: it allocates a bigger block (twice as big in libstdc++ and libc++, 1.5× in MSVC), moves or copies every element across, destroys the old ones and frees the old block.

C++verified run
vector<int> v;
size_t last = v.capacity();
cout << "size 0 capacity " << last << '\n';
for (int i = 1; i <= 33; ++i) {
    v.push_back(i);
    if (v.capacity() != last) {
        cout << "size " << v.size() << " -> capacity " << v.capacity() << '\n';
        last = v.capacity();
    }
}
cout << "sizeof(vector<int>) = " << sizeof(v) << '\n';
Output
size 0 capacity 0
size 1 -> capacity 1
size 2 -> capacity 2
size 3 -> capacity 4
size 5 -> capacity 8
size 9 -> capacity 16
size 17 -> capacity 32
size 33 -> capacity 64
sizeof(vector<int>) = 24

Why push_back is amortized O(1): doubling means that pushing n elements triggers copies of 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n/2 < n elements in total, so the average cost per push is constant. Growing by a fixed amount (+10 each time) would make it O(n) per push — O(n²) overall.

C++verified run
vector<int> a;
a.reserve(100);                  // capacity 100, size 0: no elements exist yet
cout << a.size() << ' ' << a.capacity() << '\n';
vector<int> b;
b.resize(5);                     // size 5: five value-initialized zeros
b.resize(8, 7);                  // grow to 8, new elements are 7
cout << b.size() << ' ' << b[4] << ' ' << b[7] << '\n';
b.clear();                       // size 0, but capacity is kept
cout << b.size() << ' ' << b.capacity() << '\n';
vector<int>().swap(b);           // swap with an empty temporary: really frees the memory
cout << b.capacity() << '\n';
Output
0 100
8 0 7
0 10
0
reserve(n) resize(n)
Changes Capacity only Size (and capacity if needed)
Creates elements No Yes — default-constructed or copies of a value
Use when You know how many you'll push_back You want n elements to index into
Pitfall v.reserve(5); v[0] = 1; is out of bounds — size is still 0 v.resize(n) then push_back appends after the n zeros

push_back vs emplace_back

push_back(x) copies or moves an already-built object into the vector. emplace_back(args...) forwards the arguments and constructs the element in place, saving a temporary. For vector<pair<int,string>>, v.emplace_back(1, "a") vs v.push_back({1, "a"}). With an existing object, both are equivalent.

vector<bool> is not a container of bool

It's a specialization that packs bits — 8 per byte. v[i] returns a proxy object, not a bool&: you can't take &v[i] as a bool*, auto x = v[i] gives the proxy (still tied to the vector), and two threads writing different elements can race because they share a byte. Use vector<char>, deque<bool> or bitset when that matters.

Iterator invalidation

Container Insertion Erasure
vector If it reallocates: all iterators, pointers, references. Otherwise: those at or after the insertion point At or after the erased position
deque Middle: all. Ends: all iterators, but references stay valid Middle: all. Ends: only the erased elements
list, forward_list None Only the erased elements
set, map and multi-versions None Only the erased elements
unordered_* If it rehashes: all iterators (references stay valid). Otherwise none Only the erased elements
PitfallHolding a reference into a vector across push_back

int& first = v[0]; v.push_back(x); first = 5; — if push_back reallocated, first refers to freed memory. Keep indices instead of pointers, references or iterators when the vector can grow, or reserve enough up front.

The erase-remove idiom

remove/remove_if can't change a container's size — they only see iterators. They shift the kept elements forward and return the new logical end; erase then chops off the tail. C++20 wraps both steps in std::erase / std::erase_if.

C++verified run
vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 5};
auto new_end = remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);    // [1,3,4,5, ?,?,?]
cout << "kept " << (new_end - v.begin()) << ", size still " << v.size() << '\n';
v.erase(new_end, v.end());
for (int x : v) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';
vector<int> w{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6};
erase_if(w, [](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; });   // C++20: same thing in one call
for (int x : w) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';
Output
kept 4, size still 7
1 3 4 5 
1 3 5

deque and list inside

  • deque: a "map" (array) of pointers to fixed-size blocks (512 bytes each in libstdc++). Indexing goes through two levels, which is why it's O(1) but slower than vector. Adding a block at either end never moves existing elements.
  • list: each element is a node with prev and next pointers — 16 bytes of overhead per element plus a separate allocation. splice relinks nodes in O(1). It has its own sort() (a merge sort), because std::sort needs random-access iterators.

map and set: red-black trees

A red-black tree is a binary search tree that stays balanced by colouring each node and enforcing:

  1. Every node is red or black; the root is black.
  2. A red node never has a red child.
  3. Every path from a node down to a null leaf passes through the same number of black nodes.

Together these force the longest path to be at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2·log₂(n + 1): search, insert and erase are O(log n). Inserts need at most 2 rotations and erases at most 3. Each node stores a colour, parent/left/right pointers and the element — about 32 bytes of overhead per entry, in its own allocation.

Why red-black and not AVL? AVL trees are more strictly balanced (slightly faster lookups) but rotate more on inserts and deletes. Red-black trees do fewer rotations, which suits a general-purpose container with frequent updates.

unordered_map: buckets and chains

  • An array of buckets; each bucket leads to a chain (linked list) of nodes — separate chaining.
  • Lookup: compute hash(key), take % bucket_count() to pick the bucket, walk its chain comparing keys with ==.
  • Load factor = size() / bucket_count(). When it would exceed max_load_factor() (1.0 by default), the table rehashes: allocates about twice as many buckets (libstdc++ uses primes) and relinks every node — O(n) once in a while, amortized O(1).
  • In libstdc++, std::hash<int> is the identity function: the bucket is just key % bucket_count.
C++verified run
unordered_map<int, int> m;
size_t buckets = m.bucket_count();
cout << "buckets " << buckets << '\n';
for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {
    m[i] = i;
    if (m.bucket_count() != buckets) {
        buckets = m.bucket_count();
        cout << "size " << m.size() << " -> buckets " << buckets << '\n';
    }
}
cout << "load factor " << m.load_factor() << ", max " << m.max_load_factor() << '\n';
cout << "hash(42) = " << hash<int>{}(42) << '\n';
unordered_map<int, int> pre;
pre.reserve(1000);                    // allocate enough buckets once
cout << "after reserve(1000): " << pre.bucket_count() << " buckets\n";
Output
buckets 1
size 1 -> buckets 13
size 14 -> buckets 29
size 30 -> buckets 59
size 60 -> buckets 127
load factor 0.787402, max 1
hash(42) = 42
after reserve(1000): 1031 buckets

Worst case and anti-hash tests

If many keys land in one bucket, operations degrade to O(n). Because the default integer hash is predictable, competitive-programming hackers craft inputs (multiples of libstdc++'s bucket primes) that send every key to the same bucket and turn an O(n) solution into O(n²) — a classic Codeforces "TLE after hacks". Defences: use a randomized hash, or use map.

C++verified run
struct SplitMix64 {                       // a strong, randomly-seeded hash for integer keys
    static uint64_t mix(uint64_t x) {
        x += 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL;
        x = (x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
        x = (x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
        return x ^ (x >> 31);
    }
    size_t operator()(uint64_t x) const {
        static const uint64_t seed = chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count();
        return mix(x + seed);
    }
};
// in main:
unordered_map<long long, int, SplitMix64> safe;
safe[1'000'000'007] = 1;
safe[42] = 2;
cout << safe[42] + safe[1'000'000'007] << ' ' << safe.size() << '\n';
Output
3 2

priority_queue: a binary heap

The heap lives in a vector as a complete binary tree: the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, its parent is (i − 1) / 2, and every parent is ≥ its children (for a max-heap).

Operation How Cost
top() Element 0 O(1)
push(x) Append, then sift up while bigger than the parent O(log n)
pop() Move the last element to the root, then sift down O(log n)
Build from n elements (make_heap) Sift down from the last parent to the root O(n), not O(n log n)
C++verified run
vector<int> h{4, 9, 1, 7, 3};
make_heap(h.begin(), h.end());               // O(n) heapify: h[0] is the max
cout << h[0] << '\n';
h.push_back(10); push_heap(h.begin(), h.end());
pop_heap(h.begin(), h.end());                // moves the max to the back
cout << h.back() << ' ';
h.pop_back();
cout << h.front() << '\n';
sort_heap(h.begin(), h.end());               // heapsort the rest
for (int x : h) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';
Output
9
10 9
1 3 4 7 9

Choosing between map and unordered_map (performance view)

map unordered_map
Lookup O(log n), guaranteed O(1) average, O(n) worst
Memory One node per entry (~32 bytes overhead) One node per entry plus the bucket array
Cache behaviour Pointer chasing down the tree One bucket access plus a short chain
Iteration order Sorted Unspecified, changes on rehash
Key requirements < (strict weak ordering) hash and ==
Extra operations lower_bound, upper_bound, min/max, ordered ranges reserve, bucket interface
Adversarial input Safe Can be attacked unless the hash is randomized

Interview questions

QHow does vector grow, and why by a multiplicative factor?

When it runs out of capacity it allocates a block about twice as large (1.5× in MSVC), moves or copies the elements over and frees the old block. Geometric growth makes the total copying for n pushes O(n), so each push_back is amortized O(1); additive growth would make it O(n) per push.

QExplain amortized O(1) for push_back.

Most pushes just construct one element at the end. Occasionally a push triggers reallocation costing O(size). With doubling, reallocations happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, so the total copying across n pushes is below 2n. Spread over n operations that's a constant per push.

QWhat's the difference between reserve and resize?

reserve(n) only ensures capacity ≥ n — no elements are created and size() doesn't change. resize(n) changes the number of elements, constructing new ones (or destroying extra ones). After reserve(10) you still can't write v[0].

QWhen does a vector invalidate iterators?

On any reallocation (insertion beyond capacity, reserve, shrink_to_fit) every iterator, pointer and reference is invalidated. Without reallocation, insert invalidates those at or after the insertion point, and erase those at or after the erased element.

QWhat is special about vector<bool>?

It's a space-optimized specialization storing one bit per element, so operator[] returns a proxy object instead of bool&. It doesn't meet the container requirements: you can't get a bool* to an element, generic code expecting T& breaks, and concurrent writes to different elements can race.

QHow is std::map implemented?

As a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree whose colouring rules keep the height within 2·log₂(n+1). That gives O(log n) search, insertion and deletion, and an in-order traversal yields keys sorted.

QWhy are red-black trees used instead of AVL trees?

Both guarantee O(log n). AVL is more rigidly balanced, so lookups are slightly faster, but it may perform many rotations per update. Red-black trees need at most 2 rotations per insertion and 3 per deletion, making updates cheaper — better for a general-purpose container.

QHow is unordered_map implemented?

As a hash table with separate chaining: a bucket array where each bucket points to a linked list of nodes. The key's hash modulo the bucket count picks the bucket. When the load factor exceeds the maximum (1.0 by default), it rehashes into roughly twice as many buckets.

QWhat is the load factor? What happens on rehash?

The average number of elements per bucket: size() / bucket_count(). When an insertion would push it above max_load_factor(), the container allocates a larger bucket array and relinks every node into its new bucket — O(n) for that insertion, and all iterators are invalidated (references and pointers to elements stay valid).

QWhat is the worst-case complexity of unordered_map, and how do you avoid it?

O(n) per operation, when many keys hash to the same bucket — through bad luck, a poor hash, or deliberately crafted input. Avoid it with a good randomized hash (like splitmix64 with a time-based seed), by calling reserve, or by switching to map for guaranteed O(log n).

QHow do you write a hash for a custom type?

Provide a functor whose operator() returns size_t and combines the members' hashes — for a pair, something like h(a) ^ (h(b) << 1) or packing two 32-bit values into one 64-bit value — and pass it as the third template argument, or specialize std::hash<T>. The type also needs operator==.

QHow does priority_queue work internally?

It keeps a binary heap in a vector: element 0 is the top; children of i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2. push appends and sifts up, pop moves the last element to the root and sifts down — both O(log n); top is O(1).

QWhy is building a heap O(n) and not O(n log n)?

Heapify sifts down from the last parent upwards. Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a level or two: n/4 nodes move at most 1 level, n/8 at most 2, and so on. The sum n·Σ k/2^(k+1) converges to O(n).

QWhat is the erase-remove idiom?

v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end());. remove shifts the elements to keep to the front and returns the new logical end (it can't shrink the container); erase deletes the leftover tail. C++20 provides std::erase(v, x) and std::erase_if(v, pred).

QHow is deque implemented?

As an array of pointers to fixed-size blocks. Indexing computes which block and the offset within it. New blocks are added at either end without moving existing elements, giving O(1) push_front/push_back and stable references at the ends.

Iterators & Algorithms

Iterators and their categories, half-open ranges, the algorithm families you should know by heart, how std::sort works, strict weak ordering, lower_bound and upper_bound semantics, and numeric algorithms.

Iterators

An iterator is an object that points into a sequence and can move through it — a generalization of a pointer. Every container provides begin() (first element) and end() (one past the last), so a range is half-open: [begin, end). An empty range has begin == end.

Category Can do Containers / sources
Input Read once, move forward (*it, ++it) istream_iterator
Output Write once, move forward ostream_iterator, back_inserter
Forward Read/write, multi-pass, ++ forward_list, unordered_*
Bidirectional Forward + -- list, set, map
Random access Bidirectional + it + n, it[n], <, it2 - it1 deque
Contiguous C++20 Random access + elements adjacent in memory vector, array, string, C arrays

Algorithms state the category they need: std::sort requires random access, so it can't sort a list (use list::sort).

C++verified run
vector<int> v{10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
auto it = v.begin();
advance(it, 2);                         // works for any iterator (O(n) for non-random-access)
cout << *it << ' ' << *next(it) << ' ' << *prev(it) << ' ' << distance(v.begin(), it) << '\n';
for (auto r = v.rbegin(); r != v.rend(); ++r) cout << *r << ' ';   // reverse iterators
cout << '\n';
vector<int> dst;
copy_if(v.begin(), v.end(), back_inserter(dst), [](int x) { return x > 25; });   // insert iterator
copy(dst.begin(), dst.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, ","));
cout << '\n';
list<int> l{3, 1, 2};
l.sort();                               // std::sort(l.begin(), l.end()) would not compile
cout << l.front() << '\n';
Output
30 40 20 2
50 40 30 20 10 
30,40,50,
1

Family Algorithms

C++verified run
vector<int> v{5, 3, 8, 3, 9, 1, 3};
cout << count(v.begin(), v.end(), 3) << ' '
     << *max_element(v.begin(), v.end()) << ' '
     << (find(v.begin(), v.end(), 8) - v.begin()) << ' '
     << boolalpha << all_of(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x > 0; }) << '\n';

vector<int> sq(v.size());
transform(v.begin(), v.end(), sq.begin(), [](int x) { return x * x; });
cout << accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) << ' ' << sq[2] << '\n';

sort(v.begin(), v.end());                                // 1 3 3 3 5 8 9
v.erase(unique(v.begin(), v.end()), v.end());            // unique: drops ADJACENT duplicates
for (int x : v) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';

reverse(v.begin(), v.end());
rotate(v.begin(), v.begin() + 1, v.end());               // left-rotate by one
for (int x : v) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';

vector<int> pre(5);
iota(pre.begin(), pre.end(), 1);                         // 1 2 3 4 5
partial_sum(pre.begin(), pre.end(), pre.begin());        // prefix sums: 1 3 6 10 15
for (int x : pre) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n' << gcd(84, 36) << ' ' << lcm(4, 6) << ' ' << clamp(15, 0, 10) << '\n';
Output
3 9 2 true
32 64
1 3 5 8 9 
8 5 3 1 9 
1 3 6 10 15 
12 12 10
Pitfallaccumulate uses the type of its initial value

accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) sums in int even for a vector<long long> — it overflows. Write 0LL. And accumulate(d.begin(), d.end(), 0) on doubles truncates every partial sum to int: write 0.0.

Sorting

C++verified run
vector<pair<string, int>> people{{"ravi", 30}, {"anu", 25}, {"sai", 30}, {"kiran", 22}};
sort(people.begin(), people.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
    if (a.second != b.second) return a.second > b.second;   // age descending
    return a.first < b.first;                               // then name ascending
});
for (auto& [n, a] : people) cout << n << a << ' ';
cout << '\n';

vector<int> v{9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6};
partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + 3, v.end());   // smallest 3, in order, at the front
cout << v[0] << v[1] << v[2] << '\n';
vector<int> w{9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6};
nth_element(w.begin(), w.begin() + 3, w.end());    // w[3] is what a full sort would put there
cout << "median-ish element: " << w[3] << '\n';    // O(n) average

vector<pair<int, char>> s{{2, 'a'}, {1, 'b'}, {2, 'c'}, {1, 'd'}};
stable_sort(s.begin(), s.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) { return a.first < b.first; });
for (auto& [k, c] : s) cout << k << c << ' ';      // equal keys keep their original order
cout << '\n';
Output
ravi30 sai30 anu25 kiran22 
124
median-ish element: 6
1b 1d 2a 2c
Algorithm Complexity Stable Notes
sort O(n log n) worst case No Introsort: quicksort, switching to heapsort if recursion gets too deep, and insertion sort for small ranges
stable_sort O(n log n) (O(n log² n) without extra memory) Yes Merge sort
partial_sort(first, mid, last) O(n log k) No Heap-based; top-k in order
nth_element O(n) average No Quickselect; k-th smallest
list::sort O(n log n) Yes Merge sort on nodes

Strict weak ordering

A comparator must behave like <: comp(a, a) is false, and if comp(a, b) then not comp(b, a). Using <= breaks this — std::sort may read past the end of the array and crash, or produce garbage. To sort descending use > or greater<>(), never >=.

Binary search on sorted ranges

C++verified run
vector<int> a{1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8};
auto lb = lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 3);    // first element >= 3
auto ub = upper_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 3);    // first element >  3
cout << (lb - a.begin()) << ' ' << (ub - a.begin()) << ' ' << (ub - lb) << '\n';   // count of 3s
auto [lo, hi] = equal_range(a.begin(), a.end(), 3);
cout << (hi - lo) << ' ' << boolalpha << binary_search(a.begin(), a.end(), 4) << '\n';
cout << (lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 4) - a.begin()) << '\n';   // where 4 would be inserted
cout << (lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 99) == a.end()) << '\n';   // nothing >= 99
// count of elements in [2, 6]:
cout << upper_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 6) - lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), 2) << '\n';
Output
1 4 3
3 false
4
true
4
Question Expression
First index with a[i] >= x lower_bound(…, x) - a.begin()
First index with a[i] > x upper_bound(…, x) - a.begin()
Last index with a[i] <= x upper_bound(…, x) - a.begin() - 1
Last index with a[i] < x lower_bound(…, x) - a.begin() - 1
How many equal x upper_bound - lower_bound
Is x present binary_search(…, x)

These require the range to be sorted by the same comparator you pass; on unsorted data the result is meaningless. Section 31 builds binary search by hand and applies it to "binary search on the answer".

Permutations and set operations

C++verified run
string s = "abc";
do cout << s << ' '; while (next_permutation(s.begin(), s.end()));   // all permutations, in order
cout << '\n';
vector<int> x{1, 2, 4, 6}, y{2, 3, 4};
vector<int> both, either;
set_intersection(x.begin(), x.end(), y.begin(), y.end(), back_inserter(both));
set_union(x.begin(), x.end(), y.begin(), y.end(), back_inserter(either));
for (int v : both) cout << v << ' ';
cout << "| ";
for (int v : either) cout << v << ' ';
cout << '\n';
Output
abc acb bac bca cab cba 
2 4 | 1 2 3 4 6

next_permutation rearranges into the next lexicographically greater permutation and returns false after the last one (wrapping back to sorted order). Start from sorted input to visit all n! permutations.

Ranges C++20

std::ranges versions take the container directly and accept projections: ranges::sort(v), ranges::find(v, x), ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::age). Views (views::filter, views::transform) are covered in section 22.

Interview questions

QWhat is an iterator?

An object that refers to an element in a sequence and can be advanced through it — the STL's generalization of a pointer. It decouples algorithms from containers: sort works on any random-access range, whatever container provides it.

QWhat are the iterator categories?

Input and output (single pass), forward (multi-pass, ++), bidirectional (also --), random access (jumps, <, subtraction) and, in C++20, contiguous. Each category supports everything the previous one does.

QWhy is end() one past the last element?

Half-open ranges [begin, end) make empty ranges natural (begin == end), let the size be end - begin, and let loops use it != end uniformly. end() must never be dereferenced.

QHow does std::sort work? What is its complexity?

It's introsort: quicksort with median-of-three pivots, switching to heapsort if the recursion depth exceeds about 2·log n (so the worst case stays O(n log n)), and finishing small partitions with insertion sort. It's not stable and needs random-access iterators.

QDifference between sort and stable_sort?

stable_sort keeps equal elements in their original relative order and is typically a merge sort — O(n log n) with a temporary buffer. sort gives no such guarantee and is usually faster. Use stable_sort when sorting by one key after another, or when ties must keep input order.

QWhat is a strict weak ordering, and what happens if your comparator violates it?

A comparator that acts like <: irreflexive (comp(a, a) is false), asymmetric, transitive, and with transitive equivalence. Violating it — typically by using <= — is undefined behaviour: std::sort can loop out of bounds and crash, and set/map can lose or duplicate keys.

QWhat do lower_bound and upper_bound return?

On a sorted range, lower_bound(x) returns an iterator to the first element not less than x (>= x), and upper_bound(x) to the first element greater than x. Their difference is the number of elements equal to x. Both return end() if no such element exists and run in O(log n).

QHow does remove work, and why do you need erase after it?

remove moves every element that should stay towards the front, in order, and returns an iterator to the new logical end; the elements after it are left in a valid but unspecified state. Algorithms can't change a container's size, so you call erase(new_end, end()) to actually shrink it.

QWhat does unique do?

It removes consecutive duplicates (keeping the first of each run) using the same shifting trick as remove, returning the new logical end. To remove all duplicates, sort first, then erase(unique(...), end()).

Qnth_element vs partial_sort vs sort for "top k"?

nth_element places the k-th element correctly with smaller ones before it and larger after, in O(n) average, without ordering them. partial_sort sorts just the first k, O(n log k). sort orders everything, O(n log n). For "the k smallest, any order", nth_element; "the k smallest, sorted", partial_sort.

QWhat does next_permutation do?

It transforms the range into the next permutation in lexicographic order and returns true, or, if it was the last permutation, transforms it into the first (sorted) one and returns false. Starting from sorted order and looping until it returns false enumerates all permutations without duplicates, even with repeated elements.

QWhat's the difference between accumulate and reduce?

accumulate folds strictly left to right, with the type of the initial value. reduce (C++17) may regroup and reorder the operations — which allows parallel execution (reduce(execution::par, …)) — so the operation should be associative and commutative.

QCan you use std::sort on a list?

No: std::sort requires random-access iterators, and list iterators are bidirectional. Use the member list::sort(), a merge sort that relinks nodes without moving elements.

QHow do you sort in descending order?

sort(v.begin(), v.end(), greater<>()), or sort(v.rbegin(), v.rend()), or a lambda [](int a, int b) { return a > b; }. Never use >=.

Lambdas, Functors & std::function

Lambda syntax and what the compiler turns it into, every capture form and its traps, mutable, generic and template lambdas, recursive lambdas for DFS, std::function and its cost, and when to use templates, function pointers or std::function.

Lambda syntax

Text
[captures] (parameters) specifiers -> return_type { body }
C++verified run
auto add = [](int a, int b) { return a + b; };            // return type deduced
auto half = [](double x) -> double { return x / 2; };     // explicit return type
cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << half(5) << '\n';

vector<int> v{5, 2, 9, 1};
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; });     // inline comparator
int threshold = 3;
auto big = count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [threshold](int x) { return x > threshold; });
cout << v[0] << ' ' << big << '\n';
cout << [](int n) { return n * n; }(7) << '\n';               // immediately invoked
Output
5 2.5
9 2
49

What a lambda really is

The compiler turns each lambda into an unnamed closure class with an operator(), and the captures become its data members. These two are equivalent:

C++verified run
int factor = 3;
auto lam = [factor](int x) { return x * factor; };

class Closure {                     // roughly what the compiler writes for the lambda above
    int factor;
public:
    explicit Closure(int f) : factor(f) {}
    int operator()(int x) const { return x * factor; }   // const: captures are read-only
};
Closure handwritten(factor);
cout << lam(5) << ' ' << handwritten(5) << '\n';
Output
15 15
  • Every lambda expression has its own unique type — use auto, a template parameter or std::function to hold it.
  • operator() is const by default, so value captures can't be modified unless the lambda is mutable.
  • A lambda with no captures converts implicitly to a plain function pointer, so it can be passed to C APIs.

Captures

Capture Meaning
[] Nothing
[x] x by value (a copy made when the lambda is created)
[&x] x by reference
[=] Every used local by value (and this implicitly, deprecated in C++20 — write [=, this])
[&] Every used local by reference
[=, &x] / [&, x] Default by value except x by reference / the opposite
[this] The current object by pointer (members are accessed through it)
[*this] C++17 A copy of the current object
[y = expr] C++14 Init capture: a new member y initialized from any expression, e.g. [p = std::move(ptr)]
C++verified run
int x = 10;
auto by_value = [x] { return x; };
auto by_ref = [&x] { return x; };
x = 20;
cout << by_value() << ' ' << by_ref() << '\n';         // 10 20: the copy was taken at creation

int calls = 0;
auto counter = [calls]() mutable { return ++calls; };  // mutable: modifies ITS OWN copy
counter(); counter();
cout << counter() << ' ' << calls << '\n';             // 3 0

auto owned = make_unique<int>(42);
auto taker = [p = std::move(owned)] { return *p; };    // move-only capture via init capture
cout << taker() << ' ' << boolalpha << (owned == nullptr) << '\n';
Output
10 20
3 0
42 true
PitfallReference captures can dangle

A lambda that captures locals by reference and outlives them — returned from a function, stored in a member, or handed to a thread — reads freed stack memory. [&] is fine for lambdas used immediately (comparators, for_each); capture by value (or move) for anything that escapes.

C++compiles
function<int()> make_bad() {
    int local = 7;
    return [&local] { return local; };   // dangling: local dies when make_bad returns
}
function<int()> make_good() {
    int local = 7;
    return [local] { return local; };    // a copy travels with the lambda
}

Generic and template lambdas

C++verified run
auto print = [](const auto& x) { cout << x << ' '; };   // generic lambda (C++14): a template
print(42); print(3.5); print("text");
cout << '\n';
auto sum_vec = []<typename T>(const vector<T>& v) {      // template lambda (C++20)
    T total{};
    for (const T& e : v) total += e;
    return total;
};
cout << sum_vec(vector<int>{1, 2, 3}) << ' ' << sum_vec(vector<double>{0.5, 0.25}) << '\n';
Output
42 3.5 text 
6 0.75

Recursive lambdas

A lambda can't name itself, so recursion needs a trick. The fastest is to pass the lambda to itself as a generic parameter — the standard way to write DFS inside main in contests.

C++verified run
int n = 6;
vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
for (auto [a, b] : vector<pair<int, int>>{{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {2, 5}}) {
    adj[a].push_back(b);
    adj[b].push_back(a);
}
vector<int> depth(n, -1);
auto dfs = [&](auto&& self, int u, int d) -> void {     // self = the lambda itself
    depth[u] = d;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (depth[v] == -1) self(self, v, d + 1);
};
dfs(dfs, 0, 0);
for (int d : depth) cout << d << ' ';
cout << '\n';

function<long long(int)> fact = [&](int k) -> long long {   // alternative: std::function (slower)
    return k <= 1 ? 1 : k * fact(k - 1);
};
cout << fact(15) << '\n';
Output
0 1 1 2 2 2 
1307674368000

C++23's deducing this allows [](this auto&& self, int u) { … self(v); } directly.

std::function

std::function<R(Args...)> is a type-erased wrapper that can hold any callable with that signature — function pointer, lambda, functor, bound member function.

C++verified run
int twice(int x) { return 2 * x; }
struct Triple { int operator()(int x) const { return 3 * x; } };
// in main:
map<string, function<int(int)>> ops;
ops["twice"] = twice;
ops["triple"] = Triple{};
ops["square"] = [](int x) { return x * x; };
for (auto& [name, f] : ops) cout << name << '=' << f(5) << ' ';
cout << '\n';
function<void()> empty;
try { empty(); } catch (const bad_function_call&) { cout << "bad_function_call\n"; }
Output
square=25 triple=15 twice=10 
bad_function_call
Template parameter (template <class F> void run(F f)) Function pointer std::function
Holds Any callable Captureless functions only Any callable
Call cost Direct; can inline Indirect Indirect, through type erasure
May allocate No No Yes, for large captures (small ones fit inline)
Can be stored in containers of mixed callables No (each type differs) Yes Yes
Use for Algorithms, hot paths C APIs, simple callbacks Callbacks stored for later, dispatch tables, plugin hooks

std::bind creates callables by fixing arguments (bind(f, _1, 10)), but a lambda is clearer and easier to optimize — prefer lambdas. std::invoke(f, args...) calls any callable uniformly, including pointers to members.

Interview questions

QWhat is a lambda expression?

An anonymous function object defined inline: [captures](params) { body }. The compiler generates a unique closure class whose operator() contains the body and whose data members hold the captures. Used for comparators, predicates, callbacks and small local helpers.

QWhat is the difference between capturing by value and by reference?

By value copies the variable into the closure when the lambda is created; later changes to the original aren't seen, and the copy is read-only unless the lambda is mutable. By reference stores a reference: the lambda sees current values and can modify them, but it dangles if the lambda outlives the variable.

QWhat does mutable do on a lambda?

It makes the closure's operator() non-const, so the lambda can modify its by-value captured copies. The originals are never affected.

QWhat is the type of a lambda?

A unique, unnamed closure type generated by the compiler; two identical lambda expressions have different types. Store it with auto, pass it as a template parameter, or wrap it in std::function when a fixed type is needed.

QCan a lambda be converted to a function pointer?

Yes, if it captures nothing: int (*fp)(int) = [](int x) { return x + 1; };. Capturing lambdas carry state, so they can't be plain function pointers.

QWhat are generic lambdas?

Lambdas with auto parameters (C++14), whose operator() is a template — [](auto a, auto b) { return a < b; } works for any comparable types. C++20 adds an explicit template parameter list: []<typename T>(vector<T>& v) {...}.

QWhat is an init capture?

A capture that creates a new member from an arbitrary expression: [n = v.size()], [p = std::move(ptr)]. It's how you move a move-only object (like a unique_ptr) into a lambda (C++14).

QHow do you write a recursive lambda?

Pass the lambda to itself as an auto&& parameter (auto dfs = [&](auto&& self, int u) {... self(self, v); }; dfs(dfs, 0);), store it in a std::function it captures by reference, or use C++23's deducing this.

QWhat is std::function and what does it cost?

A polymorphic wrapper that can store any callable with a given signature. It uses type erasure, so calls are indirect (no inlining) and storing large callables may allocate on the heap. Calling an empty one throws bad_function_call.

QLambda vs functor vs function pointer?

A functor is a class with operator(), able to hold state and be inlined. A lambda is concise syntax for an unnamed functor. A function pointer can't hold state and is usually called indirectly. Prefer lambdas; use functors when you need a named, reusable type (e.g. a hash or comparator type for a container).

QWhat does [=] capture inside a member function?

All used locals by value, plus — implicitly — the this pointer, so members are accessed by reference through this and can dangle if the object dies. C++20 deprecates the implicit this capture with [=]: write [=, this] or [=, *this] (a copy of the object) explicitly.

QWhen does a captured value get copied — at definition or at call time?

At the point where the lambda expression is evaluated (the closure is created). Calling it later uses that snapshot, which is why [x] printed 10 after x changed to 20.
