Preprocessor, Linking & Tools

Preprocessor directives and macro traps, header guards, the One Definition Rule, static vs shared libraries and linker errors, Make and CMake, debugging with gdb, sanitizers and Valgrind, and what optimization levels do.

The preprocessor

The preprocessor runs before compilation and works on text, knowing nothing about types or scopes.

Directive Purpose
#include <x> / #include "x" Paste a file in
#define NAME value, #define F(x) ... Object-like and function-like macros
#undef NAME Remove a macro
#if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elif, #else, #endif Conditional compilation
#pragma once, #pragma pack Compiler-specific instructions
#error "msg" Stop the build with a message
__FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, __cplusplus, NDEBUG Predefined names (__func__ is actually a variable)
C++verified run
#define SQUARE_BAD(x) x * x
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define MAX_BAD(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))
#define STR(x) #x                       // stringize
#define CONCAT(a, b) a##b               // token pasting
constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }   // the right tool
// in main:
cout << SQUARE_BAD(2 + 3) << ' ' << SQUARE(2 + 3) << ' ' << square(2 + 3) << '\n';  // 2+3*2+3 = 11
int i = 5;
int m = MAX_BAD(i++, 3);                 // i++ is evaluated twice
cout << m << ' ' << i << '\n';
int CONCAT(my, Var) = 7;                 // declares myVar
cout << STR(hello world) << ' ' << myVar << '\n';
cout << __func__ << ' ' << __cplusplus << '\n';
Output
11 25 25
6 7
hello world 7
main 202002

Macro problems: missing parentheses change precedence, arguments are evaluated more than once, macros ignore scope and namespaces, and they're invisible to the debugger. Use constexpr constants, inline/constexpr functions and templates instead; keep macros for include guards, conditional compilation and logging that needs __FILE__/__LINE__.

Include guards

A header included twice in one translation unit would define its classes twice. Guard it:

C++compiles
#ifndef GEOMETRY_POINT_H        // traditional include guard
#define GEOMETRY_POINT_H
struct GuardedPoint { int x, y; };
#endif

Or put #pragma once at the top — non-standard but supported by every major compiler, shorter, and immune to two headers accidentally choosing the same guard name.

The One Definition Rule (ODR)

  1. Within one translation unit, every variable, function, class, enum and template may be defined once.
  2. Across the whole program, every non-inline function and variable that is used must be defined exactly once.
  3. Classes, enums, inline functions/variables and templates may be defined in several translation units (that's why they live in headers) — but all definitions must be identical.

Breaking rule 2 gives multiple definition or undefined reference linker errors. Breaking rule 3 (two different definitions of a class Config in two .cpp files) is undefined behaviour with no diagnostic required — the program may silently use the wrong one.

Static vs shared libraries

Shell
# static library: object files archived; code is copied into each executable
g++ -c math.cpp -o math.o && ar rcs libmath.a math.o
g++ main.cpp -L. -lmath -o app_static

# shared library: position-independent code, loaded at run time
g++ -fPIC -shared math.cpp -o libmath.so
g++ main.cpp -L. -lmath -o app_shared
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./app_shared
ldd app_shared            # which shared libraries the program needs
nm -C math.o              # symbols in an object file, demangled
c++filt _Z6squarei        # demangle a name: square(int)
Static (.a, .lib) Shared / dynamic (.so, .dll, .dylib)
When linked At build time, into the executable At load time (or dlopen at run time)
Executable size Larger Smaller
Updating the library Relink every program Replace the file; all programs pick it up
Memory with many processes One copy per process One copy in RAM shared by all
Deployment Self-contained Library must be installed and ABI-compatible
Startup Slightly faster Symbol resolution at load time

Reading linker errors

Error Usual cause
undefined reference to 'foo()' Declared but never defined; the .cpp with the definition wasn't compiled or linked; a library is missing from the command line (or listed before the files that use it); C/C++ linkage mismatch (extern "C")
undefined reference to 'vtable for X' A virtual function of X (often the destructor) is declared but never defined
multiple definition of 'x' A non-inline function or global defined in a header included by several .cpp files
undefined reference to 'main' Linking a file without main as a program, or misspelled main
Template "undefined reference" Template definition in a .cpp file instead of the header

Make and CMake

Makefile
# Makefile: rebuild only what changed (recipe lines must start with a TAB)
CXX = g++
CXXFLAGS = -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2
app: main.o math.o
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) main.o math.o -o app
%.o: %.cpp
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
clean:
	rm -f *.o app
CMake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(Handbook CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
add_library(mathlib src/math.cpp)
target_include_directories(mathlib PUBLIC include)
add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE mathlib)
Shell
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build

CMake is the de-facto build system for C++: it generates Makefiles or Ninja files for any platform and handles dependencies between targets.

Debugging with gdb

Shell
g++ -g -O0 app.cpp -o app      # debug info, no optimization
gdb ./app
Command Does
break main / break file.cpp:42 Set a breakpoint
run [args] Start the program
next / step Next line, stepping over / into calls
continue Run to the next breakpoint
print x, print v.size(), display x Inspect values
bt (backtrace) Show the call stack — the first thing to do after a crash
frame 2, info locals Move up the stack, list locals
watch x Stop when x changes
finish Run until the current function returns

After a crash with core dumps enabled (ulimit -c unlimited), gdb ./app core and bt show where it died.

Sanitizers and Valgrind

Tool Flag Catches
AddressSanitizer -fsanitize=address Out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free, stack overflow of buffers, leaks (LeakSanitizer)
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer -fsanitize=undefined Signed overflow, bad shifts, null dereference, misaligned access, invalid enum/bool values
ThreadSanitizer -fsanitize=thread Data races, lock-order inversions (can't combine with ASan)
MemorySanitizer (clang) -fsanitize=memory Reads of uninitialized memory
Valgrind memcheck valgrind ./app Leaks, invalid reads/writes, uninitialized values — no recompile, ~20–50× slower

Every example in this handbook was run with ASan and UBSan.

Optimization levels

Flag What you get
-O0 No optimization; fastest compile; best for debugging
-Og Optimizations that don't hurt debugging
-O1 Basic optimizations
-O2 The standard release level: inlining, loop optimizations, vectorization (since GCC 12)
-O3 More aggressive inlining and vectorization; bigger code, not always faster
-Os Optimize for size
-march=native Use every instruction your CPU supports (binary may not run elsewhere)
-flto Link-time optimization across translation units

"Works in debug, crashes in release" almost always means undefined behaviour (an uninitialized variable, out-of-bounds access, a data race) that the optimizer exploited — run the sanitizers. Also remember assert disappears when NDEBUG is defined, as it is in typical release builds.

Two websites worth bookmarking: Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) shows the assembly your code becomes under any compiler and flags; C++ Insights (cppinsights.io) shows what the compiler generates for lambdas, range-for, structured bindings and templates.

Interview questions

QWhat is the preprocessor and what does it do?

A text-processing stage before compilation that handles # directives: it pastes included files, expands macros, and keeps or drops code under #if/#ifdef. Its output is a translation unit.

QWhat are the problems with macros?

They're plain text substitution: no type checking, arguments evaluated multiple times (MAX(i++, j)), precedence surprises without parentheses, no respect for scope or namespaces, and they're invisible in the debugger. Prefer constexpr, inline functions, templates and enum class.

QWhat is an include guard? #pragma once vs #ifndef?

A mechanism that makes a header's content appear only once per translation unit. #ifndef X / #define X / #endif is standard; #pragma once is non-standard but universally supported, shorter and can't suffer guard-name collisions.

QWhat is the One Definition Rule?

Each entity may have only one definition per translation unit, non-inline functions and variables exactly one definition in the whole program, and entities allowed in multiple translation units (classes, inline functions, templates) must have identical definitions everywhere. Violations give linker errors or silent undefined behaviour.

QStatic vs dynamic linking?

Static linking copies library code into the executable at build time: self-contained and slightly faster to start, but larger and must be relinked to update. Dynamic linking resolves the library at load time: smaller executables, one shared copy in memory, updatable independently, but requires compatible libraries at run time.

QWhat causes "undefined reference" errors?

The linker can't find a definition for a used symbol: the function has no body, the file defining it isn't linked, a library is missing or ordered wrongly on the command line, a template's definition sits in a .cpp file, a virtual function was never defined (vtable error), or C/C++ name-mangling mismatches.

QHow do you debug a segmentation fault?

Compile with -g, run under gdb and get a backtrace (bt) at the crash, or run the program with -fsanitize=address, which reports the exact invalid access and where the memory was allocated and freed. Valgrind is an alternative without recompiling.

QWhat are sanitizers?

Compiler instrumentation that detects bugs at run time: AddressSanitizer for memory errors and leaks, UBSan for undefined behaviour, ThreadSanitizer for data races, MemorySanitizer for uninitialized reads. They're far faster than Valgrind and should run in testing and CI.

QWhy might code work at -O0 but fail at -O2?

It almost always contains undefined behaviour: the optimizer assumes UB never happens (no signed overflow, no out-of-bounds, no data races) and transforms code accordingly, changing the behaviour of a program that does trigger it. Uninitialized variables also tend to hold different garbage.

QWhat is name mangling and how do you read mangled names?

The compiler encodes namespaces, classes and parameter types into symbol names so overloads have unique linker names. Tools like c++filt or nm -C turn _Z6squarei back into square(int).

QWhat does CMake do?

It's a build-system generator: from a platform-independent CMakeLists.txt describing targets, sources, include directories and dependencies, it generates native build files (Makefiles, Ninja, Visual Studio) and handles configuration like build type and compiler flags.

QWhat is the difference between -O2 and -O3?

-O3 adds more aggressive optimizations — heavier inlining, loop unrolling and vectorization — that increase code size and compile time. It's often but not always faster than -O2; measure. -O2 is the common release default.

26processes · scheduling · synchronization · deadlock · virtual memory · paging · IPC15 questions

OS Concepts Asked with C++

The operating-systems questions that come with C++ roles — processes and threads, fork and exec, scheduling algorithms, the critical-section problem, deadlock handling, paging and virtual memory, page replacement, fragmentation and IPC — tied back to what your C++ program does.

Program, process, thread

Program Process Thread
Is An executable file on disk A program in execution A path of execution inside a process
Memory — Own address space (code, data, heap, stacks) Shares the process's memory; own stack and registers
Creation cost — High (fork, new page tables) Low
Switching cost — High (address space switch, TLB flush) Lower
Isolation — A crash doesn't affect other processes A crash kills the whole process
Communication — IPC: pipes, sockets, shared memory Directly through shared memory, with synchronization

The OS tracks each process in a Process Control Block (PCB): PID, state, program counter, registers, memory-management info, open files, scheduling priority.

Process states: new → ready (waiting for a CPU) → running → back to ready when preempted, or to waiting/blocked for I/O, then ready again → terminated. A finished child whose parent hasn't called wait() is a zombie; a child whose parent died first is an orphan, adopted by init/systemd.

fork and exec

C++verified run
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <unistd.h>
// in main:
int shared_before_fork = 10;
cout.flush();                                // flush, or the child inherits unflushed output
pid_t pid = fork();                          // one process calls it, two processes return
if (pid == 0) {                              // child: fork returned 0
    shared_before_fork += 5;                 // modifies the CHILD's copy only
    cout << "child sees " << shared_before_fork << '\n';
    cout.flush();
    _exit(0);
}
waitpid(pid, nullptr, 0);                    // parent: wait for the child (no zombie)
cout << "parent sees " << shared_before_fork << '\n';
Output
child sees 15
parent sees 10
  • fork() duplicates the calling process. The child gets a copy of the address space — implemented with copy-on-write: pages are shared until one side writes. It returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, −1 on failure.
  • exec*() replaces the current process image with a new program (same PID). Shells run commands with fork + exec + wait.
  • Only the calling thread is duplicated by fork in a multithreaded program, so a child should call only async-signal-safe functions before exec.

User mode, kernel mode and system calls

The CPU runs application code in user mode, unable to touch hardware or other processes' memory. A system call (read, write, mmap, fork) traps into kernel mode, where the OS does the privileged work and returns. Your std::cout << x eventually calls write; new eventually calls brk or mmap when the allocator needs more memory from the OS. A context switch saves one thread's registers and loads another's; switching between processes also switches page tables.

CPU scheduling

Algorithm Rule Preemptive Notes
FCFS First come, first served No Simple; convoy effect — short jobs wait behind long ones
SJF Shortest job first No Optimal average waiting time, but needs burst lengths; long jobs can starve
SRTF Shortest remaining time first Yes Preemptive SJF
Round Robin Each process gets a time quantum in turn Yes Good response time; a tiny quantum means too many context switches
Priority Highest priority first Either Starvation, fixed by aging (raise priority over time)
Multilevel feedback queue Several queues; processes move between them by behaviour Yes What real OSes approximate; Linux used CFS, now EEVDF

Metrics: turnaround time = completion − arrival; waiting time = turnaround − burst; response time = first run − arrival.

Worked example (FCFS): P1 (burst 5), P2 (3), P3 (1) all arrive at time 0. They finish at 5, 8, 9; waiting times 0, 5, 8; average 4.33. With SJF the order is P3, P2, P1: finish at 1, 4, 9; waiting 0, 1, 4; average 1.67.

Synchronization

A critical section is code that touches shared data. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion (one at a time), progress (if nobody's inside, someone waiting gets in) and bounded waiting (no one waits forever).

Primitive What it is
Mutex A lock with an owner; only the locker unlocks
Semaphore An integer with atomic wait/P (decrement, block at 0) and signal/V (increment). Counting or binary
Monitor A type whose methods are mutually exclusive, plus condition variables — like a C++ class with a mutex inside every method
Spinlock Busy-waiting lock for short critical sections on multicore

Classic problems: producer–consumer (bounded buffer: section 23), readers–writers (shared_mutex), and dining philosophers (five philosophers, five forks: grabbing left then right deadlocks; fix by ordering resources, letting at most four sit, or picking both forks atomically).

Deadlock handling

The four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait (section 23).

Strategy How
Prevention Make one condition impossible — e.g. request all resources at once (no hold-and-wait) or impose a global lock order (no circular wait)
Avoidance Grant a request only if the system stays in a safe state — the Banker's algorithm checks that some order lets every process finish with the remaining resources
Detection and recovery Let deadlocks happen, detect cycles in the wait-for graph, then kill or roll back a process
Ignore Assume it's rare and reboot ("ostrich algorithm") — what general-purpose OSes mostly do for user locks

Memory management

  • Programs use virtual (logical) addresses; the MMU translates them to physical addresses using page tables maintained by the OS. Each process gets its own isolated virtual address space — that's why two processes can both have an object at address 0x7ffe….
  • Paging: virtual memory is split into fixed-size pages (4 KB typically), physical memory into frames of the same size; the page table maps pages to frames. No external fragmentation, a little internal fragmentation in the last page.
  • TLB: a small cache of recent translations; a TLB miss costs a page-table walk. Huge pages (2 MB) reduce misses.
  • Segmentation: variable-sized logical segments (code, stack, heap); suffers external fragmentation. x86-64 uses paging almost exclusively.
  • Virtual memory / demand paging: pages are loaded only when first touched. Touching a page not in RAM causes a page fault; the OS loads it (from disk or a zeroed page) and resumes. Touching an address with no valid mapping ends with SIGSEGV — a segmentation fault.
  • Thrashing: when the working sets of running processes don't fit in RAM, the system spends its time paging instead of running.
Fragmentation Meaning Where
Internal Wasted space inside an allocated block (asked for 13 bytes, got 16) Paging, allocators' size classes, struct padding
External Enough total free memory, but split into pieces too small to use Segmentation, long-running heaps

Page replacement

When RAM is full, a page must be evicted:

Algorithm Evicts Notes
FIFO The oldest loaded page Simple; suffers Belady's anomaly (more frames can mean more faults)
Optimal (OPT) The page used furthest in the future Impossible in practice; a benchmark
LRU The least recently used page Good; approximated with reference bits (clock algorithm). The LRU cache interview problem is this
LFU The least frequently used page Rarely used alone

Worked example: reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 with 3 frames. FIFO: 7, 0, 1 fault (3); 2 replaces 7 (4); 0 hit; 3 replaces 0 (5); 0 replaces 1 (6); 4 replaces 2 (7) → 7 faults. LRU: 7, 0, 1 (3); 2 replaces 7 (4); 0 hit; 3 replaces 1 (5); 0 hit; 4 replaces 2 (6) → 6 faults.

Inter-process communication

Mechanism Notes
Pipes One-way byte stream between related processes (ls | grep x); named pipes (FIFOs) for unrelated ones
Message queues Kernel-managed queues of discrete messages
Shared memory Fastest: the same physical pages mapped into both processes; needs synchronization (semaphores)
Sockets Communication on one machine (Unix domain) or across a network (TCP/UDP)
Signals Asynchronous notifications: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGSEGV, SIGKILL, SIGTERM
Memory-mapped files mmap a file into several processes

Interview questions

QWhat is the difference between a process and a thread?

A process is an independent program in execution with its own address space and resources; a thread is a unit of execution within a process, sharing its memory and resources but having its own stack, registers and program counter. Threads are lighter to create and switch, but a misbehaving thread can corrupt or crash its whole process.

QWhat does fork() return, and what is copy-on-write?

It returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and −1 on failure. The child's address space initially shares physical pages with the parent, marked read-only; a page is copied only when either process writes to it, which makes fork cheap.

QWhat are zombie and orphan processes?

A zombie has finished, but its parent hasn't collected its exit status with wait(), so its PCB entry remains. An orphan's parent exited first; it's adopted by init/systemd, which reaps it.

QWhat is a context switch?

Saving the state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) of the running thread and restoring another's so it can run. Between processes it also switches the address space, flushing or tagging the TLB, which makes it more expensive. It's pure overhead, so too-small time slices hurt throughput.

QCompare FCFS, SJF and Round Robin.

FCFS is simple but short jobs wait behind long ones (convoy effect). SJF minimizes average waiting time but needs to know burst times and can starve long jobs. Round Robin gives each process a time quantum in turn — fair, with good response time — but too small a quantum wastes time on context switches and too large becomes FCFS.

QWhat is a semaphore? Binary semaphore vs mutex?

An integer variable accessed through atomic wait (decrement, blocking at zero) and signal (increment) operations, used for mutual exclusion or signalling. A binary semaphore has values 0/1 like a lock, but a mutex has ownership — only the thread that locked it may unlock it — and often priority inheritance; a semaphore can be signalled by any thread.

QWhat are the necessary conditions for deadlock, and how can you handle it?

Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Handle it by prevention (break a condition, e.g. lock ordering), avoidance (Banker's algorithm keeps the system in safe states), detection and recovery (find cycles, then abort or roll back), or ignoring it.

QWhat is the Banker's algorithm?

A deadlock-avoidance algorithm: before granting a request, the OS simulates the allocation and checks whether there is still an order in which every process can obtain its maximum needs and finish. If so (a safe state), it grants the request; otherwise the process waits.

QWhat is virtual memory and why is it useful?

An abstraction where each process sees a large private address space, mapped by the OS and MMU onto physical memory and disk. It isolates processes, lets programs be larger than RAM, allows sharing (libraries, copy-on-write) and simplifies allocation.

QWhat is paging? What is a page fault?

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages mapped to physical frames through page tables. A page fault occurs when a process accesses a page that's not currently in physical memory; the OS loads it from disk (or allocates a zero page), updates the page table and resumes the instruction. An access to an unmapped or forbidden address becomes a segmentation fault instead.

QWhat is thrashing?

A state where processes don't have enough frames for their working sets, so they page-fault constantly and the system spends most of its time swapping pages rather than executing. Fixes: fewer processes, more RAM, better locality.

QWhat is the TLB?

The translation lookaside buffer: a small, fast hardware cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations, avoiding a page-table walk on most memory accesses.

QInternal vs external fragmentation?

Internal: unused space inside an allocated unit because units are fixed-size (paging, allocator size classes). External: free memory split into scattered holes, none big enough for a request (segmentation, variable-size heaps). Compaction or paging addresses external fragmentation.

QWhat is Belady's anomaly?

The counter-intuitive situation where giving FIFO page replacement more frames produces more page faults for some reference strings. Stack algorithms such as LRU and Optimal never show it.

QWhich IPC mechanism is fastest?

Shared memory: after setup, processes read and write the same physical pages without kernel involvement, whereas pipes, message queues and sockets copy data through the kernel. It needs explicit synchronization (semaphores or atomics in the shared region).

27SOLID · creational · structural · behavioral · CRTP · PIMPL · low-level design14 questions

SOLID, Design Patterns & LLD

The SOLID principles with C++ examples, the design patterns interviews ask about written in modern C++, C++-specific idioms (RAII, PIMPL, CRTP, type erasure, NVI), and a method plus a worked example for low-level design rounds.

SOLID

Principle Means C++ example
Single responsibility A class has one reason to change ReportBuilder builds the report; ReportPrinter prints it
Open/closed Open for extension, closed for modification Add a new Shape subclass instead of editing a switch over shape types
Liskov substitution Derived objects must work wherever the base is expected A Square deriving from a mutable Rectangle breaks setWidth/setHeight expectations
Interface segregation Many small interfaces beat one fat one Printer and Scanner interfaces instead of Machine with fax() that most classes can't implement
Dependency inversion Depend on abstractions; inject dependencies OrderService takes a PaymentGateway& instead of creating a RazorpayClient itself
C++verified run
struct Notifier {                                    // abstraction (DIP)
    virtual void send(const string& msg) = 0;
    virtual ~Notifier() = default;
};
struct EmailNotifier : Notifier {
    void send(const string& msg) override { cout << "email: " << msg << '\n'; }
};
struct SmsNotifier : Notifier {
    void send(const string& msg) override { cout << "sms: " << msg << '\n'; }
};
class OrderService {                                 // depends on Notifier, not on concrete classes
    Notifier& notifier;
public:
    explicit OrderService(Notifier& n) : notifier(n) {}   // dependency injection
    void place(int id) { notifier.send("order " + to_string(id) + " placed"); }
};
// in main:
EmailNotifier email;
SmsNotifier sms;
OrderService(email).place(1);
OrderService(sms).place(2);                          // new behaviour without editing OrderService (OCP)
Output
email: order 1 placed
sms: order 2 placed

Creational patterns

Singleton

C++verified run
class Logger {
    Logger() = default;                              // private: no outside construction
public:
    static Logger& instance() {
        static Logger inst;                          // created once, thread-safe (C++11)
        return inst;
    }
    Logger(const Logger&) = delete;                  // no copies
    Logger& operator=(const Logger&) = delete;
    void log(const string& m) { cout << "[log] " << m << '\n'; }
};
// in main:
Logger::instance().log("started");
cout << boolalpha << (&Logger::instance() == &Logger::instance()) << '\n';
Output
[log] started
true

Criticism to mention: a singleton is global state in disguise — hidden dependencies, hard to test and to replace. Prefer passing dependencies explicitly; use a singleton only for genuinely unique resources (a logger, a hardware device).

Factory

C++verified run
struct Vehicle { virtual string wheels() const = 0; virtual ~Vehicle() = default; };
struct Car : Vehicle { string wheels() const override { return "4 wheels"; } };
struct Bike : Vehicle { string wheels() const override { return "2 wheels"; } };

unique_ptr<Vehicle> make_vehicle(const string& kind) {     // callers never name concrete types
    if (kind == "car") return make_unique<Car>();
    if (kind == "bike") return make_unique<Bike>();
    throw invalid_argument("unknown vehicle: " + kind);
}
// in main:
for (string k : {"car", "bike"}) cout << k << ": " << make_vehicle(k)->wheels() << '\n';
Output
car: 4 wheels
bike: 2 wheels

Builder

C++verified run
class HttpRequest {
    string method = "GET", url;
    vector<pair<string, string>> headers;
    int timeout_ms = 1000;
    friend class RequestBuilder;
public:
    string describe() const {
        return method + " " + url + " (" + to_string(headers.size()) + " headers, " + to_string(timeout_ms) + " ms)";
    }
};
class RequestBuilder {
    HttpRequest r;
public:
    explicit RequestBuilder(string url) { r.url = std::move(url); }
    RequestBuilder& method(string m) { r.method = std::move(m); return *this; }   // fluent: return *this
    RequestBuilder& header(string k, string v) { r.headers.emplace_back(std::move(k), std::move(v)); return *this; }
    RequestBuilder& timeout(int ms) { r.timeout_ms = ms; return *this; }
    HttpRequest build() { return std::move(r); }
};
// in main:
auto req = RequestBuilder("/api/users").method("POST").header("Auth", "token").timeout(3000).build();
cout << req.describe() << '\n';
Output
POST /api/users (1 headers, 3000 ms)

Prototype: copy existing objects through a virtual clone() (section 09).

Structural patterns

Pattern Idea In C++
Adapter Wrap a class to give it the interface a client expects Wrapping a C library behind a C++ class; std::stack adapts deque
Decorator Add behaviour by wrapping an object with the same interface A CompressedStream wrapping any Stream
Facade One simple interface over a complex subsystem A VideoConverter class hiding codecs, buffers and files
Proxy A stand-in controlling access to an object Smart pointers, lazy-loading wrappers, vector<bool>::reference
Composite Treat individual objects and groups uniformly File system: File and Directory both implement size()
C++verified run
struct Coffee { virtual double cost() const = 0; virtual string desc() const = 0; virtual ~Coffee() = default; };
struct Espresso : Coffee { double cost() const override { return 100; } string desc() const override { return "espresso"; } };
class AddOn : public Coffee {                        // Decorator base: wraps another Coffee
protected:
    unique_ptr<Coffee> inner;
public:
    explicit AddOn(unique_ptr<Coffee> c) : inner(std::move(c)) {}
};
struct Milk : AddOn {
    using AddOn::AddOn;
    double cost() const override { return inner->cost() + 20; }
    string desc() const override { return inner->desc() + " + milk"; }
};
struct Caramel : AddOn {
    using AddOn::AddOn;
    double cost() const override { return inner->cost() + 35; }
    string desc() const override { return inner->desc() + " + caramel"; }
};
// in main:
unique_ptr<Coffee> order = make_unique<Caramel>(make_unique<Milk>(make_unique<Espresso>()));
cout << order->desc() << " = " << order->cost() << '\n';
Output
espresso + milk + caramel = 155

Behavioral patterns

Strategy

C++verified run
class Navigator {
    function<int(int)> route_cost;                   // the strategy, swappable at run time
public:
    explicit Navigator(function<int(int)> s) : route_cost(std::move(s)) {}
    void set_strategy(function<int(int)> s) { route_cost = std::move(s); }
    int plan(int km) const { return route_cost(km); }
};
// in main:
Navigator nav([](int km) { return km * 2; });        // driving: 2 min per km
cout << nav.plan(10) << ' ';
nav.set_strategy([](int km) { return km * 12; });    // walking
cout << nav.plan(10) << '\n';
Output
20 120

Observer

C++verified run
class Subject {
    vector<weak_ptr<function<void(const string&)>>> observers;   // weak: don't keep observers alive
public:
    void subscribe(const shared_ptr<function<void(const string&)>>& o) { observers.push_back(o); }
    void notify(const string& event) {
        erase_if(observers, [](auto& w) { return w.expired(); });   // drop dead observers
        for (auto& w : observers)
            if (auto o = w.lock()) (*o)(event);
    }
};
// in main:
Subject stock;
auto display = make_shared<function<void(const string&)>>([](const string& e) { cout << "display: " << e << '\n'; });
{
    auto logger = make_shared<function<void(const string&)>>([](const string& e) { cout << "logger: " << e << '\n'; });
    stock.subscribe(display);
    stock.subscribe(logger);
    stock.notify("price 101");
}                                                    // logger destroyed here
stock.notify("price 99");                            // only display remains
Output
display: price 101
logger: price 101
display: price 99
Pattern Idea Example
Command Wrap a request as an object Undo/redo stacks, job queues of function<void()>
Iterator Traverse without exposing internals Every STL iterator
Template method Base class fixes the algorithm's steps; subclasses fill some in The NVI idiom below
State Object changes behaviour when its state changes Vending machine: Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing
Chain of responsibility Pass a request along handlers until one handles it Middleware, logging levels

C++ idioms

Idiom What and why
RAII Resources owned by objects; released in destructors (section 14)
Rule of zero Let members manage resources so no special members are needed (section 10)
Copy-and-swap Exception-safe assignment (section 10)
PIMPL ("pointer to implementation") Class holds a unique_ptr<Impl>; private members live in the .cpp, so changing them doesn't recompile users and the header stays stable (ABI firewall)
CRTP ("curiously recurring template pattern") class Derived : public Base<Derived> — static polymorphism with no vtable
NVI (non-virtual interface) Public non-virtual function calls a private virtual hook: the base controls pre/post-conditions
Type erasure Hide different types behind one interface without inheritance (std::function, std::any)
C++verified run
template <typename Derived>
struct Shape {                                        // CRTP base
    double area() const { return static_cast<const Derived*>(this)->area_impl(); }   // no virtual call
    void print() const { cout << Derived::name << " area " << area() << '\n'; }
};
struct Sq : Shape<Sq> {
    static constexpr const char* name = "square";
    double s;
    explicit Sq(double s) : s(s) {}
    double area_impl() const { return s * s; }
};
template <typename T>
struct InstanceCounter {                              // CRTP: a separate counter per derived type
    inline static int count = 0;
    InstanceCounter() { ++count; }
};
struct Dog : InstanceCounter<Dog> {};
struct Cat : InstanceCounter<Cat> {};
// in main:
Sq(3).print();
Dog d1, d2; Cat c1;
cout << InstanceCounter<Dog>::count << ' ' << InstanceCounter<Cat>::count << '\n';
Output
square area 9
2 1

Low-level design rounds

A method that works for any LLD question:

  1. Clarify requirements — list the use cases and say what's out of scope (payments? concurrency?).
  2. Identify entities — nouns become classes (ParkingLot, Level, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket).
  3. Define relationships — has-a vs is-a, multiplicities (a lot has many levels; a level has many spots).
  4. Design interfaces — the public methods for each use case (park(vehicle) -> Ticket, unpark(ticket) -> fee).
  5. Apply patterns where they fit — Strategy for pricing, Factory for vehicles, Singleton for the lot, Observer for display boards, State for vending machines.
  6. Handle concurrency and edge cases — two cars racing for the last spot (lock per level, or an atomic spot claim).
  7. Write the core code — clean classes, enum class, smart pointers, const-correct methods.
C++verified run
enum class Size { Small, Medium, Large };
struct Vehicle { string plate; Size size; };
struct Spot {
    int id; Size size; optional<string> plate;
    bool fits(const Vehicle& v) const { return !plate && static_cast<int>(v.size) <= static_cast<int>(size); }
};
struct Ticket { int spot_id; string plate; int entry_hour; };
class FeeStrategy {
public:
    virtual int fee(int hours) const = 0;
    virtual ~FeeStrategy() = default;
};
class HourlyFee : public FeeStrategy {
    int rate;
public:
    explicit HourlyFee(int r) : rate(r) {}
    int fee(int hours) const override { return max(1, hours) * rate; }
};
class ParkingLot {
    vector<Spot> spots;
    unique_ptr<FeeStrategy> pricing;
    mutex m;                                          // two cars may race for the last spot
public:
    ParkingLot(vector<Spot> s, unique_ptr<FeeStrategy> p) : spots(std::move(s)), pricing(std::move(p)) {}
    optional<Ticket> park(const Vehicle& v, int hour) {
        lock_guard lock(m);
        for (auto& s : spots)
            if (s.fits(v)) { s.plate = v.plate; return Ticket{s.id, v.plate, hour}; }
        return nullopt;                               // lot full for this size
    }
    int unpark(const Ticket& t, int hour) {
        lock_guard lock(m);
        for (auto& s : spots)
            if (s.id == t.spot_id) s.plate.reset();
        return pricing->fee(hour - t.entry_hour);
    }
};
// in main:
ParkingLot lot({{1, Size::Small, {}}, {2, Size::Large, {}}}, make_unique<HourlyFee>(40));
auto t1 = lot.park({"TS09AB1234", Size::Medium}, 9);   // medium car: needs the large spot
auto t2 = lot.park({"TS10XY9999", Size::Large}, 10);   // nothing left that fits
cout << "spot " << t1->spot_id << ", second car parked: " << boolalpha << t2.has_value() << '\n';
cout << "fee " << lot.unpark(*t1, 12) << '\n';
Output
spot 2, second car parked: false
fee 120

LLD problems to practise: parking lot, elevator system, Splitwise, BookMyShow, library management, vending machine, snake and ladder, tic-tac-toe/chess, LRU cache, rate limiter, logger, in-memory file system, ATM, food-delivery order flow, notification service.

Interview questions

QExplain the SOLID principles.

Single responsibility: one reason to change per class. Open/closed: extend behaviour by adding code, not editing existing code. Liskov substitution: subclasses must honour the base class's contract. Interface segregation: clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. Dependency inversion: high-level code depends on abstractions, with concrete implementations injected.

QHow do you implement a thread-safe singleton in C++?

A static local inside a static member function (the Meyers singleton): its initialization happens once, on first call, and C++11 guarantees it's thread-safe. Make the constructor private and delete copy and move.

QWhat are the drawbacks of the singleton pattern?

It's global mutable state: hidden dependencies between classes, difficult unit testing (can't substitute a fake), tight coupling, and lifetime/order problems at program shutdown. Dependency injection is usually better.

QFactory vs abstract factory vs builder?

A factory method creates one product, choosing the concrete class from a parameter. An abstract factory creates families of related products (a UIFactory making matching buttons and menus for a theme). A builder constructs one complex object step by step through a fluent interface, useful when there are many optional parameters.

QWhat is the Strategy pattern? How does modern C++ express it?

Encapsulating interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so the context can switch them at run time. In C++ it can be a virtual interface, a std::function member, or — when the choice is fixed at compile time — a template parameter (like comparators in std::sort).

QWhat is the Observer pattern and how do you avoid dangling observers?

A subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them of events. Holding observers by weak_ptr (and skipping expired ones) prevents calling destroyed objects without the subject keeping them alive; alternatively observers unsubscribe in their destructors.

QWhat is the Decorator pattern?

Adding responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object with the same interface, which forwards calls and adds behaviour — e.g. stacking Milk and Caramel around an Espresso, or buffering and compression around a stream.

QWhat is CRTP?

The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern: a class derives from a template instantiated with itself (class D : public Base<D>). The base can call derived members through static_cast<D*>(this) without virtual functions, giving static polymorphism, mixins (counters, comparison operators) and zero run-time dispatch cost.

QWhat is the PIMPL idiom?

"Pointer to implementation": a class stores only a std::unique_ptr<Impl>, with Impl defined in the .cpp file. Private details can change without recompiling clients, compile times drop, and the binary interface stays stable. The cost is a heap allocation and an indirection.

QWhat is the Non-Virtual Interface idiom?

Public functions are non-virtual and call private (or protected) virtual hooks. The base class keeps control over invariants, logging and pre/post-conditions around the customizable step — the Template Method pattern in C++ form.

QHow do you approach a low-level design question?

Clarify requirements and scope, identify the core entities and their relationships, define the public APIs for each use case, choose patterns where they simplify (strategy, factory, observer, state), consider concurrency and failure cases, and then write clean, compilable core classes — explaining trade-offs as you go.

QComposition over inheritance — why?

Composition couples classes through narrow interfaces, allows behaviour to be swapped at run time, avoids fragile deep hierarchies and the diamond problem, and keeps classes focused. Inheritance is for genuine substitutability (IS-A) and polymorphism.

QWhat is dependency injection?

Supplying an object's dependencies from outside — through its constructor, a setter or a template parameter — instead of letting it create them. It makes code testable (inject fakes) and flexible (swap implementations), and is the practical form of dependency inversion.

QWhich design patterns does the STL use?

Iterator (all containers), Adapter (stack, queue, priority_queue), Strategy (comparators, hashers, allocators as template parameters), Proxy (vector<bool>::reference, smart pointers), Template Method/policy-based design, Factory functions (make_unique, make_shared), and type erasure (std::function).

Complexity & How to Attack a Problem

Big-O and friends, reading the constraints to know which complexity will pass, counting loops and solving recurrences, space and amortized cost, and a step-by-step method for coding rounds with a pattern-recognition table.

Big-O, Big-Ω, Big-Θ

  • O(f(n)) — an upper bound: the running time grows no faster than f(n) (up to a constant), for large n.
  • Ω(f(n)) — a lower bound: grows at least as fast.
  • Θ(f(n)) — a tight bound: both.
  • Interviews say "O" and mean the tight worst case. Drop constants and lower-order terms: 3n² + 10n + 7 is O(n²).
Complexity Name Typical example n = 10⁶ does about
O(1) Constant Array index, hash lookup (average) 1
O(log n) Logarithmic Binary search, balanced BST, heap push 20
O(√n) Square root Trial-division primality, divisors 1,000
O(n) Linear One pass, two pointers, sliding window 10⁶
O(n log n) Linearithmic Sorting, n heap operations 2 × 10⁷
O(n²) Quadratic All pairs, simple DP on two indices 10¹² ✗
O(n³) Cubic Floyd–Warshall, matrix multiplication ✗
O(2ⁿ) Exponential All subsets ✗
O(n!) Factorial All permutations ✗

Read the constraints first

A C++ judge does roughly 10⁸ simple operations per second. The constraint on n tells you which complexity the intended solution has — often the strongest hint in the problem.

Max n Target complexity Likely technique
≤ 10–12 O(n!), O(n · n!) Permutations, brute force
≤ 20–25 O(2ⁿ · n) Subsets, bitmask DP, meet in the middle (n ≤ 40)
≤ 100 O(n⁴) Small DP with several dimensions
≤ 500 O(n³) Floyd–Warshall, interval DP
≤ 5,000 O(n²) 2D DP, all pairs
≤ 10⁵–10⁶ O(n log n) or O(n) Sorting, binary search, heaps, two pointers, prefix sums, hashing
≤ 10⁸ O(n) with a small constant Single pass, sieve
≥ 10⁹ O(log n) or O(1) Math, binary search on the answer, fast exponentiation

Counting operations

C++verified run
long long n = 1'000'000, steps = 0;
for (long long i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) ++steps;                 // doubling: log2(n)
cout << "doubling loop: " << steps << '\n';
steps = 0;
for (long long i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
    for (long long j = i; j <= n; j += i) ++steps;            // n/1 + n/2 + ... : harmonic, n ln n
cout << "harmonic loop: " << steps << " (n ln n = " << llround(n * log(double(n))) << ")\n";
steps = 0;
for (long long i = 0; i < 1000; ++i)
    for (long long j = i + 1; j < 1000; ++j) ++steps;         // all pairs of 1000: n(n-1)/2
cout << "pairs of 1000: " << steps << '\n';
steps = 0;
for (long long i = 1; i * i <= n; ++i) ++steps;               // up to sqrt(n)
cout << "sqrt loop: " << steps << '\n';
Output
doubling loop: 20
harmonic loop: 13970034 (n ln n = 13815511)
pairs of 1000: 499500
sqrt loop: 1000
Loop shape Cost
for i in 0..n O(n)
Two nested loops over n O(n²)
i *= 2 or i /= 2 O(log n)
j from i to n step i, for every i O(n log n) (harmonic series)
Sieve of Eratosthenes O(n log log n)
Two pointers moving only forward O(n) total, despite the nested while

Recursion: recurrences and the master theorem

Write the cost as a recurrence: work at this call + cost of the recursive calls.

Recurrence Example Solution
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) Binary search O(log n)
T(n) = T(n − 1) + O(1) Linear recursion, factorial O(n)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Merge sort O(n log n)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) Tree traversal O(n)
T(n) = T(n − 1) + O(n) Selection sort, naive recursion on suffixes O(n²)
T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + O(1) Subsets, Tower of Hanoi O(2ⁿ)
T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) Naive Fibonacci O(φⁿ) ≈ O(1.618ⁿ)
T(n) = n · T(n − 1) Permutations O(n!)

Master theorem for T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(nᵈ): if d > log_b a the answer is O(nᵈ); if d = log_b a it's O(nᵈ log n); if d < log_b a it's O(n^(log_b a)). Merge sort: a = 2, b = 2, d = 1 = log₂2 → O(n log n).

Shortcut for recursion with memoization: (number of distinct states) × (work per state).

Space complexity

  • Count the extra memory: arrays you allocate, hash maps, and the recursion stack — a DFS on a path-shaped tree of 10⁵ nodes uses 10⁵ stack frames.
  • "In place" usually means O(1) extra space (input modification allowed).
  • 256 MB is about 6 × 10⁷ ints or 3 × 10⁷ long longs.

Best, average, worst and amortized

  • Quicksort: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case (bad pivots on sorted input) — randomized pivots make the worst case vanishingly unlikely.
  • Hash map lookup: O(1) average, O(n) worst case.
  • Amortized: the average over a sequence of operations, guaranteed. vector::push_back is amortized O(1) (doubling); a monotonic stack pushes and pops each element once, so n operations cost O(n) total; union–find with path compression and union by size is O(α(n)) per operation — effectively constant.

A method for coding rounds

  1. Understand and clarify (2–3 min). Restate the problem. Ask: input size, value ranges (negatives? duplicates? empty input?), sorted or not, what to return when there's no answer.
  2. Work an example by hand, including an edge case.
  3. State a brute force and its complexity — it shows you understand the problem and gives a fallback.
  4. Optimize: look at the constraints, find the bottleneck, and match the problem to a pattern (table below). Say your idea and its complexity before coding.
  5. Code cleanly: meaningful names, helper functions, no premature micro-optimization.
  6. Dry-run your code on the example; then test edge cases: empty, one element, all equal, negative numbers, overflow, maximum size.
  7. Analyse time and space; mention possible improvements.

Grid or network, "shortest path", "connected", "islands" BFS / DFS / Dijkstra 38

Interview questions

QWhat does O(n) mean precisely?

The running time is bounded above by c·n for some constant c once n is large enough. It describes the growth rate as input grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms — an O(n) algorithm with a big constant can lose to an O(n log n) one on small inputs.

QWhat's the time complexity of binary search, and why?

O(log n): each comparison halves the remaining range, so after k steps n/2ᵏ elements remain, reaching 1 when k = log₂ n.

QWhy is the two-pointer technique O(n) even though it has nested loops?

Because each pointer only moves forward and never more than n steps in total. The inner loop's iterations are paid for by the overall movement, so the combined work across the whole run is O(n) — an amortized argument.

QWhat is amortized complexity? Give an example.

The worst-case cost per operation averaged over any sequence of operations. vector::push_back occasionally costs O(n) to reallocate, but doubling the capacity makes n pushes cost O(n) total, so each is amortized O(1).

QHow do you find the complexity of a recursive function?

Write a recurrence for its cost (work in one call plus the cost of each recursive call) and solve it — by the master theorem for divide and conquer, or by drawing the recursion tree and summing levels. With memoization: number of distinct states × work per state.

QHow do you decide which approach will pass from the constraints?

Assume about 10⁸ simple operations per second. n ≤ 20 allows 2ⁿ, n ≤ 500 allows n³, n ≤ 5000 allows n², n up to 10⁵–10⁶ needs O(n log n) or O(n), and n ≥ 10⁹ needs O(log n) or math. Then choose a technique that hits that complexity.

QWhat is the space complexity of recursive DFS?

O(h), where h is the maximum recursion depth — O(log n) for a balanced tree but O(n) for a skewed one or a long path in a graph. That stack space counts even though you didn't allocate it explicitly.

QWhy can an O(n²) algorithm be faster than an O(n log n) one?

Big-O hides constants and ignores small inputs. Insertion sort (O(n²)) beats merge sort for small arrays because of low overhead and cache-friendly access — which is why std::sort switches to insertion sort for small partitions.

QWhat should you do first in a coding interview?

Clarify the problem and constraints, work through an example including edge cases, and state a brute-force approach with its complexity. Then optimize and explain the plan before writing code.

QWhat is the complexity of generating all subsets and all permutations?

Subsets: 2ⁿ of them, O(n · 2ⁿ) to output. Permutations: n! of them, O(n · n!) to output. That's why these approaches need n ≤ ~20 and n ≤ ~10 respectively.

The C++ DSA Toolkit

A ready-to-use template for online judges, how LeetCode expects C++ solutions, the cost of every STL operation you'll use, idioms like coordinate compression and argsort, and the overflow, TLE and wrong-answer traps that cost the most marks.

A template for online judges

C++verified run
#include <bits/stdc++.h>          // every standard header (GCC-specific; fine on judges)
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
const ll INF = 1e18;               // safe "infinity" for long long distances
const int MOD = 1'000'000'007;

void solve() {
    int n;
    cin >> n;
    vector<ll> a(n);
    for (auto& x : a) cin >> x;
    cout << accumulate(a.begin(), a.end(), 0LL) << '\n';   // note 0LL
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);   // fast I/O
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int t = 1;
    cin >> t;                      // remove when there's a single test case
    while (t--) solve();
}
Output (input: 2 ⏎ 3 ⏎ 1 2 3 ⏎ 2 ⏎ 10 20)
6
30
  • bits/stdc++.h is a GCC header that includes the whole standard library; fine for judges and practice, not for production code (slow compiles, non-portable).
  • With multiple test cases, reset global state between them, or keep state local to solve().
  • Read the input format carefully: does t exist? Are values up to 10⁹ (fits int) or 10¹⁸ (needs long long)?

LeetCode style

LeetCode gives you a class and a method signature; there's no main and no input parsing.

C++compiles
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& nums, int target) {   // nums is a reference: no copy
        unordered_map<int, int> seen;                     // value -> index
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
            if (auto it = seen.find(target - nums[i]); it != seen.end())
                return {it->second, i};
            seen[nums[i]] = i;
        }
        return {};
    }
};
  • Helper functions go inside the class (as private members) or as free functions above it.
  • Use member variables carefully: the same Solution object may be reused for several tests on some platforms, so reset them.
  • Linked lists and trees arrive as ListNode* / TreeNode* already defined by LeetCode.

STL operation costs

Container Operation Cost
vector push_back, pop_back, [], back O(1) (push amortized)
insert/erase in the middle, find O(n)
deque push/pop at both ends, [] O(1)
set / map insert, erase, find, count, lower_bound O(log n)
begin() (min), rbegin() (max) O(1)
unordered_set / unordered_map insert, erase, find, count, [] O(1) average, O(n) worst
priority_queue push, pop O(log n)
top O(1)
stack / queue push, pop, top/front O(1)
string += char, [], size O(1)
substr, find, + (new string), == O(length)
Algorithms sort O(n log n)
lower_bound/upper_bound on a vector O(log n)
reverse, accumulate, count, max_element, unique O(n)
next_permutation O(n) worst, O(1) amortized
Pitfallstd::lower_bound on a set is O(n)

lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) can't jump on a set's bidirectional iterators, so it walks — O(n). Always call the member: s.lower_bound(x) is O(log n). Same for map.

Idioms worth memorizing

C++verified run
// coordinate compression: map arbitrary values to 0..k-1, keeping order
vector<int> vals{1000000000, -5, 42, 42, 7};
vector<int> sorted_vals = vals;
sort(sorted_vals.begin(), sorted_vals.end());
sorted_vals.erase(unique(sorted_vals.begin(), sorted_vals.end()), sorted_vals.end());
for (int v : vals) cout << lower_bound(sorted_vals.begin(), sorted_vals.end(), v) - sorted_vals.begin() << ' ';
cout << '\n';

// argsort: indices ordered by value (sort indices, not values)
vector<int> score{50, 90, 70};
vector<int> idx(score.size());
iota(idx.begin(), idx.end(), 0);
sort(idx.begin(), idx.end(), [&](int i, int j) { return score[i] > score[j]; });
for (int i : idx) cout << i << ' ';
cout << '\n';

// frequency counting: an array beats a map when keys are small
string s = "interview";
int freq[26] = {};
for (char c : s) freq[c - 'a']++;
cout << freq['i' - 'a'] << ' ' << freq['e' - 'a'] << '\n';

// 4-directional grid moves
const int dr[] = {-1, 1, 0, 0}, dc[] = {0, 0, -1, 1};
int R = 3, C = 3, r = 0, c = 1, inside = 0;
for (int d = 0; d < 4; ++d) {
    int nr = r + dr[d], nc = c + dc[d];
    if (nr >= 0 && nr < R && nc >= 0 && nc < C) ++inside;   // bounds check first
}
cout << inside << " neighbours inside the grid\n";

// sort pairs: by first ascending, then second descending
vector<pair<int, int>> pts{{2, 1}, {1, 5}, {2, 9}, {1, 3}};
sort(pts.begin(), pts.end(), [](auto& a, auto& b) {
    return a.first != b.first ? a.first < b.first : a.second > b.second;
});
for (auto [x, y] : pts) cout << '(' << x << ',' << y << ')';
cout << '\n';
Output
3 0 2 2 1 
1 2 0 
2 2
3 neighbours inside the grid
(1,5)(1,3)(2,9)(2,1)

Overflow, precision and infinity

C++verified run
int a = 100000, b = 100000;
long long right = 1LL * a * b;                   // widen BEFORE multiplying: 10^10
// long long wrong = a * b;                      // multiplied in int: overflow (UB) before the assignment
cout << right << '\n';

const int MOD = 1'000'000'007;
long long x = 999'999'999, y = 999'999'999;
cout << (x % MOD) * (y % MOD) % MOD << '\n';      // each factor < MOD, product < 2^63
long long m = (-7 % MOD + MOD) % MOD;              // non-negative modulo of a negative number
cout << m << '\n';

int lo = 2'000'000'000, hi = 2'100'000'000;
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;                     // (lo + hi) / 2 would overflow int
cout << mid << '\n';

cout << (int)pow(10, 2) << ' ' << (long long)sqrtl(999999999999999999LL) << '\n';   // pow/sqrt are floating point
long long r = sqrtl(999999999999999999LL);
while (r * r > 999999999999999999LL) --r;         // fix the rounding
while ((r + 1) * (r + 1) <= 999999999999999999LL) ++r;
cout << r << '\n';

int arr[4];
memset(arr, 0, sizeof arr);   cout << arr[0] << ' ';   // 0: OK
memset(arr, -1, sizeof arr);  cout << arr[0] << ' ';   // -1: OK (all bytes 0xFF)
memset(arr, 1, sizeof arr);   cout << arr[0] << '\n';  // NOT 1: every BYTE is 1
fill(arr, arr + 4, 1);        cout << arr[0] << '\n';  // the right way

Constant Use
INT_MAX / INT_MIN Bounds — but INT_MAX + 1 overflows; don't add to it
1e9 (as int), 1e18 (as long long) "Infinity" that can still be added once without overflow
LLONG_MAX / 2 Safe infinity for sums of two distances

Trap checklist

Symptom Common cause Fix
Wrong answer on big tests int overflow in sums, products, accumulate(..., 0) long long, 1LL *, 0LL
Wrong answer, negative modulo % keeps the sign of the dividend ((x % m) + m) % m
TLE Passing vector/string by value to a recursive function Pass by const& or &
TLE endl in a loop; missing fast I/O '\n', sync_with_stdio(false)
TLE unordered_map hacked or rehashing repeatedly reserve, custom hash (section 18), or map
TLE s = s + c inside a loop s += c or push_back
TLE / MLE map<int,int> where an array would do Arrays for dense small keys
Crash (segfault) Out-of-bounds index, empty container top()/front(), deep recursion Bounds checks, -fsanitize=address, iterative version
Crash on big local array 10⁶+ elements on the stack Global array or vector
Infinite loop for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i) — unsigned never < 0 Use int
Wrong answer with doubles == on floating point, pow for integers Epsilon compare; integer arithmetic
Stale data Global arrays not reset between test cases Reset, or allocate per test
Comparator crash <= in a sort comparator Strict <

Debugging helpers

C++verified run
#define dbg(x) cerr << #x << " = " << (x) << '\n'   // prints to stderr: judges ignore it
template <typename T>
ostream& operator<<(ostream& os, const vector<T>& v) {    // print vectors directly
    os << '[';
    for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) os << (i ? ", " : "") << v[i];
    return os << ']';
}
// in main:
vector<int> v{3, 1, 4};
int total = 8;
dbg(total);                     // goes to stderr
cout << v << '\n';
Output
[3, 1, 4]

Printing to cerr keeps debug output out of the judged cout stream. For harder bugs: write a brute-force solution, generate small random tests, and compare outputs ("stress testing").

Interview questions

QWhy do competitive programmers use bits/stdc++.h and using namespace std?

To save typing under time pressure: one include brings in the whole standard library and the namespace directive removes std::. Both are GCC-specific or bad practice in real projects (slow compilation, name clashes), so mention that you'd write explicit includes in production code.

QHow do you avoid integer overflow?

Estimate the maximum magnitude from the constraints; use long long when values or intermediate results can exceed about 2·10⁹; widen before multiplying (1LL * a * b); take the modulo after each operation in modular arithmetic; compute midpoints as lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

QWhen is an array better than a hash map?

When keys are small, dense non-negative integers (letters, values up to 10⁶): direct indexing is O(1) with no hashing, no collisions and better cache behaviour. Hash maps are for sparse or large key spaces.

QWhat is coordinate compression?

Replacing values from a large range (up to 10⁹) with their ranks 0..k−1 among the distinct values, preserving order. Then they can index arrays, Fenwick trees or segment trees. Sort, deduplicate, and map each value with lower_bound.

QWhy should you pass vectors by reference in recursive functions?

Passing by value copies the whole vector at every call — O(n) per call, turning an O(n) recursion into O(n²) and often causing TLE or memory blowups. Pass const vector<int>& to read or vector<int>& to modify.

QWhy can memset(a, 1, sizeof a) not set an int array to 1?

memset writes a byte value into every byte. Each 4-byte int becomes 0x01010101 = 16843009. It works for 0 and −1 only (all-zero or all-one bytes); use fill or a loop for other values.

QHow do you take the modulo of a negative number correctly?

In C++ % keeps the dividend's sign, so -7 % 5 == -2. Use ((x % m) + m) % m to get a value in [0, m).

QWhat is stress testing?

Writing a slow but obviously correct brute-force solution and a random test generator, then running both solutions on many small random inputs and comparing outputs until a mismatch reveals a bug in the fast one.

30hashing · prefix sums · difference arrays · Kadane · two pointers · sliding window10 questions

Arrays, Hashing, Two Pointers & Sliding Window

The patterns behind most array and string problems — hash maps for lookups, prefix sums and difference arrays, Kadane's algorithm, the two-pointer family, fixed and variable sliding windows, and Boyer–Moore voting — each with a tested C++ template and the must-do problems.

Recognise the pattern

The problem says… Reach for
"Find a pair/complement", "seen before?", "count occurrences" Hash map / hash set
"Sum of a subarray", many range-sum queries Prefix sums
"Number of subarrays with sum K" (negatives allowed) Prefix sums + hash map of counts
"Add v to every element in [l, r]", many times Difference array
"Maximum sum subarray" Kadane's algorithm
Sorted array, pairs/triplets, "in place", palindromes Two pointers
"Longest/shortest contiguous subarray/substring such that…" Sliding window
"Element appearing more than n/2 times" Boyer–Moore voting

Hashing

C++verified run
vector<int> two_sum(const vector<int>& a, int target) {
    unordered_map<int, int> pos;                        // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        auto it = pos.find(target - a[i]);
        if (it != pos.end()) return {it->second, i};
        pos[a[i]] = i;                                  // insert AFTER checking (no self-pairing)
    }
    return {};
}
int longest_consecutive(const vector<int>& a) {         // O(n): start counting only at sequence starts
    unordered_set<int> s(a.begin(), a.end());
    int best = 0;
    for (int x : s)
        if (!s.count(x - 1)) {                          // x is the start of a run
            int len = 1;
            while (s.count(x + len)) ++len;
            best = max(best, len);
        }
    return best;
}
vector<vector<string>> group_anagrams(const vector<string>& words) {
    unordered_map<string, vector<string>> groups;
    for (const auto& w : words) {
        string key = w;
        sort(key.begin(), key.end());                   // anagrams share the sorted key
        groups[key].push_back(w);
    }
    vector<vector<string>> out;
    for (auto& [k, g] : groups) out.push_back(g);
    sort(out.begin(), out.end());                       // deterministic order for printing
    return out;
}
// in main:
auto p = two_sum({2, 7, 11, 15}, 9);
cout << p[0] << ' ' << p[1] << '\n';
cout << longest_consecutive({100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2}) << '\n';
for (auto& g : group_anagrams({"eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"})) {
    for (auto& w : g) cout << w << ' ';
    cout << "| ";
}
cout << '\n';
Output
0 1
4
bat | eat tea ate | tan nat |

Prefix sums

pre[i] = sum of the first i elements, so the sum of a[l..r] is pre[r + 1] − pre[l] in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

C++verified run
vector<long long> build_prefix(const vector<int>& a) {
    vector<long long> pre(a.size() + 1, 0);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i) pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + a[i];
    return pre;
}
int subarrays_with_sum(const vector<int>& a, int k) {   // works with negative numbers too
    unordered_map<long long, int> count_of{{0, 1}};     // prefix sum 0 seen once (empty prefix)
    long long sum = 0;
    int answer = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        sum += x;
        if (auto it = count_of.find(sum - k); it != count_of.end()) answer += it->second;
        count_of[sum]++;
    }
    return answer;
}
// in main:
vector<int> a{3, -1, 4, 1, -5, 9};
auto pre = build_prefix(a);
cout << pre[4] - pre[1] << '\n';                        // a[1..3] = -1 + 4 + 1
cout << subarrays_with_sum({1, 2, 3, -3, 3}, 3) << '\n';

vector<vector<int>> g{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}};    // 2D prefix sums
int R = 3, C = 3;
vector<vector<long long>> P(R + 1, vector<long long>(C + 1, 0));
for (int r = 0; r < R; ++r)
    for (int c = 0; c < C; ++c)
        P[r + 1][c + 1] = g[r][c] + P[r][c + 1] + P[r + 1][c] - P[r][c];
auto rect = [&](int r1, int c1, int r2, int c2) {          // inclusive corners
    return P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1];
};
cout << rect(1, 1, 2, 2) << '\n';                          // 5 + 6 + 8 + 9
Output
4
5
28

Difference arrays: many range updates, one read

To add v to every element of [l, r]: diff[l] += v; diff[r + 1] -= v;. After all updates, the prefix sum of diff gives the final array — O(1) per update, O(n) at the end.

C++verified run
int n = 6;
vector<long long> diff(n + 1, 0);
auto range_add = [&](int l, int r, long long v) { diff[l] += v; diff[r + 1] -= v; };
range_add(0, 2, 5);
range_add(1, 4, 2);
range_add(3, 5, -1);
long long run = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { run += diff[i]; cout << run << ' '; }
cout << '\n';
Output
5 7 7 1 1 -1

Kadane's algorithm: maximum subarray sum

At each element, either extend the best subarray ending at the previous element or start fresh here.

C++verified run
tuple<long long, int, int> kadane(const vector<int>& a) {
    long long best = a[0], cur = a[0];
    int start = 0, best_l = 0, best_r = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        if (cur < 0) { cur = a[i]; start = i; }       // a negative running sum never helps
        else cur += a[i];
        if (cur > best) { best = cur; best_l = start; best_r = i; }
    }
    return {best, best_l, best_r};
}
// in main:
auto [sum, l, r] = kadane({-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4});
cout << sum << " from " << l << " to " << r << '\n';
auto [s2, l2, r2] = kadane({-8, -3, -6});             // all negative: the largest single element
cout << s2 << " from " << l2 << " to " << r2 << '\n';
Output
6 from 3 to 6
-3 from 1 to 1

O(n) time, O(1) space. For the maximum product subarray, track both the maximum and minimum product ending here (a negative number swaps them).

Two pointers

Variant Pointers Examples
Opposite ends l = 0, r = n − 1, move inward Pair sum in sorted array, container with most water, valid palindrome, 3Sum
Same direction (fast/slow) slow writes, fast reads Remove duplicates in place, move zeroes, partition
Two arrays One pointer per array Merge sorted arrays, intersection
C++verified run
vector<vector<int>> three_sum(vector<int> a) {               // all unique triplets summing to 0
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    vector<vector<int>> res;
    int n = a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; ++i) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;               // skip duplicate first values
        int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (s < 0) ++l;
            else if (s > 0) --r;
            else {
                res.push_back({a[i], a[l], a[r]});
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) ++l;         // skip duplicates
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) --r;
                ++l; --r;
            }
        }
    }
    return res;
}
int max_water(const vector<int>& h) {
    int l = 0, r = h.size() - 1, best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));
        if (h[l] < h[r]) ++l; else --r;                         // move the shorter wall
    }
    return best;
}
int remove_duplicates(vector<int>& a) {                         // sorted input, in place
    if (a.empty()) return 0;
    int slow = 0;
    for (int fast = 1; fast < (int)a.size(); ++fast)
        if (a[fast] != a[slow]) a[++slow] = a[fast];
    return slow + 1;
}
void sort_colors(vector<int>& a) {                              // Dutch national flag: 0s, 1s, 2s
    int lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = a.size() - 1;
    while (mid <= hi) {
        if (a[mid] == 0) swap(a[lo++], a[mid++]);
        else if (a[mid] == 1) ++mid;
        else swap(a[mid], a[hi--]);                             // don't advance mid: new a[mid] is unchecked
    }
}
// in main:
for (auto& t : three_sum({-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4})) cout << '[' << t[0] << ',' << t[1] << ',' << t[2] << ']';
cout << '\n' << max_water({1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7}) << '\n';
vector<int> d{1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4};
int k = remove_duplicates(d);
for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) cout << d[i];
cout << '\n';
vector<int> c{2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0};
sort_colors(c);
for (int x : c) cout << x;
cout << '\n';
Output
[-1,-1,2][-1,0,1]
49
1234
001122

Sliding window

A window [l, r] slides over the array: extend r one step at a time, and shrink from l while the window breaks the condition. Each index enters and leaves once, so it's O(n).

C++verified run
long long max_sum_k(const vector<int>& a, int k) {              // fixed-size window
    long long cur = 0, best;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) cur += a[i];
    best = cur;
    for (int i = k; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        cur += a[i] - a[i - k];                                 // slide: add right, drop left
        best = max(best, cur);
    }
    return best;
}
int longest_unique(const string& s) {                           // variable window: no repeats
    vector<int> last(256, -1);
    int best = 0, l = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)s.size(); ++r) {
        unsigned char c = s[r];
        if (last[c] >= l) l = last[c] + 1;                      // jump past the previous copy
        last[c] = r;
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
string min_window(const string& s, const string& t) {          // smallest window containing t
    array<int, 128> need{};
    for (char c : t) need[c]++;
    int missing = t.size(), l = 0, best_l = 0, best_len = INT_MAX;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)s.size(); ++r) {
        if (need[s[r]]-- > 0) --missing;                        // s[r] was still needed
        while (missing == 0) {                                  // valid: try to shrink
            if (r - l + 1 < best_len) { best_len = r - l + 1; best_l = l; }
            if (++need[s[l++]] > 0) ++missing;                  // removed a needed char
        }
    }
    return best_len == INT_MAX ? "" : s.substr(best_l, best_len);
}
int at_most_k_distinct(const vector<int>& a, int k) {           // number of subarrays with <= k distinct
    unordered_map<int, int> cnt;
    int l = 0, res = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)a.size(); ++r) {
        if (cnt[a[r]]++ == 0) --k;
        while (k < 0)
            if (--cnt[a[l++]] == 0) ++k;
        res += r - l + 1;                                       // all windows ending at r
    }
    return res;
}
// in main:
cout << max_sum_k({2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2}, 3) << '\n';
cout << longest_unique("abcabcbb") << ' ' << longest_unique("pwwkew") << '\n';
cout << min_window("ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC") << '\n';
vector<int> a{1, 2, 1, 2, 3};
cout << at_most_k_distinct(a, 2) - at_most_k_distinct(a, 1) << '\n';   // EXACTLY 2 distinct
Output
9
3 3
BANC
7
Tip"Exactly K" = "at most K" − "at most K−1"

Windows with exactly K distinct values (or exactly K odd numbers, or sum exactly K with non-negative values) don't shrink monotonically, but "at most K" does. Count both and subtract.

Sliding window needs a condition that stays broken as the window grows (or stays satisfied as it shrinks). With negative numbers, "sum ≤ K" isn't monotonic — use prefix sums with a hash map or a monotonic deque instead.

Boyer–Moore majority vote and other array tricks

C++verified run
int majority(const vector<int>& a) {               // the element occurring > n/2 times
    int cand = 0, count = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        if (count == 0) cand = x;
        count += (x == cand) ? 1 : -1;             // pairs of different elements cancel out
    }
    return cand;                                   // verify with a second pass if not guaranteed
}
vector<int> product_except_self(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<int> out(n, 1);
    int left = 1, right = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { out[i] *= left; left *= a[i]; }
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i) { out[i] *= right; right *= a[i]; }
    return out;                                    // no division, O(1) extra space
}
void rotate_right(vector<int>& a, int k) {         // reverse trick: O(n), O(1) space
    int n = a.size();
    k %= n;
    reverse(a.begin(), a.end());
    reverse(a.begin(), a.begin() + k);
    reverse(a.begin() + k, a.end());
}
// in main:
cout << majority({2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2}) << '\n';
for (int x : product_except_self({1, 2, 3, 4})) cout << x << ' ';
cout << '\n';
vector<int> r{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7};
rotate_right(r, 3);
for (int x : r) cout << x;
cout << '\n';
int n = 5;
vector<int> missing_one{3, 0, 1, 5, 4};            // numbers 0..n with one missing
int x = 0;
for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) x ^= i;
for (int v : missing_one) x ^= v;
cout << "missing " << x << '\n';
Output
2
24 12 8 6 
5671234
missing 2

Interview questions

QHow does the hash-map solution to Two Sum work, and why insert after checking?

Scan once; for each x, look up target − x among values already seen (O(1) average); if found, return both indices, else record x → i. Inserting after the check prevents pairing an element with itself (e.g. target 6 and a single 3). O(n) time, O(n) space.

QWhat is a prefix sum and what problems does it solve?

An array where pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements; any range sum becomes a subtraction in O(1). Combined with a hash map of earlier prefix sums, it counts subarrays with a given sum, divisible by k, or with equal 0s and 1s — even with negative numbers.

QExplain Kadane's algorithm.

Keep the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index: either extend the previous one or start fresh (cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i])), and track the global maximum. It's DP with O(1) state: O(n) time, O(1) space. It handles all-negative arrays if initialized with the first element.

QWhen does the sliding-window technique apply?

When you need the longest/shortest/count of contiguous subarrays or substrings, and validity is monotonic: if a window is valid, its sub-windows are too (or if invalid, its super-windows are). Then you extend the right end and shrink the left end, each pointer moving at most n times — O(n).

QWhy doesn't sliding window work for "subarray sum = K" with negative numbers?

With negatives, growing the window can decrease the sum and shrinking can increase it, so there's no monotonic rule for when to move the left pointer. Use prefix sums with a hash map instead.

QHow do you count subarrays with exactly K distinct elements?

Count subarrays with at most K distinct (a monotonic sliding window: for each right end, add the window length) and subtract those with at most K−1. The difference is exactly K.

QWhat is the Dutch national flag algorithm?

A one-pass, in-place three-way partition with pointers lo, mid, hi: 0s are swapped to lo, 2s to hi, 1s are skipped. mid isn't advanced after swapping with hi because the incoming element hasn't been examined. O(n) time, O(1) space.

QHow does Boyer–Moore majority vote work?

Keep a candidate and a counter; matching elements increment, others decrement, and at zero the next element becomes the candidate. Since a majority element occurs more than all others combined, it survives the pairwise cancellations. O(n) time, O(1) space; verify the result if a majority isn't guaranteed.

QHow do you find the missing number from 0..n?

XOR all numbers 0..n with all array elements — pairs cancel, leaving the missing one. Or subtract the array's sum from n(n+1)/2 (watch overflow). Both O(n) time, O(1) space.

QWhen would you use a difference array?

When many range updates ("add v to every element in [l, r]") come before the values are read. Each update is O(1) (diff[l] += v; diff[r+1] -= v), and one prefix-sum pass at the end produces the final array.
